The driver of the station fly brought in her luggage, she paid him; then, closing the door behind him, she opened the windows, back and front, and passed upstairs to do the same in the two little upper rooms. The sun was slowly setting, her bedroom was full of glory, and there swept over her such a sense of reactionary delight. after the hideous, sordid life of that Portsmouth back-room that she burst into a passion of tears; and, flinging herself upon her knees, she gave thanks to God for this "little nest called home." She was not a religious girl in the best, the fullest sense of the word, but, like many another of a kindred temperament, who in moments akin to this which had come to her had leant all their souls heavily towards the Divine, so she instinc- tively praised the—to her—" Unknown God," and prayed, too, for her absent husband. Once more she began her old life, only now there was added to her income Jack's half-par.

A man-of-war's sick-bay(i.e., hospital) it - curious place to the eye of the landsman. In tir, sick-bay of H.M.S. Dappler, round a swinging cot, there were grouped three or four quiet, grave- eyed men—the ship's doctor, the sick-bay steward, his attendant, and a young sailor whose sleeve- badges denoted him to be a "leading seaman." The doctor turned, gave .a whispered word or two to the bay steward, then left the place. The steward and his mate went to the other end of the bay to get their tea, and George Forestier, the leading seaman, was left with his dying chum, Jack A.ckroyd. "I knew from the first it was all 'U P' with me, Georgie," gasped the dying man; "but I'm glad I've come round enough to talk a little." In feeble, pain-punctured, broken speech the dying man gave his chum certain instructions as to the disposal of his property. "My kit can be sold," he said; "and tell the boys from me that they are to send up the prices for my little wife's sake. Bless her ! "

"I will run down to Stoke, Mrs. Ackroyd,b George Forestier said, when he had seen Kate seated in • the train, "and will bring Jack's box with me."

Three weeks later, during which the pair had spent every available moment together (for George Forestier had taken a. lodginc, in Kate's village) a wondrous change came over'Kate ; something had touched her, glorified her. She was in love. Love, the real, mighty passion, for_the first time in her life, possessed all her being. The love was mutual and George Forestier had asked her to be his wife, and she had promised.

For three months Kate had been the wife of George Forestier Ninety days of heaven on earth had been her portion. George had left the Service, and was engaged in writing, finding a ready market for his vigorous word-pictures of sea life. The home of the pair was barely twenty miles from Charino. Cross. He had been away nearly the whole of one day, and now, on his return in the evening, he told Kate that he was going to take her into the country next day. By noon the next day Kate, full of wonder, a sense of mystery all about her, a sense which she could not explain, so intangible was it, drove up with him through a wide avenue of glorious trees to a house that was a palace almost. "What does it mean, George ? " she gasped. "Wait another minute, my darling," he replied, with a smile.

The next moment a white-haired butler in irre- proachable black was opening the door of the fly. Th nk God for this day, Master George—my lord, I should say." - It was all true, though Bate but slowly grasped the wonder of it all. George Forestier was now Lord Hallowbore, and she, the tri-coloured widow, was "my lady." It had all come about very suddenly, and was in this wise. When— "Oh, bother the rest 1" readers may interpolate. "It is enough for us that things have 4urned out so lovely." Very well, readers, I leave you with my Lord and Lady Hallowbore, with a hearty au revolt.. [THE END.]

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. A Deputation to London and Its Cost.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. A Deputation to London and Its Cost.

A meeting of the Warrington Board of Gaardians ava.s held on Wednesday morning. Mr. 3. W. Knowles 'presided in the absence of the Chairman, and there were 41.150 present t—Ars. Clay, Rev. Father Wilson, Dr. Tkurray, Messrs. A. J. Jolley, T. H. Ashcroft, S. Davies, P. Longton, T. Ritchie, J. Billinge, W. Houghton, G. Mather, A. Jolley, R. Forshaw, J. :futon, J. Billinge, '.vith J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), J. F. Awbery (workhouse master), and A. Wright (superintendent Padgate schools). LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD COMMUNICATIONS. The CLERK read ,a letter from the Local Government Board consenting Co the proposal of the Guardians to add four years in each case, for the purpose of super- annuation, to the services of Mr. and Mrs. Woodhouse, the tailor and foster mother of the Padgate sckools. The Board also wrote approving of the proposed alteration of the relief districts of M. Ankland and Mr. Bowes, whereby Mr. Aukland's district was increased by the addition of several townships pre- viously included in Mr. Bowes' district. THE RECENT POOR LAW CONPERENCE. THE COST OF THE WARRINGTON DEPUTATION. The CHAIRMAN presented azeport on the recent Poor Law Conference in London which was attended by Mr. Brooks, Mr. Sutton and himself. On the first day, he said, the Guardians paid a visit to the training ship "Exmouth," where some hundreds of lads were being trained for the navy and army or mercantile marine. Mr. Knowles gave a racy description of his visit and said all the lads were very healthy and were well cared for. He thought it would be advantageous to the Guardians if the Padgate Schools Committee would consider the advisability of sending a few lads to this ship if the opportunity arose. The lads were removed away entirely from . their former associations and it was not likely that they would return to town life in back streets if they went on the" Exmouth" and were trained for a seafaring life. Mr. ASHCROFT : We have several Padgate lads in the navy. The CHAIRMAN: This would be a grand training ship for them. Mr. Prt.tixo : Ibelieve the deputation that went to this training shiphad the finest luncheon that was ever known. (Loud laughter.) The CHAIR3IAN: Yon were not there. lam afraid you are only speaking from hearsay. (Laughter). Mr. PILLING: I have heard it on good authority. (Laughter.) The CHAIRMAN proceeded Ito refer to other topics dealt with at the Conference including a new system of out-relief and Mr. Cleaver's paper on the co-opera- tion of Boards of Guardians in relieving their institu- tions of different types of cases. , Mr. A. JOLLEY: Has this report cost us about £l3? (Laughter.) The CHAIRMAN: That is about the cost of the deputation. (Laughter.) Mr. A. JOLLEY : It is only right to let the ratepayers know. Mr. S. DAVIES thanked Mr. Knowles for his report.

Mr. fORSHAW said there seemed to be a joke from begimainc, to end. He never saw a Chairman act like that. (Laughter.) The CHAIRMAN : You can never tell what will emanate from Mr. Forshaw (Laughter). The subject then dropped. THE OVERSEERS OF WARRINGTON.

The CLERK read a communication stating that Alder- man James Fairclough, Alderman A. Bennett, Councillor John Wilkinson and Councilor J. G. Craik had been appointed overseers for Warrington. APPOINTMENTS FOR PADGATE SCHOOLS._ _

The ia-Clga-te Schools Committee recommended the appointment of Miss Ethel Foxley, of Birmingham, as foster mother of No. 3 home. It was also recommended that Miss Basketter be engaged as seamstress to assist the matron in making up girls' dresses for a period not exceeding 12 weeks at £1 per week. The minutes were approved on the proposition of Mr. ASHCROFT.
• THE HOUSE COMMITTEE. A NEW SYSTEM OF DIETING.

At a meeting of the House Committee on February 12th, the Master reported that he had re-organized the system of distributing bread to the inmates by giving to each according to appetite and not as per scale allow- ance. Each inmate was first served with a portion of the prescribed allowance and the remainder if desired. By this means 207 lbs of bread had been saved, in 5 days, the value of which was 13s. 11d. It was resolved to promote the hospital housemaid Miss Marion Murton to the post of children's caretaker at the salary of £2O per annum, increasing yearly £2 10s., until £25, was reached, together with uniform, rations and furnished apartments. The resignation of Mrs. Lowe from the Brabazon Committee vas accepted. An application from the Master's Clerk, Mr. Alfred Turpin for an advance of salary was considered, and it was unanimously resolved to increase the same from £3O to £4O, the same as paid to his predecessor. At a meeting of the committee on February 19th John Mason, 182 Padgate-lane was appointed night porter and stoker at the Workhouse at 265. per week. With respect to the recent decision of the Court of Appeal that a Workhouse was a place within the mean- ing of the Factory Acts, it was resolved to ask the Board to lay this decision before the Poor Law Unions, Association for their consid3ration as the matter opened up new possibilities and obligations with respect to injuries to officers, which was of general interest to all Boards of Guardians. At a meeting on February 26th it was resolved to sell Mr. Hickman the Workhouse hearse for 20s. It was re- solved to vote the sum of £lO 10s. to Dr. Bmide for attention to vagrants from December 18th to February 12th for daily examination re smallpox. The tender of the British Westinghouse Company, Ltd., for the sum of £49 10s. for the erection of two motors in the wash- house was agreed to. At a further meeting on March 4th, the Master drew the committee's attention to the unsatisfactory diet as supplied to the old and infirm, and suggested that some improvement might be made therein. It was resolved to ask Messrs. Pilling, A. J. Jolley, Ashcroft and For— shaw to form a committee to investigate the whole matter and to furnish a report. The committee con- demned the present weighing machine and it was also resolved to recommend the Board to purchase another and larger one. Mr. PILLING moved the confirmation of the minutes. Mr. FORSHAW seconded. %1

div.head: CRITICAL PERIOD. Bile Beans as a Woman's Medicine.
div.p: A CRITICAL PERIOD. Bile Beans as a Woman's Medicine.

Mrs. Hannah Gill, of Park Gate Farm, Ernley, near Wakefield, says :—" For between six and seven years I suffered most acutely from ailments connected with that critical period in a woman's life which I had reached. At times I was so ill that I could neither eat nor drink, work nor sleep. My flesh and bones seemed to ache all over, my memory left me, and I used to n wander about ice one lost. ._ _ _ _ _

_ - "I was also very greatly troubled with constipation, and ray food s3emed to do me no good. I used to fancy I could eat all sorts of things, but when I got them could never enjoy them. I was much subject to terrible sweats, although all the time I was shivering. Instead of enjoying life as I had been accustomed to do, I wished many a morning, after a long night of sleepless tossing about, that I might rtrst in death before the day closed. Of course, I was seen by the doctor, but his medicine did me very little good. "One;day my sister advised me to try Charles Forde's bile beans. I began to take them, and you can imagine my joy to find about three weeks after commencing with them that my memory had retulined. "I began mending straight off, and became able to sleep. Altogether I pulled up very quickly. I con- tinued taking bile beans until I was quite well again. "I have had twelve children and , twenty grand- children, and a heathier family never breathed. I lam now fifty-five years of age, but I feel as bright and buoyant as when twenty." Chas. Forde's bile beans are the acknowledged remedy for female ailments, constipation, biliousness, indiges- tion, liver complaints, ana3mia, debility, headache, loss of appetite, skin eruptions, and the numerous ailments arising from disorders of the stomach and liver. They are purely vegetable, and their great success as a " wonian's medicine" has led to several harmful imita- tions and substitutes being put upon the market. Against these you are warned. See the name "Chas. Forde " on every box. Stocked by all chemists at is. lid. and 2s. 9d. per box containing three times Is. 10. size. div.head: Concert at Hollinfare.
div.p: Concert at Hollinfare.

Miss Lucy Davies, of Hollinfare, gave her first concert on Saturday in the Temperance Hall, HoHin- fare, submitting a programme deserving of afar larger audience than the hall could accommodate. Miss Davies, who is possessed of a.soprano voice, of excep- tonal range and expression, is already known to local I audiences, having created a very good impression in ; the district on several occasions. On this occasion she received enthusiastic encores for her contributions, "Songs of Florian " aid Edwin Green's "Sine me to sleep," her beautiful r&dition of the latter,with violin obligato played by Mr. Whitfield, being especially heartily received. She was also heard to great advantage in the duets ." The Spider and the Fly," with Mr. George Whitfield, and "Over the heather," with Mrs. Hudswell. Mrs. Hudswell (contralto) sang "The Enchantress" and "There's a land" in a very pleasing manner, securing a mell-merited encore for the latter. Mr. G. Whitfield, who has a powerful baritone voice, gave "Song of the Desert" and "The Veteran's Song " and, in response to an encore " Friar of Orders Gray." Mr. Harry Whitfield delighted the audience with his brilliant playing of the violin solos " Gipsy Dance," " Sarabande " and "Tambourin " ad " Witches' Dance," all of which were encored, the last receiving a double encore. Mr. Fred Walmsley was a very successful humourist, being recalled for, all his selections, the happiest of which was a very humorous Scotch song about a certain " McKay," some very funny " patter " being introduced. Mr. John Tinkler, who was an excellent accompanist, also con tributed a fine pianoforte solo "Polish Dance." Owing to the number of recalls, the last item on the programme, a trio by Miss Davies, Mrs. Hudswell and Mr. G. Whitfield had to be omitted. Miss Davies is certainly to be congratulated on the success of her first concert, a success which was very clearly indi- cated by the continuous applause of the appreciative audience which filled the hall.

The Stockholm court has pronounced the Arctic explorer Andree to be dead in law, the legal term of disappearance having expired. Andree left Spitzberaen on .luly 11th, 1897, with two companions in a balloon with the object of reaching the North Pole.

Rabe Ackroyd 'drew her tall, lithe; graceful form 'up to its full height in an unconscious act of .straightening as she gave mental utterance to he.' last resolve, and behind her veil her handsome `brunette face filled with an expression that could ;only be described as heroic. Her way to 'the .railway station, whither she was bound, led her through one of the busiest thorough- fares of Portiea, the main street from the dockyard 'to the station. At every few yards the mingled odours of many liquors, coarse sawdust, and vile tobaccos, and the babel of thick, coarse-voiced talk and raucous laughter floated out from the "pubs" to the ears and nostrils of the passers-by. In the doorways of dark little dens of Jew-shops, where everything bought and sold was nautical, the Hebrew trader lurked like some spider in its hole ready to dart out upon the passing fly. Crowds of bold-eyed, shameless girls, with flushed, drink- smitten, painted faces passed to and fro, their loud voices and hideous- laughter filling the air, their laughter used to hide their misery, as the paint on their faces was used to mask the effects of -their life upon their once fair skins. Once something of all this struck upon the finer sense of Kate Ackroyd, and she shuddered ; s she let her sweeping, comprehensive glance take in the main features of her surroundings, and murmured: "It is easy enough to find fault with our sailors for looseness of life, but they need to be of sterling stuff to escape all the bird-lime spread hereabouts for their feet." Then the girl-wife's thoughts went back to their former theme, and once more repeating her lament "Yes yes; it has all been a horrible blunder," she quickened her steps, having none too much time in which to catch her train. Kate Ackroyd was the daughter of a well-to-de tradesman in a small cotintry-town. Her life, ever since the death of her mother, which had happened when she had been barely twelve years old, had been a very lonely one, for neither her father nor brother (who were fashioned in very much coarser moulds) ever understood her, and had seemed to take a delight in snubbing and thwarting her in a wantonly cruel way. Her natural tastes—inherited doubtless from her mother, who had been a refined and educated woman—had led her into a pathway of a culture unusual for a girl of her years, and in such a sordid little town as Hangerford. It was this natural and cultivated superiority of mind, and consequent superiority of manners, that her father and brother had hated; not that Kate acted the superior person by any means, but their coarse souls felt the contrast between her and themselves, and with the petty meanness of their kindred dis- positions they each resented it. With all her culture of heart and mind Kate had yet ever been of a most practical turn, and even at twelve began to prove herself a wise little house- keeper. As the years passed on she developed into a handsome girl ; but though "worshipped dimly at a distance" by more than one young fellow of Hangerford, not one of them had ever presumed to pay her court, for she appeared to these more or less empty-headed youths as someone of a different yace to themselves. The giggling, dressy, flirting girls of the town they could understand better than Kate; so while they admired the tall, handsome, cultured brunette they paid court only to the lesser stars in the Hangerford firmament. When Kate was seventeen her father suddenly married again. The second Mrs. Merchant was a coarse, vulgar girl of twenty, with a passion for over-dressing and display of all kinds. This stepmother took an immediate, unfounded, invincible dislike to Kate, and within twenty-four hours of her return from the honeymoon with her middle-aged husband, she purposely quarrelled with the girl, and declared that either Kate must find a new home or else that she herself would leave the house and return to her parents' home. It was Kate who left, of course. But the details of this little affair are of small concern to the reader. It may be remarked, however, that both the father and brother rather welcomed the result of the new Mrs. Merchant's quarrel with the girl. Kate had a little money of her own, which had been made over to her by a deed of gift by her mother's sister a Year before the rupture in her home, and OR this slender income of ten shillings a week, supplemented by what she could earn with her pen as an occasional contributor to magazines, and by her needle at millinery (she was very clever in this art) she managed to exist comfortably in a village about thirty miles from her old home. She had been living this quiet, independent life about six months when an incident happened which changed the whole course of her life and thought, and made it possible to pen this story of her. Taking one of her favourite walks one afternoon she had to cross some water-meadows, when with a bellow of defiance and rage a bull, which she had not noticed, suddenly rushed out from a cluster of willows and raced towards her. it was an awful moment. She ran with every nerve strained. The beast gained on her. Its head was lowered for the final attack when suddenly a huge flint came hurtling through the air and struck the bull heavily on the side of the •head, seeming for a moment to stagger it. With a fierce bellow of paip and rage the beast turned on its assailant and--" Well, things moved swiftly during the next three minutes, by which time she had been helped over a stile into a safe place by the man who had probably delivered her from death. Her saviour was a good-looking young man-of- war'sman, about four-and-twenty, with a pleasant voice, and, for a sailor, a singular correctness of

speech. This is how she and Jack Ackroyd first met. As the days went on they saw more and more of each other, and into Kate's lonely life there entered a new, a warmer interest. There had always been a strong strain of quiet romanticism in her character, and this helped to blind her for the time to some failings of her sailor-lover—for this was the character he soon assumed.

And Kate, mistaking a warmth of gratitude towards him for his brave rescue of her for love, and further deceived by the pleasure of his more or less constant society with her, believed she was serving her own and his best interests when she agreed to a swift marriage. This event took place the day before Jack Ackroyd's six weeks' leave of absence had expired. They were married at a registry-office, then started ,for Portsmouth, where Jack had to report 'himself next day, and where he had secured a room for the bridal home.

Forty-eight hours of life in this one apartment, in a noisy back street of Portsmouth, completely disillusioned Kate, and, lying alone on her bed that first night of her husband's absence on the receiving ship, she stared with aching mental eyes into the darkness of a future that was denser than the darkness of the room, and learnt in that hour how hopelessly she had ruined her life. Only one ray of light, of hope, came to her, and that was connected with her husband's probable early call to sea, when she could at least get back to the quiet, sweet purity of the village where her tiny little thatched cottage was still furnished as she had left it, she holding a tenancy of the house for nearly another year. Jack's call to a newly-commissioned ship came earlier than either expected, though even the bare two months' purgatory in that Portsmouth lodging was a penance which Kate felt sometimes to be beyond all her powers of endurance. Jack had sailed •on the day of the opening of this story. Less than an hour before Kate had been strained convulsively, passionately, to the serge- covered breast of her departing husband. She had seen the anguish in his eyes, had heard the break in his voice as he prayed God bless her; she had seen his barely successful efforts to strangle the thick sobs that choked him; and when their lips* met in a laq farewell kiss two great scalding tears had fallen from his eyes upon her cheek. Her own heart had been very miserable at the parting, yet, as the train conveyed her more and more rapidly every moment from the great naval town, she was conscious of a lightening of heart, of a sense of calm. a more cheerful outlook.

, He paused for a moment, then, looking his chum full in the eyes, he went on: "I've come to think of late that Bate was somehow disappointed in her marriage, though she never let on, by look or word, that she was so. But I can see now, I hurried her on to marry me, and she was so different to sich a lady everyhow, that I can see now. She sort of woke up to—well, many things. But she'll be free now, and I hope she'll marry again, and marry well, for she's fit fur an Empress, Bless her ' " All this had been brokenly uttered, and now there came a lengthier pause. When he spoke again, he said: "Don't sell my ditty-box, let that go to her, George. Take it to her yourself, will you, and tell her my last thought was of her." . He paused again, was silent a moment, then the eyelids drooped, and he dozed. He never woke again, but he had died a hero's death. A boy had fallen overboard when the ship was steaming ten knots. Jack had leaped over to save the boy, had caught him, and had held him up until the lowered boat had reached them. Then, just as he passed the boy into the boat, a shark had seized one of his legs. There had been a struggle between the boat's crew and the hideous "ocean scavenger," some of the men holding on to their shipmate by his arms while others attacked the ravening shark with boathook and oars. Jack had been rescued, but with the loss of a limb, the leg being literally torn from his thigh by the shark. George Forestier missed his chum very sorely, for, in spite of their manifold differences of character, they had been very close friends. Who this George Forestier really was, or how such an one came to be a common "flat-foot" on the lower deck of a man-of-war was a puzzle alike to officer and man. "Gentleman Georgie " his shipmates had christened him, and a gentleman by birth and education he certainly was. He was about twenty- six, tall, well set-up, without a trace of the "slackness," the looseness of limb and gait of the ordinary sailor, but with more the cut of the trained athlete, or the Guardsman. Everyone liked him, for, in spite of his nickname of "Gentleman," he was a strong, cheerful, ready, all-round worker, and a friend to all his mates. _ _ _

Sorrowfully, he carried out all his dead chum's wishes, and, taking charge of the ditty-box, he wrote to the young widow, whose photo and history had long ago interested him—for Jack had told him all the story of his marriage, and had mare than once shewn him the cabinet photo of Kate.

• Kate laid the letter down upon the table, and, gazing away into space out of eyes that were filled with tears, felt a deeper grief for the death of the man whose name she bore than she had ever sup- posed she could have done. "And what a death!" she sobbed. "So pitiful in its horrors, so heroic in its cause. My poor dead Jack, you were a true hero ! " • In that first hour of her bereavement Kate came nearer to loving Jack Ackroyd than ever before. • When, as was inevitable, the subject of mourn- ing dress forced itself upon her mind, she came to a strange decision. "I'll dress as I believe he would have me dress for him," she mused; "and as to the conventional notion of mourning garb, with which I have no sympathy, I'll just ignore it, let people think or talk as they may." And people did talk about her; even the curate of the parish, who was a genial, kindly-hearted fellow, fond of saying smart little things, had a word to say about his fair parishioner, and smilingly alluded to her as "The Tr-coloured Widow," for Kate's mourning garb, chosen to do silent honour to the dead hero, consisted of a costume of dark navy blue, braided with a deep, dark red; the strings of her dainty little navy blue bonnet were white; and at her throat she wore the Union Jack brooch which had been Jack's last gift to her. Two years sped swiftly by, and that first tri-coloured costume had been replaced by a second almost identical with the first, only really daintier, and Kate, happier in freedom and in her simpler life than ever before, had developed a new and rarer beauty. _ _ -

- More than one man had sought her hand, and though no one knew it but themselves, the curate, who had dubbed her as the "Tr-coloured Widow," had paid much quiet court to her, winding up by imploring her to marry him—but Sate had refused him.

Now, after two years'- widowhood, she receives a second letter from George Forestier, this time announcing that by a certain date—four days from the time of her receiving the letter—the Dappler might be expected at Portsmouth. "We are coming to payoff," the letter said, "and in oomph. ance with dear old Jack's express wish, I shall take the earliest opportunity of seeing you person- ally, that I may hand over Jack's ditty-box. I suppose it will be too much to expect to see you at Portsmouth." The writer signed himself "George Forestier."

Intensely interested and excited, Bate made up her mind to go to Portsmouth. Then, as she re-read the letter, her thoughts took a channel very similar to one in which they had rim after her receipt of that first letter from her dead husband's chum, and she murmured: "George Forestier may only be a seaman as regards rank, but he is a gentleman, I believe."

George Forestier watched the crowd of privileged visitors who were pouring in over the gangway of the newly-berthed ship. He had no idea, no thought, of seeing anyone whom he knew, but watched in the generally careless fashion a a man to whom his fellow-men are always an interesting study. Suddenly the graceful figure of a tall girl, evidently alone, arrested his attention. There seemed something familiar about her figure, and her costume was an arrestive one.

As she crossed the wooden brow she put up a small, daintily-gloved hand and lifted her veil, revealing a face of singular power and beauty. "By Jove It's Jack's wife ! " gasped the young sailor; and byathe timeolCate had stepped over the gangway he was there to greet her. Lifting his hat, with a smi eof greeting, he said: "Mrs. Ackroyd ? Surely I cannot be mis- taken? lam George Forestier." • She gave him one swift look, and in that one look knew that what she had felt was true, ane that this chum of her dead husband's was al gentleman by birth. She gave him her hand, and he drew her away, from the bustle of the gangway. Re did not take her on the lower deck, for the babel there, he knew, would be awful, but choosing a quiet nook on the off-shore side of the ship, he made her comfortable while they talked long and earnestly. "I can get ashore for an hour or two, Mrs. Ackroyd," he said by-and-bye, "if you would care for me to accompany you. I .should be pleased to see you to the station: Besides, lam longing for ;a cup of shore tea, and you would join me in this, am sure." So it came to pass that presently the pair were seated in a clean little quiet refreshment parlour taking tea together like old friends.

div.head: PLAGUE OF PLAGUES.
div.p: THE PLAGUE OF PLAGUES.

There are few events about which greater misconcep- tion exists than the "great plague of London"—that terrible visitation which caused 100,000 deaths in the year 1665, almost depopulating England's capital. Corn-, Ipiratively few people know what manner of sickness that plague was, for happily it has not for many years revisited the world. Yet London is not without its plague to-day, though it be less deadly than that of 1665. A great many Londoners regard the levying of taxes as a plague; others so describe influenza; while some (and these with strongest reason) apply the term to indigestion. Some people suffer from it the greater part of their lives; others wisely tight and conquer the malady. But indigestion is not only the plague of London; it deserves the greater distinction of the plague of the world, for wherever there are people there is indigestion. Mr. 3. Harris, who lives at the Market Hotel, Birstall, near Leeds, is one of many thousands who know this truth from experience. Further, Mr. Harris also knows from experience that the one great, sure remedy for this complaint is Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. Writing on the 2nd of January, 1904, Mr. Harris says: "I used to be a martyr to in- digestion and biliousness. I consultd many doctors, but none of them did me any real good. My condition was truly wretched—too ill to work, not ill enough to leave my business. What- ever I ate lay like lead in my stomach for hours afterwards, causing great pain. There was pain also in my back, between the shoulders; and I was hardly ever free from headaches, which were terribly severe. With hardly any appetite, and afraid to gratify even the little that I had, I became extremely weak. Sleep did not refresh me; I felt as weary in the morning as at night. It was while in this state that I chanced to hear of Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, and decided to try it. The result astonished me. My weakness and depression vanished; my appetite returned; and I found I could eat without any pain resulting from it. The headaches and other troublesome symptoms soon left me, and I gathered strength fast. Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup made a new man of me.

The experience of Mr. Harris differs in no respect from that of thousands of other men and women in every part of the world, victims of the plague of indi- gestion. Unfortunately, some of the habits and cus- toms of modern life favour indigestion. Fortunately, modern science has provided us with its antidote. You hardly need be told its name Mr. Harris ha 3 told it in earnest words.

div.head: ACCIDENT AT MESSRS. MONKS HALL AND COMPANY'S WORKS.
div.p: THE ACCIDENT AT MESSRS. MONKS HALL AND COMPANY'S WORKS.

Mr. Brighouse conducted an inquiry on Tuesday morning relative to the death of Thomas Childs, a large labourer, who was kilted at the Works of Messrs Monksliall & Company on Friday evening last.Mr.E.A Connor (for Mr. Steel) appeared for the relatives ; Mr. Draper for Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co ; and Mr. Willett for the Ocean Accident Assurance Company Mr. Augustus Lewis, Factory Inspector, was also present,— In opening the inquiry the coroner pointed out that from a report furnished by the company to the Factory Inspector, it appeared that the deceased was assisting three other labourers to bar round the number 3 forge ermine. The engine driver told the men to draw the 'bar out when the engine started. They pulled the bar out but it did not fall clear of the arms of the fly-wheel. When the arms caught the bar, the bar rose with great force and struck the deceased on the head, death being almost instantaneous.—Frederick Childs, sbingler' said the " deceased, who was his brother, was a forge labourer. He had been with Messrs. Monks, Hall and Company , for about 12 months.—By the Inspector : Deceased was a temperate man.—By Mr. Conner: The deceased , was a strong man, had good sight, and his hearing was all right.—ln answer to Mr. Draper, witness said he could not . say whether the deceased had been en- gaged at this particular class of work before.—Arthur Massey,the driver in charge of the No. 3 forge engine, I said the men as soon as they saw the engine start took the bar out, and it dropped on the ground, and the fly wheel struck the each of the bar, causing it to fly up. It hit the deceased a fearful blow. By Mr. Connor : He had previously had to call in help to start the !, engine. He could not say that the deceased had been I called in on witness's turn to start the engine. He i could not say whether the deceased had been used to this kind of work. The bar would weigh from 701 b. to 801 b., and would be Oft. in length.—ln answer to Mr. Draper, witness said there was : ample time to take the bar out. The act of taking the bar out was in itself a very simple operation —A juryman said he had assisted to bar round the engine many a time. He had never known the fly ; wheel tilt up the bar before. The bar was laid on the floor too near the fly wheel.—The Inspector said the usual method had been adopted here, and he did not see that blame attached to anyone. This was a kind of accident that would happen sometimes. In some works,automatic modern barring engines were in use. Messrs Monks, Hall and Company had such engines !in the new mill. He could only suggest that they might be introduced into other parts of the works.— The jury returned a verdict of 6` Accidental death," and added that no blame was to be attached to anyone.

AMBULANCE COMPETITION AT EARLESTOWN. I On Wednesday afternoon a competition uneer the rules of the St. John Ambulance Association in con- nection with the Wigan and District Ambulance Centre of the London and North-Western Railway Company took place in the Viaduct Institute, Earlestown. Dr. Handyside the Company's surgeon at Earlostown offici- ated as examiner. Only three teams competed, and in the result the Preston Loco. team was declared the winner, and this team will take part in the final com- petition at Belle Vue, Manchester, the trophy being a cnallenge shield. The best all round man was S. Barrow of the Preston team and he was awarded a silver cream jug. Mr. H. D. Earl presented Barrow with his prize and addressed a few encouraging remarks to the com- petitors.

A resident of Harlesden' on his way to Willesden Junction on Tuesday morning left in the train, Ameri- can bonds of the face value of 100,000dols. He notified the police of his loss, and the bonds. were soon after- wards found at Pinner Police Station, where they had been left by a passenger who found them in the train after the owner had alighted.

Miss Bessie Dutton, of Moore, wrote stating that the Ladies' Visiting Committee had long felt that it was highly desirable that the inmates of the Union should have more frequent change and recre- ation in the shape of occasional rational entertainment which would probably assist to maintain good health, &c. The Guardians kindly signified their approval of their desire to organize occasional pleasant musteal evenings. They had, how- e_ver, found the absence of a piano a very great obstacle to the carrying out of the proposal, and a concert had been given only once a year when an instrument had to be brought from Runcorn or Warrington at consider- able expense. They had taken steps to remedy this serious drawback, and felt sure the Guardians would further their efforts. Mrs. Congreve Promoted an entertainment at Moore which realized £5 and Mrs. Whitley had kindly collected something for the fund. The comm;ttee earnestly begged the Board to recognize these exertions by making a grant to the piano fund, for the committee felt sure the members had all a true desire to ameliorate the monotony of Workhouse life to the inmates. A piano also would be of signal ser- vice in the instruction of the young and for the clan- duct of prayers and worship in the House. The Chairman: That is something new. The Deputy-Clerk : If the Board decide to make a eubscriptiou out of the rates, the sanction of the Local Government Board will have to be obtained.
Mr. Linaker : I believe it is not unlikely that they will be able to purchase a piano with the money they have in hand.

Mr. Norman thought the best thing would be to find out hvw much money the committee required and then application for a definite amount could be made to the Board. Mr. Linaker suggested that the balance required should be raised by subscriptions from the members of the Board, and not out of the rates. He moved that the matter be deferred until they knew exactly what the committee needed. Mr. Woodward seConded.
Mr. Roylance said he did not think the committee had much in hand.

Mr. Linaker did not think the Board would be justi- fied in asking the permission of the Local Government Board to contribute to a piano for the amusement of the inmates. If they could find the monvy from private purses he would not quarrel with the proposal. Mr.Roylance :I shall have great pleasure in ,giVinglOs. to the fund and I hope there will be other subscriptions offered to-day. These ladies give their services and it is for the welfare of the inmates. If we can raise the money by subscription, I think it will do us all good to help the cause. Mr. Norman: We are willing to do that when we know what we have to raise. _
Mr. Linaker's motion that the nutter be deferred, pending more definite information, was carried.
THE BOA RD OBJECT TO THE EMIGRATION OF BUS.

A letter was read from the condiiCi-o-r-s. of Bukley - Hall orphanage asking the Board's approval of the emigration of two Runcorn boys to Canada. The Board were asked to contribute the expenses, amounting to £l2. The boys, it was stated would be sent out through the Catholic Emigrating Society, which was recognized by tie Local Government Board.

Mr. Norm'in thought that in the matter of homes for the children, the Board ought to act on uniform lines. He did not know whether it was the habit of other orphanages to come upon the Guardians, or those who stood in the position of parents to the children, for the cost of the first move in life. He understood that when the Bo trd sent children to the institutions, the . con- ductors of the homes took the responsibility of giving them a start in life.
--1-6.-11-a-x-t-e-r-took exception to the giving of grants and the sending of boys to Canada. Mr. Edwards : r have no sympithy with the letter. and move that it lie upon the table.

Mr. Norman : I shall not support that. I feel that if a lad wants to go to Canada it is our duty, as far as we can, to give him a start, in life. The only point I raise is whether it is our duty or the duty of the insti- tution to make provision for sending the children out. Mr. Antrobus seconded the motion, which was agreed to, but the deputy-Clerk was instructed to acknowledge the receipt of the letter. ALTERATIONS AT VIE WORKHOUSE. An agreement was produced and sealed between the Board of Guardians and John Littler,Frodsha,m, for the alteration and addition to the new bath-room, lavator- ies, &c., at a total cost of £209.
THE BOARDING OUT OF CHILDREN. SECTARIANISM .INTRODUCED.

Mr. Wright moved that the Board's subscription to the Pantasaph (Roman Catholic) orphanage be in- creasedifrom 4s. to ss. per week for eachchild sent to the institution. He said most of the Guardians had visited,the orphanage and knew perfectly well what advantage it was for children to go there. It was almost impossible to keep growing children on 4s. per week and, in fact, the Board had granted a subscription of Gs. per week to the Brothers of Charity (Rochdale) who manageka similar institution.

_ Mr„. Wood said that when he proposed that chil- dren be sent to the orphanage at a cost of ss. per week, Mr. Wright objected on the ground of expense. He said it was very much cheaper to keep the children at the Workhouse, where they were very comfortable. He (the speaker) thought the Board ought to serve all the children alike. (Hear, hoar.) Mr. Wright : I do.i't think I did object to the price. Mr. Moseley-Williams seconded the motioq He said that when it was decided to send the childreli to the orphanage, the allowance would probably have been greater, but for his objection. He then looked upon it almost as a sectarian matter—that they were making a distinction between Catholics and Protestants--and he proposed that the same amount be voted to the institu- tion as was spent on the children in the Workhouse. After visiting the orf3hanage he was prepared to support a grant of ss. _ _

Baxter said it was his intention in future that if children be sent to Buckley Hall or Pantasaph, the cost should not be larger than the sum that was being spent on the children in the Workhouse. It was very unfair that they should treat Catholic children better than the children in the House. They were very well cared for at Dutton at a cost of about 3s. 6d. per week. He moved that the subscription be not increased. Mr. Edwards seconded. He considered that Mr. Williams's seconding of the proposition came with rather bad grace, inasmuch as he resided in another union.

--ki.Woodward deprecated the introduction of person- alities (A voice : Election time). He did not agree , with Mr. Wright's proposal. on the grounds that they were not dealing with the whole of the children under their control. Until they applied one common rule to all the children he would oppose any advance in the interests of one ' party. It seemed to him that I if the TPantasaph orphanage complied with the

Mr. Roylance strongly supported Mr. Wood's pro- position. He pointed out that the Northern Nursing Association had withdrawn their nurses from the House. They coMplained that the accommodation was insuffici- ent, that there was no-one to cook their food, and that some of tke food especially the eggs, was not satis- factory. The Chairman said a number of applications had been received for the vacant posts on the nursing staff. Roylance thought the present system should be done away with, and that a house should be built for the accohtmodation of the nurses. Mr. Wood agreed to defer the resolution. THE WORKHOUSE WATER SUPPLY. The Deputy Clerk stated that at the last meeting of the District Council, the question of the extention of the'water supply to the new hospital at Dutton was under consideration. It was thought that the Guardians might be approached, with advantage to themselves, to extend the main to the Workhouse, so that water would be available in case of fire and also for domestic purposes. The estimated cost of the work was £Bl. The Beard agreed to the extension. THE ASSE.SSMENT COMMITTEE. Mr. Woodward reported that the Assessment Com- mittee recommended that the salary of the clerk should be at the usual rate of £lOO, but that an additional sum of £lO be allowed him for considerable extra work dur- inLthe past ye 11...
he recominendation Was approved. A NEV NURSE. ' •
On the recommendation of the Visiting Committee, the Board agreed to the appointment of Nurse Margaret Duncan, of Liverpool, as a temporary nurse at a salary of 31s. per week and expenses.

Total! expenses for the half year, £11,659; probable balance at Lady Day, 1904, £1,714; amount required from the over- seers, £9,945 ; assessable value of the Unions £215,478 A rate of 11d. in-the £on the assessable value produces £9,878, and a call of £9,915 was recommended, being an. increase of id. in the £ upon the rate for the last half-year.

div.head: YOUNG MAWS TROUBLE.
div.p: A YOUNG MAWS TROUBLE.

Pain and illness may come to anyone, but it is not often that a vigorous young man is stricken. Few men of his age have suffered as much physical pain as Mr. H. Herbert, Selsley West, near Stroud, Gloucester. Mr. Herbert says:

"I was a great sufferer from Kidney Trouble and under the doctor's treatment for six months without getting the slightest benefit. There was always a sharp, cutting pain across mY. loins, and when I moved, my limbs seemed so heavy that I could hardly lift them. I could not sleep at night, and in the morning my face - was bloated, there was a bitter taste in my mouth; I was nervous, always tired, and I had a pain as if someone was pressing on the top of my head.. I commenced taking Dodd's Kidney Pills and they soon made a marked change in my condition. My pains. gradually disappeared. I slept better, and after I had completed a treatment or Dodd's Kidney Pills, I can now say lam completely cured. I have no pains what. ever and am well and strong."

Among other latest publications, the "Leap Year " series, the "Fiscal" series, the "Bartolozzi " series,the "Raphotype "series,'the latest "Phil May" series and the "Write-away" series are remarkably popular. Altogether, as pioneers of the picture postcard trade in the British Empire, Messrs. div.head: TRANSFERENCE OP THE " ASHES:"
div.p: THE TRANSFERENCE OP THE " ASHES:"

Warner's team went out as the "M.C.C. XI." amidst general criticism, some of which was none too fair or generous, but it Will re- turn as the "England X 1.," if it cares to, after its glorious success. At last a team has managed to win the test match rubber in Australia once more, and thus bring back the "ashes," in the parlance of cricketers. This phrase, which has been so much quoted of late, originated in 1882, when the Australian XI. beat England in the single test match at the Oval, causing tremendous surprise in the Mother Country; and one of the papers pub- lished an epitaph on English cricket, saying that the body would be cremated and taken out to Australia. Now, owing to the prowess of " Plum " Warner and his team, the " ashes " are deposited on this side, and it is for the Australians to recapture them. This fact will lend a fillip to their next visit, and give, an additional interest to .the " test " series. The result, on the other hand, has deprived the fifth and last of the present rubber, now proceeding, of its chief interest, though it is being very keenly followed. The

HAYWA. -ES. results hitherto have been decisively in favour of the M.C.C., and it is generally acknowledged by the Australian press that the team won on its merits, and is a fine all-round combination, keen, and well captained. Undoubtedly the wet wicket was in our favour, as our men are more accustomed to it than the Australians, and they pronounced Rhodes unplayable at times. Bosanquet, too, got marvellous work on. the ball. Of the batsmen, Hayward, as usual, has proved himself invaluable, whilst each has done his share at one time or another to contribute to the combined success, and " Tip " Foster's record innings will never be forgotten. After the match Noble declared that Warner's team was the finest ever sent out to the Antipodes, -and in view of their success it would be ungenerous to argue otherwise.

div.head: NEW ARMY COUNCIL.
div.p: THE NEW ARMY COUNCIL.

There is no question that the Army is at present in a state of evolution; but how far or how fast it is progressing seems to be a debateable point, to judge • from the Premier's recent statement in the House of Lords. How- ever, it seems that, whether the recommenda- tions of the Triumvirate are being adopted in their entirety or not, they are certainly being administered in their details. This reads like a paradox, or it may simply be part and parcel of War Office muddling,which people were be- ginning to hope might under the new regime cease to exist. Anyhow, the facts remain that Lord Rob
erts has ceased SIR BRUCE HAMILTON, K.C.B. to be Comman-

. der-in-Chief, the office itself having ceased to exist, and the Duke of Connaught has been appointed to the new post of Inspector-General of the Army, which he will take up on May Ist, after the King's visit to Ireland. This appointment is in many respects a very popular one, ' as the Duke is very popular throughout all ranks in the Army, and is, moreover, a thoroughly good and practical soldier, who is keen upon his profession and works hard. In addition, Sir Henry Hildyard has been gazetted to succerl General Sir Neville Lyttelton in South Afeca ; and Major - Generals Douglas, Plumer, and Wolfe-Murray have been chosen as the other military members of the new Army Council. The appointment of the first of these three has created a vacancy in the command of the second division of the Aldershot Army Corps, which is to be the only one to survive the drastic changes, and .will therefore act as the first striking arm of the Army. This command has been conferred on Major - General Sir Bruce - Hamilton, K.C.8., who distinguished himself so greatly at the front in the pursuit of De Wet. He has already joined at Alder- shot, and will at once take up his duties. Sir John French will, of course, retain com- mand of. the whole Army Corps, as he has been doing since its inception; but Lord Grenfell will leave the half-organised Fourth Army Corps, which is to become once more a district, and succeed the Duke of Connaught in Ireland.

div.head: I'HE LYCEUM'S NEW ROLE
div.p: I'HE LYCEUM'S NEW ROLE

Last week saw the last link of the Irving days cut at the Lyceum, when all its contents were sold by auction, fetching, curiously enough, very little as relics. Even the various articles in Sir Henry Irving's and Miss Ellen Terry's dressing-rooms were knocked down for a mere song, instead of falling to curio-hunters at in- flated prices, as many had anticipated. Now the work of dismantling the historic house begins; and soon the Lyceum with all its many theatrical memories will be razed to the ground to make way for an entirely new form of entertainment. In the past; its tradition has been Shakespeare and serious drama under the
THE LYCEUM THEATRE., LONDON.

mgis of Irving : but for the future it is to be devoted to variety entertainment under the tutelage ot Mr. Thomas Barrasford. It •is doubtless a very radical alteration, but in such hands it should prove a great success in every way. Financially nothing pays better nowa- days than a music-hall with its isolated turns and freedom for the audience: and, although London is admirably supplied in this respect, there is surely room for another hall right at the top, as the new Lyceum is sure to be.

div.head: LATEST ADDITION TO OUR NAVY.
div.p: LATEST ADDITION TO OUR NAVY.

H.M. torpedo-boat destroyer Erne, just completed, is now in charge of a navigating party from Devonport, where the Erne will in all probability shortly join the destroyer flotilla. This class of vessel, from which naval authorities anticipate splendid results in time of war for attacking purposes, has already played an important part in the Russo-Japanese encounter. The Erne pre- sents the newest features in the science of warship building, and the trials which have been ;ecentty carried out by the Adm ralty

kave been eminently Successful. In the ditifi of this ship there is no attempt to break speed records. The Erne will have a speed of 23+ knots, and her displacement has been increased from 360 to coo tons. An extra deck has been fitted for the lecigth of . the forecastle, thus affording better accommtda- tion for the crew, and increasing the height of the forward gun platform, which arrange- ment gives the captain of the gun a greater range of vision. There are. four water-tube

KM. TORPEDO BOAT DESTROYER ERNE. boilers placed in three stokeholds, the middlt stokehold containing two boilers, face to face. The armament consists of one i2-pouuder and five 6-pounder quickfiring Hotchkiss guns. There are two torpedo tubes, one forward and one aft, on .the upper deck, on the centre line of the vessel, which can revolve, and thus fire a torpedo to port or starboard without turning the ship round. These are provided with 18 in. torpedoes of the latest type, fitted with gyroscopes, which ' enable them to run true for 3,000 yards.

div.head: BIBLE CENTENARY.
div.p: THE BIBLE CENTENARY.

Probably no one was more surprised than the Bible Society itself at the international interest aroused by its centenary last Sun- day. For one hundred years the society has been working silently and unobtrusively with the one object of giving the Scriptures to every human being in his mother tongue and at prices which the poorest can afford to pay. Considering the nature of the work carried on by the society it was but natural that it should seek to commemorate its century by special services of thanksgiving in various places of worship, but in organising these it was no part of its programme to achieve a celebration absolutely unique in the world's history. And in nothing is the universality of the Bible Society more evidenced thait in the impressive way it has thus been able to unify Christian people who may be most widely sundered on other points. The strik- ing feature of this demonstration is its world- wide character and the way in which it is
THE BIBLE SOCIETY'S HEADQUARTERS IN SpOZEM

VICTORIA STREET. appealing to people of all races and tongues no less than to those of all grades of society. The Bible Society was founded on March 7, 1804, in consequence of the great famine of Bibles in Wales. Its first issue was St. John's Gospel in Mohawk for the Indians on the Mohawk River. During its centenary of work it issued 186000000 copies of the Scriptures. Last year it circulated nearly 6,000,000 copies, a total which exceeds all previous records by 870,000 copies. The Bible Society has been called the world's greatest philological institution. When the society was founded the Bible was current in about forty languages. To-day 370 appear on the society's list, the majority of these having never before been reduced to written form. In the same way, at the time the society was founded liot a line of the Scriptures had been issued for the blind in any language. To-day not only has the society issued portions of the Scripture in raised type in twenty-eight different languages but an entirely new system of Braille is being brought out for the use of the blind in the East, who far outnumber those in our own land.

div.head: THE. VETERAN WALKER
div.p: THE. VETERAN WALKER

Dr. Deighton,, of Durham, is well-known is. the athletic world, above all for his marvel- lous walking feats. Last week he started upon another of his long walks: and so far he has been eminently successful, The feat which he has set himself to do this time is to walk, fair heel and toe, from Land's End to John o' Groats, roughly a thous- and miles, within a month. Resting upon Sundays, he is confident he will accomplish itin twenty-nine days though this requires an average of forty miles a day. At the end of the first week Dr. Deighton had reached Bristol, where he spent Sunday, being well up to time, despite the wretched weather and the state of the roads He is accompanied on his great trip by a motor-car containing friends and refreshments to cheer him on his way. The latter consists of meat extract, oranges and beer; and he uses a special embrocation of his own for cases of chafing and for rubbing down. He has also half-a-dozen spare pairs of boots with him. The most marvellous part of it all is that Dr. Deighton is sixty-one years of age. Yet he is as strong and active as he ever was, standing over six foot high and weighing over thirteen stone. He has for the last fifteen years been professional athletic instructor at Durham University, where he obtained the now uni- versal nickname of " doctor " ; and all his life he has been a keen all-round athlete, having won no less than between sixty and seventy competitions of various sorts.
R. DEIG
ITON

div.head: ANOTHER DOOMED LINK WITH THE PAST.
div.p: ANOTHER DOOMED LINK WITH THE PAST.

The venerable ruin of All Saints' Church, Dunwich, the last of the many churches which once existed in the former capital of last Anglia, has suffered from the 'recent severe weather, and fears are entertained that before very long this interesting remnant will entirely disappear. The church stands in crumbling decay upon the edge of the low s d Jiff conspicuous landmark on
if THE RUINS OF ALL SAINTS' CHURCII, DUNWICII

Suffolk coast. Ancient Dunwich extended some three or four miles ;.;-; the seaward of the sleepy little fishing village of to-day, and it is .recorded that in the reign of Edward lll.—about the time that All Saints' was built—the sea devoured 400 houses. In its prosperous days Dunwich possessed a busy harbour, a king's court, a bishop's palace, and more than fifty churches 4

OLDHAM v. WARRINGTON.

Played at Watersheddings in the presence of about 5,000 spectators. Oldham won the toss, and Ferguson started. The Warrington lines were crossed with a rush, but Hallam managed to touch down. His side then got away, and Davies and then Fish almost got over. From the succeeding scrummage Oldham attacked. Spottiswoode was conspicuous, and Oldhann appeared to have scored a try, but the ball was ordered back,. and a scrummage took place near the line. The Warrington halves failed to clear, and W. Thomas scored. Ferguson failed at goal. The home team were soon again forcing the game,and Tyson scored but was rulledoff-side. Civil however, soon ran in a try, but failed at goal. Dicken- son enabled his side to make a temporary incursion to the Oldham. "25," and shortly after Dicky Thomas failed to check kWarrington rush,and Boardman scored Fish failing to convert. Then Warrington wereaggressive, and Dickenson put in a fast run for Warrington,ending up by scoring a try, but Fish again failed at goal. Oldham then pressed, and after smart play by Lee; Dixon dropped a goal. Shortly afterwards, from a penalty, Ferguson steered the oval safely over the bar. The members of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council were unanimous at their monthly meeting on Tuesday in condemaing the proposed introduction of Chinese labour into the South African mines. The Secretary (Councillor Stott) opened the discussion by moving the following resolution :—"That this Council strongly protests against the proposed introduction of Chinese ,labour into South Africa under a system. of slavery, and calls upon all Trade Unionists to do all that lies in their power to prevent such a scandalous proposal being put into operation, and that copies. of this resolution be sent to the Prime Minister, the Colonial Secretary, and Mr. Robert Pierpoin,t, ALP." He said the question was one to 'which he thought every working man ought to give earnest consideration. He rememberedsome four or five years ago when the war commenced he was one of those individuals—rather scarce at the time—who were dubbed Pre-Boers. He was against the war from the beginning to the end,and he thought events had justified the position he, with others took up. He never was a Pro-Boer, but he was one who believed in justice and in the cause of righteousness: He liked to consider a question from both sides, but the more he considered the side which supported the importation of Chinese labour the less reason could he see for working men taking up the side which was taken up by one of the representatives for Sheffield .at Parr Hall last week. Personally, he believed there was no reason whatever for the introduction of cheap labour. (Hear, hear.) A Labour Commission was formed some , short time ago in South Africa, and the result of the inquiry was that it was stated that there was a lack of unskilled labour, and that they were unable to secure natives in such large numbers as were required. But he remembered that two of the gentlemen who formed the Commission issued a minority report stating that almost the whole or the greater portion of the evidence given before the Commission was given by men interested in profits on the Rand. They could therefore imagine what kind of evidence it would be. The report of the. two gentlemen he had referred. to said that there was no need whatever for the introduction of Chinese labour. The fact of the matter was that the men who had interests on the Rand were not satisfied with the extent to which their profits were increasing. It had been said that unless they got this Chinese labour the minas could not be made to pay. The dividends paid by mining companies last year he contended, disposed of that argument. He would, give them the three highest and the ;three lowest percentages of the dividend paid: 187 per cent., 155 per cent., 110 per cent.; and 45 per cent., 40 per cent. and 33 per cent. In the face of those figures and immense profits they were told that the mines would not pay unless they got Chinese labourers at 71d. a day. An industry that would not pay a living wage to the men engaged in it should not be allowed to continue. Mc. Stott quoted some of the conditions of the labour ordinance, and said that if they did not mean slavery he was at a loss to understand what slavery was. The real grievance was that the mine owners were not willing to pay the price which white labour or even native labour demanded at the present time. If they were prepared• to pay a reason- able wage they could get either white or native labour. (Hear. hear.) He believed there would be plenty of our own unemployed who would be willing to go out there for a reasonable wage. It had been argued that the climate was not suitable for white labour, but white labour was employed on the soil and could do the work below the surface oeeing that the change of tem- perature was not as great as it MIS on the surface. It was the duty of every Trades Unionist to protest against the proposal, w -Lich if carried through, would no doubt lead to the introduction of Chinese labour in other industries.

Mr. BULLOCK seconded. Considering the great ex- penditure of money and loss of life in the South African war, there could be no two opinions on the Chinese labour question. Mr. PLuata (railway servants) supported on behalf of his society.

Mr. PLINSTON said the war would never ,have been commenced if it had not been a capitalist fight from beginning to end. Undoubtedly its object was to bring profits to the mines. The Government now sought to reintroduce the system of slavery which was so strongly condemn?cl and finally abolished years ago. Not only Trade Unionists but Christian ministers all over the country were endeavouring to bring pressure to bear against this monstrous action of the Govern- ment. He was unable to attend the wonderful meeting at Parr Hall, but he read what was said there, and he thought it was ridiculous that men should listen atten- tively to the speeches of two gentlemen who happened to be financially interested in the movement which they were trying to show was not in any degree slavery. If the mineowners could get Englishmen to work for 6d.a day they would drop Chinese labour. It was simply an effort to obtain larger profits out of the blood and sinews of the Chinese. It was monstrous to think that in the twentieth century there shouW be a Goverment, and supporters of it, that would bring such a system as was proposed into operation. -

Mi. PODMORE said it was only another example of the greed for gold. The men who had the power in South Africa were what he might call "cosmopolitan graspers," who seemed to have no soul for anything except getting rich, and who, unfortunately, appeared to have got control, to a great extent, of the Houses of Parliament. He believed their old friend Mr. Pierpoint voted for Chinese labour, but he ventured to think that in doing so he was not voicing the opinion of Warring- ton. (Hear, hear.) The resolution was carried unanimously. DEMONSTRATION TO BE HELD.

Mr. RANDLES, as instructed by the local branch of the Gas Workers and General Labourers' Society,moved: "That this Council;hold a public demonstration protesting against the importation of Chinese labour into South Africa." He said that the members of his society were quite prepared to pay their share of the expenses, along with other trade unionists.

Mr. ROWLAND 3 seconded and considered the condi- tions under which the Chinese would work were worse than slavery. Under the old slavery system it paid the masters to clothe and feed the slaves well, but in South Africa the Chinese would receive 7d. a day, be fed on rice, and after two or three years' service they would be sent back to China ruined. Mr. BUCKLEY then moved:—" That the secretary be instructed to write to the Free Church Council and the Labour Representation Committee asking them to co- operate with the Council in holding a demonstration to protest against the introduction of Chinese labour." The system he said, could not be condemned too strongly, and there was a religious as well as a political aspecL of the question. As Mr. Plinston had pointed out, a great many ministers of various denominations were taking up the question very strongly. By inducing the other bodies to co-operate in the demonstration the expense to the Council would be reduced. Mr. PLUMB (railway servants) seconded. _ _ .

Mr. SHEPHERD serongly condemned the Chinese labour proposals. The mine owners would take the blood and sinew from the Chinese, and send them back physical wrecks. There ought not to be a minister in the country who would not condemn the proposals from the pulpit. . . _

The CHAIRMAN said that if they invited the Free Church Council they confined the meeting to one section of the religious community. If the Church of England clergy felt strongly on the matter why not invite them as well ?

Mr. Porriz suggested that the Church Society should be asked to co-operate. Mr. BUCICLEY said he was willing to accept that pro- posal as he did not in any way wish to make it a party question. Mr. R LNDLE'S asked if they intended to invite the Catholic Association and other organizations to take part. His idea was that the Trades should protest from a labour standpoint. On a vote being taken there were twelve votes for each resolution.

Mr. EDWARDSON thought they should make the meet- ing purely a labour demonstration, although ministers and clergy might take part if they wished. The matter was again put to the vote, 9 voting for Mr. Backley's proposition and 14 for Mr. Randles's. The meeting then unanimously approved of Mr. Randles's motion, and the committee was empowered to make arrangements for the demonstration.
George Steadman, a famous wrestler, who had held the championship of the world in the Cumberland and Westmorland style, died on Saturday at Brough, West- morland.

div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Workingmen's Mission, Bank Quay.

The special services in connection with the opening of the New C'aapel, were continued in the above place of worship on Sunday. Mr. Arthur Mounfield conducted the service in the morning, and preached an eloquent sermon on" Prayer." Councillor James Evans preached in the evening to a crowded congregation, taking for his text" The Glory of the latter house shall exceed that of the former." He urged upanhis hearers Oe im- portance of giving their best for the Church of God, as the people of old had done at the time of the repairing of the first temple. The choir rendered the anthem "God is love," in an efficient manner. Mr. F. Atkinson presided at the organ.

The Rev. F. Vaughan praached his first sermons as curate-in-charge of the Emmanuel (Reformed Episcopal) Church, Bold-street, on Sunday when the centenary of the Bible Society was celebrated. There were good congregations both morning and evening. In the morn- ing the preacher took as his subject "The living word of God," the text bsing from Isaiah v. 10, 11 ; and in the evening his discourse was on "The Victories of God's book." Mr. J. Lloyd presidel at the organ.
St. Ann's gam Victoria IVlrnorial Vicarage.
Bishop of LiV2P,1331 Uovails the Tablet.

The comm)dious new vicarage which the parishioners of St. Ann's have erected in Orford Avenue was on Saturday delicated to the late glean Victoria. The Lord Bishop of Liverpool performed the ceremony and unveiled a tablet which has been fixed on the front wall, and bears the following inscription :—" St. Ann's Vicarage,built to the memory of Queen Victoria the great and good, and to the Glory of God." A special service was conducted in the church by the Vicar, the Rev. JlllO3 Davies. The Bishop, in the course of his sermon, referred to the useful purpose which the new vicarage would serve in bringing the Vicar into closer touch with his people. He proceeded to allude to the virtues of oar late revered Queen. He then offered up the prayer of delication. After the service a procession was formed, headed by the Bishop and clergy, followed by the choir, congregation, and the Sunday school scholars. The vicarage was reached by way of Winwick-road, Longford-street, and Orford-lane. On arrival, the Sunday school scholars, the ehoir and congregation assembled in front of the building, and the Bishop unveiled the tablet.—On the proposition of the Vicar, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Bishop.

div.head: Bible Society Centenary.
div.p: Bible Society Centenary.

At most Warrington places of worship on Sunday, sermons were preached and collections made on behalf of the British and Foreign Bible society. The excellent work which the organization has carried on in every past of the world during the hundred years of its exis- tence was dwelt upon from various aspects. At Wycliffe Church the Rev. John Yonge preached two appropriate sermons and heartily commended the society as deserving of liberal support. The Rev. R. Wilkins Reps was the preacher at Bold-street Wesleyan Church in the morning, his subject being "The voice of God in the Bible." In the evening the Rev. G. H. Carnson spoke upon "The hidden treasure." Mr. Rees's subject at Bevvsey-road Wesleyan Church in the evening was "The Bible in its simplest aspect."—At Holy Trinity Church in the morn- ing the Van. Archdeacon Midden occupied the pulpit. The Bible, he said, was the backbone of the reformed religion in the Church orEngland. In regard to the Bible Societz, it had done a threefold work— a mission work, a paThotic work, and a personal work, as it appealed to them personally. Voltaire once gave the Bible 100 years of existence. At that time there were from 6,000,000 to 8,000,000 in existence, now the number was over 100,030,000, while the annual circulation was Over 6,000,000.

div.head: Services for the People.
div.p: Services for the People.

The Rev. H. Dannico gave the second of his serieFia "Services for the People "in the Royal Court Theatre on Sunday evening, when the hall was again crowded. The text was taken from i Kings 18-21 "Elijah came unto all the people, and said, How long halt ye between two opinions? If the Lord be God, follow Him; but if Baal, then follow him." After brieVrelating the scene which led to the utterance of these words and des- cribing the position of the Jewish people at that time, the preacher went on to say that he believed scarcely anyone present was directly hostile to the Christian faith, but that many were halting between two opinions. The attitudelof hesitancy and indecision was asi much opposed to success in the sphere of religion as in every- day life. The important question was, " What do you think about Jesus ?" If they could not accept all the doctrines concerning Christ, every honest man must admit that in Christ was summed up all that was high- est and noblest and best in human life and character. Christ stood for the Fatherhood of God and the Brother- hood of man, and in the Brotherhood of man was in- cluded the Sisterhood of woman. The very founda- tion upon which their trade unions and socialidms were built was that laid by Jesus Christ, 'who had shown to , the world that a life spent in the service of one's fellow- men was the grandest and most sublime thing in the world. The choice must be made between accepting and rejecting the Christ who died because he loved men, who went about doing good and lived a life of self-sacrifice. Were they living the Christ-life? The pursuit of pleasure was one of the things which hindered many, and through which they were wasting their lives and fosing their souls. Men and women were dying for theiwant of spiritual heroes,and the preacher in the last appeal, urged men, if they refused for their own sakes, to live for God and for righteousness for the sake of others. The singing was led by a large choir, and Miss Gladys Roberts, R.A.M., an accomplished con- tralto, rendered vc4llk admirable taste and feeling a solo from the "Elijah" entitled, "0, rest in the Lord."

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.—Anniversary Meeting.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.—Anniversary Meeting.

The NVycliffe P.S.A. Society celebrated its eleventh anniversary on Sunday and commenced another year with favourable prospects of a continuance of the suc- cess which has attended the society since its formation. There was a very large attendance, the members bring- ing their lady friends on this occasion. The proceedings were presided over by Mr. J. E. Farrar, of Blackpool, brother of the honorary secretary of the Wycliffe Society. In the course of a five minutes' address he said he was delighted to attend the anniversary meeting and to see the Wycliffe Society in such a healthy con- dition. He was one of the founders of the Halifax P.S.A. Society. He knew the great amount of good it did there, and he felt confident that it was doing just us much good in Warrington. They must strive to make their homes happy, and one way to do this was to seek guidance from Above. He believed that if there were more happy homes in the land there would be fewer men resorting to public-houses. Many misunderstandings, he pointed out, occurred in homes through the husband or wife insisting upon having their' own way. He was the better able to give advise on this subject, he added, because he had celebrated his golden wedding, aid in his long married life had, been able to obviate misunderstandings in the home by not insisting too much upon having his own way.—Mr.C.E. Parker delivered the address, and in an interesting way he recapitulated the incidents which occurred during Christ's visit to Ca,pernaum as recorded in Mark 2nd chapter. He asked his hearers to notice how mach of Christ's time was taken up by acts of healing to the body and proceeded to point opt that all disease, all malformation and early death ftre opposed to the principles upon which the kingdom of Christ ought to be based.—The President (the Rev. John Yonge), referring to the anniversary, said he did not knowhove many were present that after- noon who were present at the first service, but he was perfectly sure that those who had been faithful to the movement during the last slevenlyears were better men, and had better homes. Attendance at a P.S.A. not only improved the individual man, but his family and his home. They had altogether 412 members, and he was very glad to state that of that number 74 were new members. (Applause.) The soloist was Mr. Levi Richardsog, and he sang with marked ability "0 love that will not let me go," and "Be thou faithful unto death."

FAILURES IN ENGLAND AND WALES.—According to "Kemp's Mercantile Gazette," the total number of failures recorded in England and Wales during the week ending Friday, March 4th, was 187, viz.:—New Bank- ruptcy Proceedings published in the London Gazette, 80; deeds of arrangement registered, 107. The res- pective numbers in the corresponding week of last year were : Bankruptcies, 78 ; deeds of arrangement, 85— total 163; being a net increase in bankruptcies of 56, and a net increase in deeds of arrangement in 1901, to date, of 114.
