SCRIPTION LIST:
There was a good attendance at the monthly titeetrilg of the Trades and Labour Council held in Bolcktrent school on Tuesday evening under the presidency of ltr. J. Podmore, jun.

CONCESSIONS TO GAS CON'SIIMIRS. The SECRETARY referred to the welcome concessiong to users of slot meters by the Gas Committee. He thought they could safely say that it was owing to a great extent to the agitation of that Council that the step had been taken.

CORPORATION OFFICIALS' SALARIES. The SECRETARY alluded to the resolution of the Council protesting 'against the imams of Corporation officials' salaries and suggesting that an advance in workmen's wages might be considered. The matter, he said aroused a long discussion at the meeting of the General Purposes Committee, bo.t he had to acknow- ledge that the motion was very indefinite, especially in regard to workmen's wages. The question was referred to the various committees to deal with as they thought fit. That seemed to be a wise course as any grievance which the Council might have in the future in regard to any section of employees, could be brought forward.

- -s- IRONWORKERS REJOIN THE COUNCIL. The SECRETARY reported the receipt of a letter from the secretary of the Bewsey Lodge of the Iron and Steelworkers of Great Britain, intimating their decision to rejoin the Council. That was welcome news, especi- all in view of the criticism which had appeared in the press, stating that the ironworkers left the Council owing to the revolutionary debates. Only a very small section seceded from that cause,eleven or twelve years ago.

TREASURER AND AUDITORS. Mr. A. WARBURTON was elected treasurer in place of Mr. E. IVlalone. who has resigned. Messrs J. Fargher and W. Rathbone were re-appointed auditors. WHAT THE CORPORATION IS DOING FOR THE UNEMPLOYED. • The SECRETARY said he was recently waited upon, by a deputation of ironworkers who were suffering very keenly from the trade depression. He suggested that they should write a letter to that Council, asking them to use their influence with the Mayor with the object of calling a meeting to open a public subscription list. He believed the distress in Warrington could not be met by the amount of work which the Corporation were able to provide. Later he received a. letter stating that the distress was so keen that the iron-workers could not defer action any longer, so they had decided to open a subscription list. Several mem— bers of the Town Council were waited upon and the appeal met with a very fair response, one Councillor having promised £lO. Tt had been suggested that a public fund should be opened to deal with all classes of destitution, although the ;iron workers were suffering the most. The Town Clerk and the Borough Surveyor had really aeted magnificently with the object of alleviating the distress. Mr. Longdin laid his plans before a committee meeting on Monday, and it was decided that as much work as possible should be immediately commenced. It was intended to widen Padgate Lane near the" King and Queen "hotel, and thus find work for 40 or 50 of the. unemployed at the pay of 3s per day. One diffi— culty was that before the Corporation could proceed with steel works the sanction of the Local Govern- ment Board had to be obtained. The Town Clerk was, however, instructed to write explaining the position and asking the Board to send an inspec- tor to conduct an inquiry at the earliest oppor- tunity, so that street paving could be proceeded with. Other work that would be undertaken was the pulling down of buildings. The Town Clerk had also been instructed to ascertain as far as possible the number of children who were being sent to school without or short of food. He (Mr. Stott) believed it was intended to forma committee to provide at least one meal per. day for the children. The Mayor was prepared,to open a public subscription list if the Town Clerk procured evidence of its necessity.

The CHAIRMAN alluded to the acute distress and ex- pressed satisfaction that the Town Council was giving the matter more sympathetic attention than it had received for many years. He proposed that the Mayor be asked to open a public subscription list. Mr. WARBURTON seconded and the motion was agreed n

Mr. BUCKLEY expressed the hop 3 that the Corporation would employ labour directly and not through contrac- tors. The builders in Warrington had already more men than they actually needed, and strangers were also flocking into the town. It was a grievance with Trade. Unionists that many builders preferred to employ these outsider:- If the Town Council employed labour directly, Warrington men would no doubt receive the preference. Councillor STorr said it was the intention of the Borough Surveyor's department to employ labour directly when buildings had to be pulled down. _ _

THE TARIFF PROPOSALS. The SECRETARY said he had received a letter from the Tariff Reform League offering to send a speaker to address the Council on the tariff question. Mr. PLIXSTON MOVAd that the letter lie on the table, pointing out that the Council had already condemned Protection and in doing so they were following the example of trade union leaders all over the country. Mr. RAN-IDLES : I move the letter be sent back. (Laughter). Mr. PLINSTON'S motion wan carried. The Tariff Commission had forwarded a series of questions with a request that the Council would answer them. The committee was instructed to consider the matter.

Public opinion on the CHINESE LABOUR. Chinese labour ques-

tion in the Transvaal is fairly summed up by the declaration of the ARCHBISHOP of CANTERBURY in the House of Lords.. If the importation of Chinese workmen is a necessity, it is the most regrettable nece.sity ever imposed on a British Colony. The necessity is strongly disputed; and, at any rate, the Opposi- tion have done their duty by urging upon the Government the most precise regulations for the well-being of the unwelcome immigrants. There was a considerable risk that the Chinese would be handed over to task-masters, who might not.shew the most scrupulous consideration for the liberties which flourish under the British flag. The Colonial Secretary was inclined to separate the Labour Ordinance from the regulations, as if the manner in which the Ordinances were to be administered did not concern the House of Commons. Against this assumption the Opposition offered a vigorous and successful protest. It has certainly had the effect of making the regulations more stringent and pacific than they would probably have been if the Colonial Office had been left alone. Mr. LYTTELTON now explains that every contract will be made with the express approval of the Chinese Government, who cannot be accused of any desire to send their coolies into slavery. The indentured workelan will not be held in bondage ; at the expiration of his term he will be free to g) ; and if he should want to break the contract he will be allowed to return home at his own expense. He may even take forty-eight hours' leave of absence from his compound. If all these conditions are carried oat, Chinese labour in the mines will not be slave labour. The Times is eager to accuse the Opposi- tion of employing contradictory arguments by asserting that to make the Chinaman as comfort- able as possible is to heighten the objection to his presence in the Transvaal. There is no contradic- tion whatever. It was intolerable that any system resembling slavery should be sot up in a British Colony; it is equally intolerable that the coolies should have the chance of leaving a permanent mark on the social fabric in South Africa.

The more the restrictions on the immigrants are relaxed, the greater is this particular danger; and to point this out is simply to express the natural repugnance to the immigration. There is nothing to prevent the Chinese from inter-marry- ing with the natives, or to prevent the children of such unions from becoming settlers in South Africa. The Attorney-General, at all events, has not thought it safe to promise that they will be sent to China. Mr. LYTTELTON assures us that the numbers of the immigrauts can never reach 300,000, that they will always be treated as supplementary to Kaffir labour,. and that no efforts will be spared to increase the supply of miners from native sources. But it stands to reason that the mine-owners will be disposed to rely more and more on the cheap and plentiful Chinese, if they can get these without difficulty. In that case the supplementary labourers will gradually become the mainstay of the minidg industry. This consideration alone would justify the strenu- ous resistance to the policy of Mr. LYTTELTON and Lord MILNER. They are undoubtedly convinced that the importation of Chinese coolies is an immediate necessity ; bu'-, they do not see that they need have the eff3,:t of slacken- ing the zeal of the mine-owners for the employ- ment of Kaffirs. Lord MILNER. is somewhat impatient of criticism in this matter, because he believes that upon the prosperity of the mines depends the financial stability of the Transvaal. This is unquestionably true, but it makes none the less imperative the duty of safeguarding the colony against evils which would be quite as 'grave as financial instability. All the criticism in this country has been directed to this object ; and it will certainly be justified by the increased care it has enforced upon the authorities at home and in the Transvaal.

The reply of the Liberals to Sir Ho ,vard Vin- cent M.P.and Mr. R.Pierpoint, M.P., at Parr Hall on Wednesday, was something like the reply of the Japs to the Russian fire at Port Arthur. It de- moralised the enemy. To begin with,the audience was much larger than that which heard the Pro - tectionist_ case stated, and with regard to the enthusiasm manifested there is no comparison between the two meetings. Even Conservatives admit that the Howard Vincent oratory fell !tat, ' and they must also grant that the opposite was the case on Wednesday when fully two thousand people were roused to a , pitch of enthu- siasm which is rare, even at political meet- ings. There have been fears among local Free Traders that Protectionist and retaliatory fallacies had got a firm hold of the Warrington public. The irmi-workers were said to be bitten with the craze to such an extent that their vote was likely to be a solid one for Protection, and election prospects were painted a particularly vivid blue. This week's Free Trade meetings, however, shed such a quantity of strong light on matters political that party spectacles are not required in order to see the brightest of prospects for local Liberalism. Mr. William Long's return to the colours, and his earnest advocacy of the grand principles enunciated and fought for by. Cobden and Bright were productive of an unmis- takable effect, while the oratory of Mr. Joseph Howes was magnetic. The disappointment due to Sir John Brunner's non-appearance was speedily forgotten in the delight and excitement of the moment. We are not exaggerating when we say that no man ever delivered a more pungent,pithy, and forcible address in Warrington on any politi- cal question than did Mr. Howes. It is, of course inspiring to be a critic, and Mr. Howes possesses considerable popularity locally, but nothing more nor less than enthusiasm for the cause of Free Trade and disgust at the vacillating, reactionary policy of the Government can account for the

"vigour of the demonstration •on Wednesday. 'Cheer after cheer roared from the throats of Warrington workingmen when Mr. Howes resumed his seat and one thought for a moment that the audience was going to demand something in the nature of an encore. They were loth to Part with the speaker of the evening and we should Judge that his oratory was worth a good many votes at the nexo election. Liberals have safe ground for the most sanguine hopes. The tide is turning witha swirl all over the country, and even lethargic Warrington appears to be awakening to the imperative necessity for making a change in the administration. Mr. R.Pierpoint as a "whole- hogger and a supporter of the Chinese Labour Ordinance is likely to find himself in desparate straits.

If our readers will peruse Mr. Howes' speech on .page 8, they will find therein a complete answer to fallacious Protectionist argument. The speaker's points were excellent and put in such language that they appealed irresistibly to the dullest person present. There were not many assertions made by Sir Howard Vincent a week before which Mr. Howes had any difficulty in knocking the bottom out of.' A favourite com- parison with the whole-hogger is between this country and the United States. The British workman is invited to look across the Atlantic at the Protectionist States and admire, •but he is not told how many of the workers there are out of employment or how serious and difficult the labout problem there is. Mr. Howes, by one illustration, showed the absurdity of the com- parison as a Protectionist argument. If, he said, it were possible to freeze up the waters round the American Continent the inhabitants would be able •to produce all they wanted and revel in luxury, 'whereas under similar conditions of isolation the Teo* of these islands would. commsnce to starve in less than six months. The dependence of this country on the rest of the civilised world for the Means of actual subsistence is, we think, one of the strongest possible argumentß in favour of Free Trade. Protection would merely be a kind of national suicide, and no sensible person will invite any such fate.

"Thank God for another dump! " was Mr. Howes' closing commentary after an elabor- ate and amusing dissection of the dumping fallacy, but the audience was roused to its deepest sense of personal responsibility for the doings of the Government when Chinese Labour was men- tioned. The first reference to this nauseous topic Was responded to by a murmur of unmistakable resentment which travelled right through the huge audience. There was no mistaking the temper of the meeting here,nor could the evident abhorrence of virtual slavery in South Africa be put down to any Party feeling. Less even than Protection is this a party question. and we are very much mistaken if the Chinese Labour Ordinance does not lose the Government more votes at the polls than even their colossal blunders during the war and in reference to education. British workmen won't stand "yellow preference," and Warrington itself will take very little rousing on this subject. We are glad to note,in this connection, that the Trade Unionists are getting up a local demonstration against:Chinese labour for South Africa, and we hope Free Churchmen and Liberals in particular Will ally themselves with the movement. All branches of thought and opinion should be solidly united against such a step as Lord Milner and tie Home Government propose for the benefit (sic) of South Africa.

Judging by the evident soreness of the Presi- dent of the Trades Council and the members of the Labour Representation Committee that important body despairs of getting a Labour candidate to contest Warrington. And looking a little further, the evident annoyance with the " Examiner " proves that we are to a considerable extent responsible for Mr. Alexander Wilkie's refusal to stand in the Labour interest. We humbly admit the soft impeachment. Had we deemed the time opportune we should have been glad to show our sympathy with the Labour men by supporting them in their endeavour to obtain a candidate of their own: But it will be in their own interests to wait a while,and we cannot regret that circumstances and the " Examiner " have conspired in compelling than to do so. Even txte Labour leaders should be able—in these nerd times—to see that half a loaf is better than io bread at all, and if the Trades Council mem- bers would put their aloofness in their pockets and approach Mr. Crosfield they might obtain assur- ances which would guarantee them perhaps more than the proverbial "half-loaf." It is ,not too late, even now,for them to come in line with those Trade Unionists who have already Satisfied them- selves with Mr. Crosfield's bona fides. Such a Policy would be more to their credit than display- ing an almost savage jealousy of the men who have dared, in the name of Trade Unionism, to come to some understanding with the prospective Liberal candidate.

A National Municipal Reform Conference is to be held in Manchester to-day, and all persons specially interested are cordially invited. ,The special objects of the Conference are: (lrrhe public inauguration of a National Municipal Re— form League, in which local associations repre- senting the ratepaying interest, under various names, may be linked together for united effort. (2) The discussion of urgent municipal questions and united action thereon. Meetings are to be held in the Coal Exchange, Market Place, and in the afternoon Councillor James Dodds will be the Chairman. The evening meeting will be nresided over by Mr. George Harwood, MA., M.P., and addressed by Mr. S. Norbury Williams, Mrs. Pankhurst, and Mr. S. G. Hobson (London).

The parochial electors of Stockton Heath attended the annual Parish Meeting in surpris- ingly large numbers, the schoolroom being packed to the doors. No fewer than nineteen well-known residents in the district were nominated for the twelve seats, including all the retiring coßncillors. Election by show of hands in these cases is far from satisfactory, and seeing the number of can- '!'dates it can occasion no surprise that a poll ha 3 been demanded. One of the principal ohjectioni to the form of election at the Parish Meeting is that it practically disfranchises the ladies, who do not, naturally care to attend a crowded meeting and compete with the men in a show of hand 3. Trouble is also liable to ensle when A. is observed to vote for B. and not for C., especially.if C. happens to be A.'s employer, as is not at all unlikely. The voters have by no means a "free hand" on these occasions. Another -°,biection, which was made noticeable at Stockton ateath occurred when it was necessary to have a lal-count. In those eases the candidace usually Polled more votes every time hands were shown, 'W. hich clearly indicated either that some people_ liked to change their minds or they voted when 111,ElY were not eligible to do so. Seeing the interest "alten in parochial affairs at Stockton Heath, and the growing importance of the district,it is just as. 'well that the final choice of the electors will have to be by the ballot.

The Warrington Board of Guardigns is not such call influential body as to inspire K. 3011 COMp9tit;Oa .4or seats upon its Board, but nevertheless too Illneh importance cannot be attached to the wise administration of the poor laws. There is room, even yet, for reform in poor law administration nd in humanising the treatment ex - ended to the deserving poor. Much has 'been done by the Warrington Board in .ecent years by adopting new methods lin the treatment of the sick poor and in introduc- Ug a system of classification amongst the aged and inarrn inmates of the Workhouse. The days of herding paupers together, good, bad,and indiffer- fetal and treating them alike, are, we trust, gone ,(11. ever so far as Warrington is concerned. f• feature of recent poor law administration has ibleen the introduction of women on the governing :dies. Mrs. Clay has for many years performed _useful work on the Warrington Board. There a time when she was assisted by Mrs. Vrelsten in her beneficent work, but latterly _B. Clay has been the only woman Guardian it the ) Warrington Union with its 28 representatives

In the forthcoming election of Guardians, the representation of women is to be brought more prominently to thb front. 'Mrs. Clay has been returned unopposed as the Guardian for White- cross ward, but three other ladies have been nominated for other wards, and if they go to the poll Mrs. Clay may no longer occupy her position of splendid isolation. Miss Constanceßroadbent, who has been So prominently identified with the Brabazon Employment Scheme at the Workhouse has been nominated as a candidate for Latchford Ward, and anotner lady candidate has been found in Mrs. Wilkinson in the Orford Ward. Then Haydock which returns three Guardians to the Warrington Board, has ' a lady candidate in the person of Mrs. Hayward, so that at the present time Caere is a likelihood of three ladies seeking the suffrages of the electors as members of the Warrington poor law authority. In the care of pauper children, and in the administration of relief to the poor and aged, there is a distinct sphere of usefulness for lady Guardians. Many of the recipients of the poor rates are women, and at the Workhouse and Padgate Schools there are offices which can be performed with mote tact and consideration by lady Guardians than by members of the sterner sex.

Personal. Mr. A. H. Crosfield has arranged to take a tean?. of golfers to Cannes to play a match against a side to be organized by the Grand Duke Michael of Russia. The team, which leaves almost immediately, will probably be made up of the following players !—Lord Eldon, Hon. 0. Scott, and Messrs. A. H. Crosfield, John Ball, jun., H. H. Hilton, J. Graham, jun., C. F. Hutton, T. Stone, and W. Ryder-Richardson.
Crippled Girls' Floral Exhibition. £251 was the amount realized by this exhibition which was brought to a close at the Parr Hall on Saturday evening.

Alderman Bennett and Federation. Alderman Bennett, of Warrington at the 44th annual meeting of the Association of Chambers of Commerce of the United Kingdom, held on Tuesday, at the Hotel Metropole, London, advocated a closer union with the Colonies. . UNDER the CLOCK for GOOD Boon.—Advt. Sudden Death. Peter Ashton, 64 years of age, a filecutter, residing in Haydock-street, and empioyed at Messrs. Stubb's Scotland road, died very suddenly on Monday morn- ing. He commenced work at seven o'clock, being apparently in his usual health and spirits, and at eight suddenly complained of feeling ill, and expired. He was a widower.

PUBLIC BENEFIT. UNDER the CLOCK for BEs BOOTS in LA.NCASIIIRE.—Advt. A Promising Young Singer. Miss Carrie Hastings, pupil of Mrs. A. Booth, won first prize in children's solo at Earlestonrn Eisteddfod last Saturday. She also won first prize in soprano solo competition' singing " The Swallow Song" from " Esmeralda.% Miss Hastings is 13 years of age and in soprano solo was competing against much older singers.

H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC IS the KING Of' TONICS.--63, SANKEY-STREET, Warrington.—Advt. Women's Employment Bureau. The Register of CharwQmen at the Gymnasium is open for inspection every morning - from. nine till twelve, and every afternoon, except Friday and Satur- day, Irom two till four. Inspector Hackett calls once a week, and marks the names of those women whom he knows to be clean and respectable. If ladies, when suited, will send is. to Miss Broadbent, Latch- ford, the office can be made self-supporting. AsK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS MINEICA. WATERS.—Advt. Bewsey Road Wesleyan Church. The Rev. George Harbottle will preach at .Bewsey Road Wesleyan Church to-morrow at 10.30 and 6.30 in connection with the Guild Festival. A. few years ago, Mr. Harbottle was in charge of the Bewsey Road Church, and during his stay in Warrington he was well known. throughout the town and district. Many of his old friends will be glad to gee and hear lilin again, and it is hoped that he will draw largo congregations. At 7.30 on Monday evening Mr. Harbottle will de- liver his lecture entitled "Through Germany by Cycle and Fourth Class." The chair will be taken by Mrs. Robert Garnett of Penketh.

Local Divorce Case. On Tuesday afternoon, in the Divorce Court, Mr. George Lawrence was granted a decree nisi for di- vorce by reason of the adultery of his wife with peti- tioner's brother. Mr. Barnard said the petitioner was married in 1883, at Radford, near Nottingham, and there were four children of the marriage. In 1897 they were living at Langley Mill, and the co-respon- dent was living in the house with them. They left the house together,and petitioner could not find where they had gone till last year, when it was found that Mrs. Lawrence had been living with petitioner's brother, William Lawrence, at Pierpoint street, War- rington, and they had had three children.

BASSINETTES AND MAIL CARTS in latest art shades.—J. S. G MU. AND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Ambulance Men as Naval Reserves. - The men of the Warrington Corps St. John Ambu- lance Brigade who have been enrolled as members of the Royal Naval Sick Berth Reserve fore paraded at the Patten Arms on Tuesday last before Inspector General Wood, R.N.C.V.O, to be examined as to their knowledge in first aid &c. They were tested with abcidents likely to occur on board ship, and as this calls for a rather different training than is required on law:, such as working in confined positions, getting an injured man out of an exposed position on deck with the least possible delay, and working without a stretcher &c. In the words of the Inspector General, they compared very favourably with any men he had examined so far. The men were also tested in stretcher work, fireman's lift, &c. The .Royal Naval Sick Berth Reserve is being formed from thd Ambu- lance Brigade men all over the country, to supplement the Naval Sick Berth Attendants in maritime war. Mr. Draper said he was not prepared to go into the case that day, and he 'asked for a remand for seven days. He hoped by next Monday he would be able to go into the case. He was bringing counsel down. The Chief Constable said he received the prisoner at 7.39 on Thursday morning, from the Jersey police. A Railway Detective's Retirement. Detective-Inspector John Howells, who resides at 709, Knutsford-road, has just retired after twenty- seven years' service with the London and North- Western Railway Company. He has been attached to the Crewe and Warrington District since 1896 and by the able discharge of his duties has gained the confidence of the company and the esteem of a large circle of friends. Previous to coming to Warrington, Mr. Howells was stationed at Leeds. He will have the (good wishes of many friends in Warrington and district in his well-earned retirement. Death of Mr. W. P. Skelton. Many Warrington people will regret to hear of the death of Mr. William Partington Skelton, formerly of this town, who passed away at his residence, Talana Villa, Rosebank, South Africa, on Wednesday. The deceased gentleman had been ailing for some months, consumption of the throat being the cause of death. It is about seven years since he left Warrington for the Cape. He was a member of the firm of Skeltons Limited (formerly Messrs. W. P. and W. Skelton), ironmongers &c., Horsemarket-itreet. In 1893 he successfully contested Orford Ward in opposition to Mr. William Pierpoint, and sat in the Town Council for three years. He then resided at Hill Crest, Sankey, and was prominently identified with St. Mary's Church, having held the office of warden. Girls' Club, Silver-street. The above Club was visited on Monday evening by several members of the British Women's Temperance Association. Short earnest addresses were given by Mrs. Simpson, Mrs. Norman, Mrs. Milne and Mrs. Landon. Mrs. Milne related some of her experiences with:Christian girls in China which were interesting to all. Miss Elsie Taylor gave two violin sOlos,which gave great pleasure,judging from the smiling faces of the girls, who, throughout the evening wore most attentive. They sang several sacred songs, and a few pledges were taken. Their behaviour is a credit to the patient enduring matron--Mrs. Davies—who has been with them for the past 11 years. FOR CLASS AND CHINA. of every description try J. S. GARLAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. The Work of the Brabazon Society. Through the agency of the Brabazon Employment Society a great deal is done to brighten the lives of inmates of the Workhouse hospital by providing them with light and interesting work. Warrington people were afforded an opportunity of lending much- needed financial aid to the local branch on Thursday, when the annual sale of work done by the inmates who come under the influence of the society was held at the Town Hall. Several stalls were laden with a variety of articles and there was also a display of choice flowers. Mrs. Edelsten, who was a pioneer of the movement in this town, opened the sale in the presence of a large gathering. Mr. William Hickman presided, and Miss Broadbent, the able hon. secretary, presented the annual report, which we hope to be able to give in extenso next week. LADIES BEST GLACE BOOTS and SFIOES, UNDER the CLOCK, BRID GE-STREET.—Ad7t, Bold-street Choir Concert. The annnal concert was given Jut Wednesday to a large audience. The items consisted of part songs by the choir, given in Splendid style, and choruses by the Warrington Male Voice Choir ;(conductor, Mr. S. Hassall). The soloists were Mrs. A. Booth, Misses Prince, Wilson, Osborne, Taylor, Hastings, and Dunn, and Messrs.-J. P. Taylor, B. Jennings, and W. War- burton. Instrumental items were given on the violin by Miss Elsie Taylor and Mr. Arthur Dunn. The humorist was Mr. H. 11. Ashton. The Chairman (Mr. Alfred Silcock) was received very heartily, and he expressed his delight and pleasure at being present. —Encores were numerous, and altogether a very I pleasant evening was spent. H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC is the KING OF TONICS.-63, SANKEY-STREET, Warrington.—Advt. Bold-street Band of Hope. The Bold-street Wesleyan Band of Hope on Mon- day evening held a children's concert in the Wesleyan schools. Mr. Sherburn presided. Owing to the in- clemency cf the weather the attendance was not as good as expected. Miss Lloyd Williams' orchestra gave selections which were well appreciated as were the ,pianoforte duet by Miss Ethel Pickup and Miss Edith Birch, and the banjo solo by Miss Clara Grace. Songs were sung by Miss Lena Duckworth, Miss May Isherwood, and Miss Nellie Kershaw; recitations by Master John Greenhalgh, Miss Annie Wood and Miss Nellie Lunt. The dialogue " The Band of Hope Fiscal Polley " rendered by Stanley Jones ' and Arthur Whitfield was exceedingly good. The fan song by the Band of Hope girls waa very pretty and very well done. The main feature of the, evening was a dialogue " Cinderella," in which the principal characters were :—Cinderella, Miss Ethel Cooper and the Prince, Master Gerald Doncaster, the remaining characters being taken by members of the Band of Hope. A vote of thanks was proposed to Mr. W. H. Sherburn for his kindness in presiding and to Miss Lloyd Williams and her pupils and to all who, in any way, helped to bring the entertainment to such a successful issue. Drowning Mysteries. At the Police Station yesterday afternoon Coroner Brighouse held an inquest touching the death of George P. Chappell (28), a clerk, of 7, Wash-lane, whose body was recovered from the Bridgewater Canal at Stockton Heath on Tuesday.—The evidence of Alexander IChappell, deceased's brother, and P.S. Dean, showed that deceased left home at 8 a.m. on February 4th for the Cable Work.s,where he was em- ployed. Nothing further was seen of him until the body was recovered. It was almost devoid of clothing and the arms and legs were broken, it is believed by passing boats.—A verdict of" Found Drowned. was returned—At Moore on Tuesday Coroner Dobson inquired into the circum- stances surrounding the death of A-my de Prez, aged ! 26, who resided with her parents at .Laburnum. Cottage, Moore—Deceased who had been rather un- well and depressed in her mind, was last seen alive on Sunday night, when she left the house stating that she was going to bring some sticks for the fire. As she did not return a search was inst•tuted, and her body was recovered from the canal at Kekewick by P.C. Ellis—Verdict " Found Drowned." •BIOE BOOTS FOR ALL.—UNDER THE CLOCK.—Advt . Debate on Chinese Labour. At a meeting of the Cairo-street Unitarian Sunda y School Debating Society held on Tuesday evening,the subject discussed was "The Chinese Labour Question." Nearly all the members present took part in the de- bate, and, as the opinions expressed were candid and well-conceived, an interesting and instructive evening I was spent. Str.-ing objections ware raised to the recent determiniation of the Government to import Chinese coolies into South Africa on the following (amongst other) grounds, namely : —That the scheme was calculated to operate for the sole benefit of a certain class of capitalists ; that it would be the means of ousting the employment of white men in South Africa, for whose protection and welfare the late war NVVI waged; that the proposed treatment of the coolies dnring the term of their engage- ment would be inhuman and degrading and would border on slavery; and that the Government proposals, if carried into effect, would eventually leid , to the adoption of a permanent system of importation ; I the resulting evils of which it would be impossible to I I define, It was pointed out, that the imported coolies would have no power to vote, and would therefore be unable to use their influence against tyrannical mono- polies. It was also argued, that the development of the mining industry in South Africa would open out fresh fields of ernoloymont for white men ; though on the other hand, the opinion was expressed, that the proposals to ininort Chinese had not been made in the I interests of British labour, but were due to a desire on the part of the capitalists to " rush " the wealth of the mines. Various speakers condemned the common idea that the Chinese as a race were lacking in good qualities, and strongly deprecated the low I conditions of labour to which the coolies would be ' subjected in consequence of their so-called inferiority. In order to close the proceedings, a resolution was unanimously passed to the effect that on moral, sani- tary, and political grounds, the meeting did not I approve of the proposed introduction of Asiatic labour into South Africa.

div.head: Local Distress.
div.p: Local Distress.

The Mayoress of Warrington (Mrs. Bolton) convened a meeting of ladies which was held at the Town Hall yesterday morning to consider whether the distress in the town was of such an extent as to necessitate the appointment of a committee to raise funds in aid of the distressed poor. The Mayor presided over a fairly-large attendance, about thirty ladies being pre- sent. It was ultimately decided to instruct the Town Clerk to make inquiries of all the large employers of labour and also of the head teachers in the public elementary schools respecting distress.ln the meantime it was decided to appoint a small sub-committee to take steps to provide relief in the Bewsey district, and Mr. Coun.cillor Rogers undertook to collect and place at the disposal of the sub-committee a sum of £lO until a definite decisiop. had been arrived at. A further meeting of the committee is to be held at an early date.

div.head: ELECTION OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: ELECTION OF GUARDIANS.
Probable Contests at Warrington.

The Warrington Board of Guardians consists of 28 members, and of these 10 are returned by the Borough i and 18 by adjoining townships included n the Union. The triennial election takes place on Monday, March 28th. Thursday was the last day on which nominations could be received by Mr. J. C. Sutton, the returning officer, The following have been nominated for the ten seats in Warrington -- WARDS. CANDIDATE. Town Hall: Mr. A. J. Jolley. Whitecross : Mrs. Clay. Bewsey : Mr. James Payton. Orford: Maria Jane Wilkinson. James Robinson. James Henry Smethurst. St. John's: Rev Neville Wilson. Rev. Dr. Mercer Fairfield: Mr. Robert Bolton, Howley: Mr. S. Davies. St. Austin's (1) Mr. Wm, Hickman (2) Mr. T. H. Ashcroft. Latchford: Mr. George Pilling Miss Constance Broadbent.

It will be seen that unless there are withdrawals on or before the 15th inst, contests are probable in three Wards of the Borough. It is anticipated that one of the two Catholic priests nominated for St. John's Ward will withdraw in favour of the other. The only Guardian who has not sought re-election is Mr. Alfred Jolley who represented Latchford Ward. Mr. George Pilling, who formerly represented Fairfield I Ward has de- cided to seek the suffrages of Latchford Ward, and his retirement from Fairfield Ward has enabled Mr. Robert Bolton to obtain a seat on the Board without a contest. In Latchford Ward, Mr. Pilling finds himself opposed by Miss Constance Broadbent of the Hollies, who has been deeply interested in the Brabazon Employment Scheme, for finding pleasant and light employment for workhouse inmates. A lady candidate has also been nominated in Orford Ward, where a triangular contest seems probable. Mr. James Robinson is the candidate who retires, and the candidates nominated to oppose his return are Mrs. Wilkinson, of Orford-lane and Mr. James Henry Smethurst.

div.head: NEWTON AND HA.YDOCK GUARDIANS.
div.p: THE NEWTON AND HA.YDOCK GUARDIANS.

The Guardians representing Newton-in-Makerfield which forms part of the Warrington Union are: Rev. T. It. 'Matthews, Dr. Patterson, Messrs. Thomas Ritchie, E. L. Bent and John Clarke. The first three named gentlemen have been returned unopposed. but in opposition to the return of Mr. E. L. Bent in Wargrave Ward a candidate has been nominated in the person of Mr. Astley King, of 33, Queen-street. There is also a probability of a contest in Viaduct Ward, Earlestown, where Mr. Thomas Lythgoe has been nominated in opposition to Mr. John Clarke. Haydock is represented on the Warrington Board of Guardians by the Rev. J. H. Riddette, Mr. Jacob Billinge and Mr. John Turton. The two last named gentlemen have been returned unopposed. The Rev.J. H. Riddette does not seek re-election, and the seat is to be contested by Catherine Hayward, of Clipsley-lane and William Flanagan, 4, Park-street.

div.head: TRADES COUNCIL AND MR. CROSFIELD'S RECENT SPEECH.
div.p: TRADES COUNCIL AND MR. CROSFIELD'S RECENT SPEECH.

The position of the Labour party in regard to the nett general election was again alluded to at the monthly meeting of the Trades and Labour Council on Tuesday evening. Mr. Buck,ley presented a report of the pro- ceedings at the last meeting of the L'aboar Represen- tation Committee when it was made known that Mr. Alexander Wilkie's executive declined to advise him to contest Warrington, and a resolution was passed asking the National Labour Representation Committee to provide a candidate. He also referred to the result of the poll for elective auditors, which, he said, showed that labour was awakening. Some people seemed to think it was a rather insignificant victory, but to his mind it was very significant. It only needed a few more efforts of that kind to rouse the working classes, and they would have not only a labour representative for their elective auditor, but also a labour representa- tive in Parliament.

The CILIIRM IN (Mr. J. Podmore, jun.) said the result of the contest was a striking example of what could be accomplished if labour made up its mind. Mr. Ball had many friends who were not always allied with the labour movement, but there was no doubt that the labour vote after five o'clock in the evening gave him his thumping majority. The election proved that if labour would unite and work they could accomplish anything they liked in Warrington. They had been told by the *Solomon of one of the local papers that they on the Labour Representation Com- mittee were poor, misguided individuals. It was mar- vellous how raisguidefd they were when they happened to do something which was opposed to that paper's par- ticular side, whereas they were clapped on the back if they said anything favourable to it. The labour move- ment would go on in Warrington. He believed firmly that they were entitled to a direct labour representative. He did not believe in second- hand representation. Warrington was an indus- trial constituency and, as such, labour had a direct claim upon it. In his opinion Warrington could be better represented by a labour man, affiliated with a labour group independent of both parties, than by any man belonging to the capitalist or landed classes. It had been 9. matter of astonishment to him that his fellow workingmen had not, long ago, awakened to the importance of being represented in Parliament. Councillor STOTT- said great stress had been laid upon an incident which occurred recently. One of the local papers, in alluding to Mr. • Crosfleld's speech at the Liberal Club, referred to the statement that responsible and important trade union leaders of Warrington had met Mr. Crosfield and decided to work shoulder to shoulder with him. Whoever those responsible leaders were, he did not think they were members of that Council or of the Labour Repre§entation Committee, and it was not fair for them to meet a Parliamentary candidate and speak in the name of trade unionism. Mr. BCCKLEY wished to utter a strong protest against any individual Trade Unionist expressing an opinion for the whole. If Mr. Crosfield or anyone else had wanted the opinion of trade unionism in Warrington in regard to Labour Representation, the Trades Council or the Labour Representation Committee or even the Building Industries' Federation could have (riven fairly the opinion of trade unionism. All those bodies would have spoken with no uncertain voice in favour of inde- pendent and direct labour representation. He could give the lie direct to the trade unionists who. went to Mr. Crosfield, and say that they had no right to speak on behalf of trade unionism in Warrington. The report was then passel.

div.head: RICHIOND GAS STOVE AND METER COMPANY LIMITED. Annual Mnting of Twain'tiers at Warrington.
div.p: THE RICHIOND GAS STOVE AND METER COMPANY LIMITED. Annual Mnting of Twain'tiers at Warrington.

Last year was not a very favourable one for gas stove and heating apparatus manufacturers, but notwithstand- ing the unfavourable weather, bad trade and the state of the money mtrket, the directors of the Richmond Gas Stove and Meter Company were able to present a satisfactory balance sheet to the shareholders at the annual meeting held in the showrooms of the company at Academy-streest, Warrington, on Thursday. Mr. Thomas Dwerryhouse, chairman of directors, presided and the other members of the directorate present were: Mr. Hb M. Thornton (vice-chairman and managing directa), Mr. John A. Ransoms (managing director), Dr. J. F. Atkins (Birmingham), Mr. John Coxon (War- rington), IVIr. J. W. Glover (Chelsea), Therewere also present: Messrs. J. A. Ewart, David Garnett, L. A. Voisey, C. R. Adamson,J. F. Davy, .T. Pollitt, J. Barlow, William Duff, J. Plant, James Booth, William Goodall, and J. W. Slack (secretary). THE REPORT OF' THE DIRECTORS. In submitting the balance sheet of the company, as on the 31st December last, the directors stated that the balance standing to the credit of profit and loss account (after deducting debenture interest and the managing directors' co.-Emission as per agreements), in- eluding the amount brought forward as per balance shaet,is £27,754 us 2d., which the directors recommend be appropriated as follows :—dividend on the preference share capital,at the rate of 6 per cent. perannum,for the year ended 31st December 1903, £5,737 14s 6d ;dividend, free of income tax,at the rate of 10 per cent.,on the ordi- nary share capital, for the year ended December 31st, 1903,£7,911 Os 8d; write off depreciation from buildings patterns, plant and showroom fixtures, &c., .21,099 4s lid carried to reserve fund, making this fund £21,500, £4.442 2s 6d ; carried to branch reserve fund making this fund £1,500, £5OO Os Od ; balance forward to next year (subject to vote for director's remuneration) £5,081 8s 7d. The directors proceed to state that the business of the company continues to be satisfactory, and it is gratifying to them that they are able, after placing entire (lost of advertising' as in former years, against revenue. to recommend a dividend at the rate of 10 per cent, per annum. The company's works and various branches are in good condition and have been maintained out of revenue. The directors retiring by rotation are Mr. James Atkins, Mr. John F. Atkins and Mr. John A. Ransom°. Taeir re-election by the Board is hereby reported in accordance with the company's articles of association. The auditors, Mr. L. A. Voisey and Al3ssrs. Hopps, Banka.rt and Warmington, chartered accountants, retire, and are recommendad for re- appointment.

_ _ SPEECH BY THE CHkIRMAN. The CHAIRMAS, in moving the adoption of the direc- tors' report and statement of account, said he was cer- tain the shareholders would derive satisfaction from the balance sheet. Twelve months ago he said he anticipated they would have a good year, and they had had a good year. (Hear, hear.) Inireviewing the balance sheet, the. Chairman painted out that a resolu- tion was to be submitted that the existing 12,500 £1 preference shares in the capital of the company be con- solidated in such a manner that every five of, the said shares should constitute one £5 preference share. This would not affect the general shareholders,andsome of these £1 preference shares were held by workmen as profit-shar- ing ',shares. When this alteration had taken place, the share capital .of the company would comprise ordinary shares of £1 each and preference shares of £5 each. The assets of the company, so far as works, buildings, patterns, plant and fixtures were concerned, were very little different from those of a year ago. The trade stock showed a reduction of £3,000 upon, that of last year, and that reflected credit upon the people who had been looking after.the business and had kept the stock a,s low as possible. (Hear, hear.) That was a very good feature of the balance sheet. The invest- ments of the company were in connection mainly with the two meter companies which the shareholders practic- ally owned, and they were first class investments. The net result of the year's work was that there was a balance of £20,009 to bs disposed of. The dividend on the 6 per cent. preference share capital would absorb £5,737, and the 10 per cent dividend which it was proposed to Tay on the ordinary capital would require £7,911. It was proposed to write off £4,099 for depreciation from buildings, patterns, plant and showroom fixtures and to carry,a sum of £1,412 to the reserve fund, making this fund £21,500, as well as 1500 to the branch reserve fund. They would thenhave a very respectable reserve fund. This satisfactory cohdition of affairs had not been attained by sitting down quietly and taking things easily. Competition was getting keener and they had to work harder for a profit than they did sorae years ago. The company was in a much better position for making profit, but more work had to be done for the money. A year ago, he recollected introducing to them the new managers, Mr. Thornton and Mr. Ransoms. They had now had twelve months' experience in their respective positions andhe could give them both a good character, because he knew them. (Hear, hear.) From his own observation he was quite satisfied that they deserved all the good things he said of them twelve months ago. They had done admirably, as witness the report which was presented that day, and he hoped the oompany would have their services for many years to come. (Hear, hear.) He must also add that the firm's travellers and the staff generally had worked zealously and contributed a good deal to the prosperity of the company. There .was another matter which he must mention. For some time the directors had been talking of having the company's works more compact together. It was a great drawback, no doubt, to have two or three works in different parts of the country, and the directors thought some change ought to be made on economical grounds which would benefit the company. (Hear, hear.) Those who lived in Warring- ton would have heard rumours that the company had bought land here, there and everywhere. (Laughter.) Asa matter of fact they had leased some land at Latch- ford, on which, at some future day, they hoped to erect some works. He could not say anything further at present. It tvas a suitable plot of land for works. It was difficult to obtain a good site for works and the directors had had some trouble in looking after it. The directors hoped to do something with it in course of time, and they hoped it would help them to make profit. He believed the company was in a stronger position to-day than at any other time in its existence. (Hear, hear).

MR. THORNTON AND THE COMPANY'S POSITION. Mr. THORNTON, in seconding the proposition, stated that he anticipateda year ago that they would have a better balance sheet this year, and that prophesy, he was pleased to say, had come true. It would be noticed that the dividend of .ten per cent. was paid free of income tax. They all knew what a very onerous matter that was at the present time,and if that income tax were not paid by the company, it would enable them to pay an increased dividend. The directors felt that the pay- ment of the income tax by the Company was a very desirable thing from the shareholders' point of view. With regard to the amount set apart for depreciation, it should not be forgotten that out of revenue-the com- pany maintained the works in first-class condition ; and as a matter of fact, depreciation was a great security for the business generally. After referring to the satisfactory character of the reserve fund, Mr. IThornton turned his attention to the trade stocks which he said had gone down from £56,000 to £42,000. In re- viewing the trade of the year, Mr. Thornton said they had passed through an extremely trying year. They had had bad weather against them, bad trade against them and the money market against them. Some of theshareholders hardly realised what the money market meant. The company dealt largely with municipal Cor- porations,and urban councils and at the present moment every authority was staying its hand and was unwilling to expend where curtailment was possible. The result was that the company had suffered through these authorities curtailing expeuditure'on the company's com- modities. He felt that they had cause for congratulation onthe results obtained. One reason for the splendid results, which the balance sheet represented, was the careful consideration which had been given to all points of expenditure in advertising and the general working of the business. A great deal had been saved in this direction. Further they had been endeavouring at all points to reduce the cost of manufacture. Much had been done already and the directors hoped to do still more. All departments had contributed splendidly to the general result and he was glad to say they had secured some important contracts, including those of Dublin, and the Gas Light and Coke Company, of London, which helhooed would prove profitable to the shareholders generally. He would like to say that their thanks ware due to their travellers . and all connected with the outside and inside stalls for the capable manner in which they had discharged their duties. (Ap- plause.) . . _ .
The aaoption of the report; wiq oarriei unanimously.. THE DIVIDEND.

The CHATECH AN MlVei tha-t—a—dividend'at the rate of ten oar cent. on tha ordinary share capital be declared. gr. JOHN COKON in seconding, thought that if the company could do so well in a had year like 1993, they might look forward with confidence to the future. (Hear, hear). The proposition was carried unanimously. 'MS AUDITORS. Mr. DUFF moved the re-aonointment of Mr. L. A. Voisey as auditor for the Warrington works at a re- muneration of .£33; and the re-appointment of 'Messrs. Hopp, Bankart and Wlrrnington as auditors for the Stratford works at a retnuderation of £BO. Mr.ENVIRT seconded and the proposition was carried.

THE REMCNERATIO.N OF- THE DIRECTORS. Mr. Bona meved that £lO9 be placed at the disposal of the directors for their services during the year 1903. Mr. PLANT seconded, and the resol‘,ltion was carried unanimously. Dr. ATKINs acknowledged the compliment on behalf of the directors. THE SHARE CAPITAL. The CHA.IRMA,N moved "That the 12,500 £1 prefer- ence shares in the capital of the company be consoli- dated in such manner that every 5 of the said shares

shall constitute one £5 preference share ; and that of the 6,605 shares (part thereof) already issued, when so consolidated as aforesaid, every 5 of the said 6,605 shares shall constitute one £5 preference share, upon which the sum of .25 shall be credited as having been paid up." In answer to a question by Mr. David Garnett, the CHAIRMAN said the resolution meant that those who held odd shares would either hava to sell them or buy others to make them into £5 preference shares. Mr. DUFF seconded and the resolution was carried. The meeting terminated with an acknowledgment of the Chairman's services.

div.head: WARRINGTON BUILDING SOCIETY'S AFFAIRS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BUILDING SOCIETY'S AFFAIRS.
THE ACTION AGAINST THE LATE SECRETARY.
B3nkruptcy PrOCB3llilgS to ba
Instituted.

Thera was a large attendance at the thirty-seventh annual meeting of the Warrington Permanent Benefit Building Society held in the Cairo-street schoolroom on Wednesday evening. In the absence.through illness, of the president of the Society (Mr. W. 4. Shaw), Mr. S. W. Da!low presided. He WAS supported by Messrs. John Critchley, Thomas Critchley, T. Ice, J. Mather, P. C. Price, R.Shack-leton, and F.Timperley (directors), A. Cook (treasurer), A. J. Willett (solicitor pro tem), W.H. Woodcock (auditor), and A. El. Clive (secretary.)
THE YEAR'S' WORKING. A DIVIDEND EXPECTED NEXT YEAR.

Tee report and balance sheet were fully explained by the CfrAIRMA.N, who pointed out that the whole of the Warrington property was now tenanted. Oat of the 259 houses owned by the Society only 11 were empty and those were situated in Widnes. (Applause.) The increase in the amount of rents received as compared with the previous year was £123 4s. 3d., a fact upon which he thought they were in a position to congratu- late themselves. There had been a reduction of £99 paid by the society in income tax, a redaction which was entirely due to the efforts of their secretary. That was not a temporary reduction, but meant that Air. Clive had saved the society £99 a year for all time. They would see from the balance sheet that the directors had that year paid out of revenue old standing accounts which had been passed by the board in previous years, which they had believed had been paid, but which had not been paid— "Shame ")—accOunts to the extent of £646 4s. sd. During the year the society had made a profit of £1,211 Cs. 6d.—;applause,—eut of which they had had to pay the outstanding accounts to the extent of the sum he had named, and out of which they pro- posed to-pay off shareholders on notice of withdrawal to the extent of £l5O. Hai they not had to pay off old debts they would have been able to pay a dividend of 4 per cent. which would have absorbed £B6O of the profits. They could, however, look forward with confidence to the payment of a dividend next year. (Applause.) They would sea in the balance sheet an item of £2,342 18s. id.. as having been expended on properties in the possession of the society. That sum included £678 9s. ss. for repairs, £721 Os. rates and taxes, £194 175., ground rents, £365 15s. 7d. street paving and making, and £79 7s . id. commission. The itells •he had mentioned included the out standing aecounts which they thought had been paia. He pro- posed the adoption of the balance sheet. Mr. HresERT scended. The report, he thought, was highly satisfactory throughout, and twelve months ago none of them anticipated that the society would be in such a position. (Applause.) Mr. JOHN CarrefiLEY remarked that in aboat three years they hoped to have paid off about £593 due for street making, which had always been a drawback to the society. (Hear, hear.) Mr. HIRRISON asked if he was to understand that all the outstanding accounts had been paid as he saw in the balance sheet the item " due to creditors £239 3s. Id."

Mr. DA.LIOW explained that that account was the amount of the law costs incurred by thesociety through the prosecution of their late secretary. Their late solicitors had acted in a very fair manner indeed. From their original bill they had refunded £lOO and merely charged them out of pocket expenses. There was, however, a condition attached to the re-funding of that £lO9. Messrs. Robert Davies and Company originally intended that it should be ex- pended in relieving the necessitous Cases which existed among the members of the society. They had since, at the express wish of the managers, agreed to allow £5O to be utilized for the society generally and £5O to be used in relieving necessitous cases. A committee con- sisting of Messrs. Davies's representatives and the re- presentatives of the society had beda appointed to pay off those small shareholders in the society who were in poor circumstances but who would not accept charity. The committee would also expend the £5O for the alleviation of distress amongst the members of the society. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Joss eq POTTER,: Might I ask what benefit we have derived through incurring the law costs?
Mr. DALLOW : No benefit. W 3 have obtained a judgment for about£2,soo, but up to naw wa have r - ceived nothing. The matter is still in the hands of the Board. _ _
WILLETT explained that they could enforce the judgment for £2,399 Hs. 51. which they obtained against their late secretary.
Mr. POTTER : Walt farther proceedings are to be taken? -

Wrr.J.Err : It is for the shareholders to enforce judgment either by execution onby bankruptcy pro- ceedings. Mr. DA:now : It would be as wall to ask the feel- ing of the 'meeting alto whether they would take bank- ruptcy proceedings or not. We do not wish to involve the Society in unnecessary expense, but the additional proceedings would only cost from £l5 to £2O. and I do not think it would be money badly spent. (Hear. hear.) We spent mlney more foolishly many times—(A. voiee 'Spend more then ")—and if we spend the £2O we: 'might be more satisfied. So far we have bean met in a very bad spirit. We have tried every way possible, both by friendly means and by the law, but we are treated as though we were dirt. (A Voice : "Go on to the bitter end.") Mr. HARRISON asked whether the family had been approached in the matter. It had been stated that they were willing to come to a compromise. Mr. R. COOK: Do you remember the Words of the barrister in the civil action, and the reply made by the judge? The barrister said he had nothing, absolutely nothing, and that he defended him as an act of charity. The judge in reply said "Why nrcQoeci ?" I personally would not spend another halfpenny upon him. (A. Voice: "I would.") A SHA.REHOLDEFt : I would send him to gaol if possible, as I or anyone else would be sent. Mr. DALLOW : We were told that he had no assets. Some of you may be aware that catalogues were issued of a sale held in London last Saturday week in the name of a member of the family, of old flshinz books. That sale realized £512. (Hear, hear.) Where has that money gone? With regard to what my friend has said about the family we have approa,ehed the family but can get no reply. We are treated as dirt. Mr. DA.T.LOW explained that some of the members had transferred a part of their shares. Mr. F'. TiMPERLEY: You Twist not take last year's balance sheet as being correct. It showed a balance at the bank of £99, whereas we actually owed the bank £535. ("Shame.") On being asked to vote, those present decided to take bankruptcy proceedings against the late secretary, only one voting against the proposal. • _ _

Mr. R. COOK said that some reflectiops had been cast upon the members of the family. If his information was correct the family offered to refund some of the money in the earlier stages of the unfortunate affair, but their offer was refused as the matter was in the hands of the lawyers. Mr. DA.LLOW said that when the offer was made the matter was in the hands of Messes. Robert Davies and Co. who on being consulted advised that the offer could not be accepted, as if it was, the directors would be compounding a felony, and that the society would be held responsible for their action. Mr. R. COOK: That shows that the family are not so bad as they have been painted this evening. Mr. D ALLOW : When W 3 obtained judgment after the civil action wa did try to c unpromise matters. We wrote, but have not received a reply to 'our letter. (A voice : "That shows what they are.") lam not casting any reflection upon anyone. .The family have a parfect right to please themselves what they do. The ofacial receiver will find that out for us. (A voice: Let us have satisfaction and I don't care). _

div.head: ~ THE CLARA BUTT-RUMFORD CONCERT.
div.p: ~ THE CLARA BUTT-RUMFORD CONCERT.

-- 1 The unexpected happens in musical as in all other matters. It was as unusual as it was gratifying to find that in mid-Lent the seating accommodation of Parr Hall was requisitioned to its fullest extent on the occasion of the visit of Madame Clara Butt's (Mrs. Kennerley Rumford's) concert-party, arranged through Mr. Pearson's agency. The hail was en Thursday filled in every part with an audience which, overflowing into all the available space on the platform, shewed by its interest in the music, as by its numbers, both a keen discrimination and a determination to enjoy itself. And there is no doubt that it does one goad to hear singing of the Clara Butt sort. There is about it a directness of purpose so unmistakable and an abandon so entire and unrestrained as to compel rather than invite the sympathy of the audience. No wonder then that a high degree of enthusiasm was aroused by Madame Clara Butt's songs ; a thing too seldom experienced in a Warrington concert-room. In the dranaatic aria from Saint Saen's "Samson et Daltila"as in songs such as "Abide with me" which she has made in a sense her own, Madame Clara Butt's sing- ing showed for how much thoroughness of intention iii interpreting a composer's ideas coupled with a high- strung temperament, count in these successes. It has been truly said that an artiste is powerless to move an audience unless that emotion is also subjectively felt. IHow true this is, Madame Clara Butt's singing more perhaps than any other's, brings home to us. Mr. Kennarley-Rumford himself rendered some most interest- ing songs and one received a distinct impression that he had improved in many ways since he was last heard in Warrington. "The old black mare" and "The little red fox" especially were .given so brightly and so pointedly that they could scarcely fail to achieve their evident purpose. Nor was Mr. Jack Robertson less successful as a vocalist, albeit his sweet tenor voice is rather light for a large room and his songs, as exemplified in "The bird and the rose," somewhat too trivial for such occasions as that under notice. The sisters Misses Pauline and Ethel Hook sang the duet "Quis est homo" from "The Stabat Mater" and "The four sunbeams" in the best of 'taste and won thereby well-merited applause, a little more animation in both their singing being, perhaps, the one thing lacking in these joint efforts of two gifted vocalists. The 'cello solos by Mr. W. H. Squire—ono of the Spanish Dances and the well-worn Gavotte by Popper—were played with a finished technique and a briskness of tempo which left nothing to be desired in their interpretation. In this capacity and as the com- poser of "The old black mare" and "The harbour lights" Mr. Squire received quite an ovation, Alp Johannes Wolff's abilities as a violin soloist are already known and highly appreciated here. But what- ever induced him to elan- upon an interminable unaccompanied solo in response to a vociferous recall following his performance of two bracketted items already sufficiently long, passes one's comprehension. The playing of the E flat Rhapsodie Op. 119 (Brahnts) by Mr. Prank Merrick betokened high attainments by that gentleman as a piano executant, and resulted in a hearty encore to which due response was made. Mr. F, A. Sewell played the accompaniments at the organ and the piano'with conspicuous ability. The next noteworthy engagement at Parr Hall is that for Wednesday April 13th, when the world-famous Mr. George Grossinith will give one of his well-known humourous and musical recitals.

div.head: WARRINGTON ARTIST'S WORK.
div.p: A WARRINGTON ARTIST'S WORK.
Exhibition in tha Art Gallery.

James Charles is a iVarrington man whose work as an artist has gained him n high place among modern painters, but hitherto the Warrington public have not had an opportunity of judging his capabilities. Such an opportunity now presents itself as an exhibition is at present being held in the local art gallery of oil paintings and studies by Mr. Charles. There are about thirty pictures in all, many of them having been lent by local gentlemen, principally by Alderman Bolton (Mayor of the Borough). The ten studies are of animals and are intended to illustrate to students methods of modern painting, One study is of a goat that was painted for a picture Mr. Charles exhibited in the New Gallery. The paintings are of pastoral scenes in Sussex and vividly reflect country life in its quiet, old-world moods. Mr. Charles is an Associate of the French National Society of Fine Arts, and the treatment of his pictures is that adopted by the modern French school. Mr. Charles carries out the most advanced notions in painting with a vigour which is refreshing. The two pictures purchased by the Corporation are included in the collection. One de- picts a scene in an orchard in which the members of I Mr. Charles's family are seen disporting themselves whilst the other—the best in our opinion—is a quiet pastoral scene in which a group of cattle occupies the foreground. Most of the landscapes are of scenes within easy distance of Mr. Charles's house in Sussex and he depicts some of the picturesque old country houses which are fast disappearing from view, as well as giving us an insight into some of the beauties of the natural surroundings. The pictures will remain on view for about a fort ' night and the gallery will be open daily from 10 a.m. to 9 p.m. We might add that the position given to some of the pictures does not show them to the best advantage and the centre of the room is so fully occupied with show cases as to detract from the plea- sure of viewing the pictures.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
WARRINGTON MAN IN TROUBLE FOR BURGLARY.-
COVERED WITH A REVOLVER.

On Tuesday, at Wrexham, Owen Jones, wire puller, Winwick-road, Warrington, was charged with attempt- ing to break into Little Acton, the Wrexham residence of Mr. Sydney Crosfield, the well-known Lancashire cricketer.—Prosecutor stated that shortly after mid- night last Tuesday he heard a noise downstairs, and on going down he saw the prisoner crouching against some ivy. He covered him with a revolver, and asked him who he was. He gave his name, and then ran away. Later on it was discovered that the windows in the drawing-room and pantry had been broken. The following day the prisoner was arrested by Police-Sergeant Rees at his home at Warrington —Mr. Thomas S. Steel, solicitor, Warrington, said he appeared OR behalf of the prisoner's family, and asked the Bench not to commit the prisoner, but to deal with him as a wandering lunatic. He had been several times confined in an asylum, and was well-known at Warring- ton as a harmless lunatic. His wife was in a dying condition, and the conduct of prisoner had caused much anxiety to his family.—Prisoner acted in_n most extraordinary manner in court, and eventually the Magistrates ordered him to be detained in Wrexham Workhouse for 14 days, and at the end of that time to be medically examined with a view of being sent to an asylum.

div.head: CHAMBERLAIN'S STATESMANSHIP.
div.p: CHAMBERLAIN'S STATESMANSHIP.

"The great difference between the real statesman and the pretender is,that the one sees into the future,while the other regards only the present. The one lives by the day, and acts on expediency ; and the other acts on en- during principles, and for immortality."—Burke. lam not one of those critics who blame a man for changing his mind, so long as he has got a mind that grows, and develops, and takes in new ideas. Sir Robert Peel started life as a Protectionist, but nhe became a convinced Free Trader. Gladstone entered Parliament as an old-fashioned Tory, and he became the leader of the Liberal party. Lord Beaconsfield began his public career as a radical, and he ended it as a Tory, and a Jingo, and an Imperialist. Chamberlain has boxed the compass all round. He set out as a Republican, and then he became a Radical and a Free Trader, and a municipal reformer. Then he changed to a Liberal Unionist, and became more reactionary than the Tories themselves. He developed into a fire-eating Jingo, and an avowed Imperialist, and finally he has gone the whole hog on Protection and Retaliation. He has been all things by turns, and nothing long, and his political coat of many colours is getting decidedly threadbare, and shabby, and worse for wear. .

Now when a man who calls himself a politician and a leader of men carries on these games continually, and swings round like a weather-cock with every wind that blows, it is time to ask whether he has go; any fixed beliefs or conscience, or principles of any kind. We have a right to know whether our rulers are shifty time-servers and reckless expediency mongers, or sober, honest statesmen. _ .

I have been hunting up some of Joseph's doings at the Colonial Office during the last seven years, and I wantyou to apply Burke's test to his policy and tell me whether he has the hall-mark and stamp of Statesman- ship, or whether he is only Brummagem tinsel and base metal after all.

div.head: 1.-WHAT ABOUT HIS HUT TAX POLICY.
div.p: 1.-WHAT ABOUT HIS HUT TAX POLICY.

Did he foresee all the trouble and unrest it would cause? And was he prepared to risk so much to gain so little? When he took charge of the Colonial Office in 18.15 this was one of the thorny problems he had to solve. Our" Crown Colonies "as they are called, that have no form of representative government are ruled in London, and they can imposeno new taxes and make no new laws without the consent of the Colonial Secretary. The governors of those colonies are usually military men who can undertake a little war at any time, but they are the worst rulers of subject races that can be found. They reteive big salaries from poor people, and they boss the nmives as they rule the Tommies in the army. Our West African Settlements at that time were com- plaining of financial difficulties, and some of them were drifting into debt. They must either reduce their ex- penses, or they must impose new taxes or they must borrow money to pay their way. Joseph,in his wisdom, decided that they must impose some new tax and the puzzle was to raise money out of people who had not got any. The poor nigger whose entire wardrobe con • sists of a few yards of calico and who carries all his worldly goods in a bundle on his head, will defy any tax-gatherer to get much money out of him. These natives have no visible property of any kind to tax. They do not even live in houses. They build gipsy huts of sticks and twigs and roof them with grass and straw. Some genius suggested that these miserable shanties should be taxed a pound each every year and Joseph gladly tumbled to this idea. But the people on the spot, who knew more about the matter than he could 'possibly know, objected. They told him that he might as well ask a naked nigger for one hundred pounds as one, while he was about it, and he would be just as likely to get it. They showed him that the average hut was wit worth more than a pound, and if he tried to collect the tax he would turn a settled population into a migratory one, and no tax-gatherer could keep pace with their movements. He was warned by those who knew the temper of the native that they would sooner fight than pay, and if the hut tax were levied at all it would have to be collected at the point of the sword.

, And yet in spite of all these warnings, Joseph would have his own way. He deliberately took the most peril- ous path he could find, and provoked a series of little wars, in which we gained neither honour nor glory, and we squandered our blood and our treasure in wars that might have been avoided. You may call this policy folly, and stupidity, and madness, but it certainly was not statesmanship.
IL-WHAT ABOUT OUR WEST INDIAN SUGAR

PLANTERS. The representatives of this "ruined industry" were soon on Joseph's track wanting to know what kind of outdoor relief he would give them. These sturdy beggars date their misfortunes from the days of the French Revolution, when we blockaded the French ports and would not allow any West Indian sugar to be sold there. The French learned by their misfortunes to supply their own needs, with sugar made from beet- root, so they were not only independent of us, but they were able to compete with us in our own markets. So long as our old Protective taxes were in force, sugar was dear, and the West Indian planter sheltered himself behind the tariff walls. When Free Trade came, he was driven from his last refuge and compelled to rely on his own merits and his own exertions. He came to grief, and now he is everlastingly wanting to know what we are going to do to revive his ruined industry? This raises the whole question of Free Trade, or Pro- tection, in its most acute form. We have coddled and nursed our cane sugar industry till it cannot live with- out artificial help. Is it worth our while to keep it alive any longer, or shall we let it die and give it a I respectable funeral? There are some other people in the world to think about, beside sugar planters, and Joseph might have suggested many ways out of that difficulty. He could have advised them to plough up I their sugar canes, and give over growing crops that do not pay and begin growing cotton or tropical fruits that will pay. He might have given them another grant in aid to improve their harbours, and roads, and railways, and to help them to place their produce on the markets quickly. He might have cut down expenses and administered government more economically and relieved the burdens of the colonists; or he might:have , promised them Protection at our expense. He could , have proposed to close every other sugar market against us by prohibitive tariffs, as our fathers did a hundred 11 years ago. Whether he could have carried his schemes is another matter, but at any rate he might have tried. What did,he do? He voted for the Sugar Convention , Bill which cut off our supplies of cheap sugar and ' threatens one hundred and twenty thousand work- people in our confectionery, marmalade, jam, and cocoa trades, and he did not put any money into the pockets lof the West Indian Planters. This policy of injuring everybody and benefitting nobody is worthy of Colney Hatch, or Bedlam, but I fancy that Joseph himself, in his sane and sober moments, would hardly call it statesmanship. lII.—WHAT ABOUT HIS GAME OF BLUFF IN SOUTH AFRICA.

The worst feature of Joseph's policy is that he always sins with his eyes open, and walks into traps that he knows all about. He invariably knows the right, and does the wrong. Long before the Boer War, he told us that a war with the Boers would be a long war, and a costly war, and a bloody war, and its effect would last for generations. No truer words of warning were ever uttered than these, and yet he had not wit enough to keep us out of it. The very man who pointed out the peril, deliberately led us into it, and then left us to stew in our own juice. He had not been long at the Colonial Office before the restless spirits who coveted the gold and diamond mines outside our own territory organised the Jameson Raid. If the Boers had hanged or shot every mother's son of them that fell into their hands I should have said it served them right. But .with wonderful magnanimity they handed them over to us. Did Joseph punish them. Not much! We had a formal, friendly trial, and we locked up some of them as firstclass misdemeanants, and fed them like fighting cocks all the time, and finally we honoured them and promoted them. The Boers never trusted Joseph again. They began arming and preparing for a war that they believed to be inevitable. Joseph knew all this, and yet he used his saucy, impudent, irritating tongue as•recklessly as ever. The man who could tell France to" mend its manners," and tell Germany that " its territory was limited," and tell Russia those who sup with the devil would need a long spoon," could say anything. Unfortunately for us, he did nothing but talk, and threaten, and bully the Boers. He talked about the "squeezed sponge," and the "sands running out of the hour-glass," and did all he could to provoke a war, and yet he made no preparation for it. At the very time he was playing with gunpowder and fire after this fashion he said to Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman: "You need not be alarmed; there will be no fighting. We know these fellows won't fight. We are playing a game of bluff." This game of bluff cost us two hundred and fifty millions of motley, and tens of thousands of lives, and did infinite harm to our reputation for wisdom and honour. Joseph can claim the dubious honour of having played the costliest game in the world, but no man in his senses will call these games statesmanship. It was the memory of this kind of "statesmanship" that prompted the Manchester Radicals recently to sing: Oh, Joseph! you may never Be a Minister again; Joseph! We'll remember you, When you're numbered with the slain.
