div.p: The ExamineT, Saturday, March 12 1904 LOCAL PARISH ME:ANGS.

Ebenezer England, Whitefield-road, accountant and estate agent; John Fairhurst, London-road, grocer and draper ; Ebenezer James Hall, Whitefield-road, chartered secretary; John Hallows, Fairfield-road, retired postmaster •, Ashton Hayes, Grappenhall-road, gentleman; John Lord, Ellesmere-road, draper; Wm. Mclntyre, Bedford-street, manufacturers' clerk; John Miller, Gaskell-street, contractors' assistant; Frederick Pearson' Wilderspool, cashier • John Pemberton, Fair- field-road, builder; William Henry Sherburn, Grappen- hall-road, designer; Frank Warburton, Whiteffeld-road, builder; James Whitley, Walton-road, grocer; Samuel Fitzgerald Welsby, Walton-road, cycle agent; Herbert James Westbrook, Whitetleld-road, solicitor; Thomas Boyle Westbrook, solicitors'. clerk; Thomas Williams, Whitefield-road, builder.

Voting proceeded by show of hands, Messrs. F. Timperley and Ft. Isherwood acting as tellers. The following were the votes recorded for each nominee :—Pearson, 82; Mclntyre, 80; Warburton, 78; FL J. Westbrook, 72; Clarke, 71.' Fairhurst, 66; Hallows, 66; Bonchier, 65; Whitley, 63; T. R. West- brook, 53; Williams, 52; Welsby, 50; Pemberton, 45; Lord, 44; lives, 41; Hall, 39; England, 32; Sherburn, 24; and Miller, 20._ _ _

- The Chairman said that, subject to no poll being de- manded, he declared the first 12 to have been elected. Mr. Lord demanded a poll and was supported by four ratepayers as required by the Act. Mr. H. J. Westbrook asked the Chairman if he could give the meeting some idea of the cost of a poll. The Chairman: About .£l5. Mr. Hallows expressed his willingness to withdraw in favour of Mr. Lord to save a poll. The Chairman.—Mr. Pemberton is next on the list,and I: dont think, therefore. that your suggestion would avail.

Mr. Hallows explained that his object in offering to retire was to save the cost of the election. (Elear,hear) The Chairman : lam afraid you are too late to withdraw. You can only withdraw through the re- turning officer. He added that the election would take place on March 28th. Any candidate desirous of with- drawing could do so not later than 12 noon on the 15th inst. tTnesday). The withdrawals must be sent to Mr. G. F. Ashton. returning officer. A vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman, on the motion of Councillor Lord.
On Tuesday Mr E. J. Hall withdrew his candidature.
THE SCHOOL ACCOIDIODATION QUESTION.

Mr. England said he wished to address the meeting on behalf of the children of the parish. They would be aware that the County Council of Cheshire and the Educational body had arranged to build six or seven schools, but he was sorry to say that Stockton Heath was not one of the places that had been mentioned for a new school. Therefore their school interests had been somewhat neglected. (Hear. hear.) That was his opinion, andithe opinion of others. It had been clearly shown that a school was urgently needed there. It was the desire of many parents that their children should be educated in a manner equal to the education that was given to the children of other districts, and he con- tended that it was the duty of the ratepayers to see that a new school wag erected at Stockton Heath. That district would have to bear its due cOst of the expense of the erection of the new schools to which he had alluded and the least they could do was to see that the other parts of Cheshire should contribute towards a school for that parish. He made no reflection on the teaching in that school. The authorities were doing their best, but they were so handicapped by the num- bers in the classes that they could not do their duty. He hoped that whoever was elected would take the school question in hand. (Hear, hear, and applause.)

need fear nothing. He (Mr. Thompson) asked if the inqpector would protect them in the matter, and he said, "Certainly." When the Winwick Asylum sewage was turned into Sankey Brook the Parish Council wrote to the Local Government Board, and had that nuisance stopped. He thought the Parish Council had done all they could in the mAtter—(hear, hear)—but he was glad Mr. Furness would be on the new Council, and would be able to put them in order to enlighten them on the matter.

The Chairman said he quite agreed with Mr. Furness in bringing the matter forward, and he believed that in doing so he was actuated by the purest motives and a desire to do good for Great Sankey. Was it not a fact that a man living in the neighbourhood, and who had to pass the Sanatorium sewage every day, had died from smallpox? ("Yes.") Then where did he getthe germs of smallpox from? That was the question. There was no doubt that so long as the colliery people at Bold were pumping water into the brook, the germs were carried away, but if that pumping stopped and they had a dry summer, they would see what would happen. He believed a great deal of the rubbish that was turned into the brook could be utilized, but that was away from the question. He thought Mr. Halton had been blamed wrongly by Mr. Furness, though quite inadvertently. Mr. Furness: I never mentioned Mr. Halton's name. I said the District Council and Parish Council. The Chairman: But Mr. Halton is our representative on the District Council, and I have known him to be laughed at for bringing the matter forward so often. Continuing, Mr. .Clarke said he knew also that the Parish Council had often had the matter under their consideration. With reference to the sanitary arrange- ments referred to, there was no doubt an evil existed, which required remedying. There was no doubt that a sewage scheme would have to be faced eventually, but he hoped it would not be for a few years. (Hear,hear). Mr. Hope asked whether the Local Government Board had given any promise in writing with reference to the protection of the district. The Clerk said there was no undertaking in writing. Mr. Hope complained of the unsatisfactory arrange- ments in the Hood-lane district. The Chairman was thanked for his services in the chair and the meeting terminated.

div.head: POLL DEMANDED AT STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: A POLL DEMANDED AT STOCKTON HEATH.
THE EDUZATIONAL HEEDS OF THE VILLAOE.

More than usual interest was lent to the annual parish meetings held in the country districts on Monday even- ing by the fact that the triennial election of parish councillors took place. Most of the gatherings in the Warrington district appear tso have passed off har- moniously. At Stockton Heath there were no fewer than nineteen nominations for the twelve seats, and after a vote had been taken, a gall wis demanded. The election will therefore take place on 'March 28th.
STOCKTON HEATH FARrsa COUNCIL. URBAN POWERS TALKED OF.

Prior to the annual ptrish meeting of ratepayers, the Stockton Heath Parish Council held its anal meeting for the year in the National Schools. Mr. J. H. Clarke presided, and there were also present :—Messrs. F. Pearson, J. Whitley, J. W. Bouchier, J. Fairhurst, W. Mclntyre, and E. Bradshaw (clerk).
SECONDARY EDUCATION. THE COUNCIL AND WARRINGTON CORPORATION.

The CLERK reported that in accordance with instruc- tions given at the last meeting,he wrote to the Director of Education for the Cheshire County Council. suggesting that the County Council should approach the Warrington Corporation with a view to Stockton Heath children who desired to receive second- ary instruction being allowed to attend the secondary, school at Warrington. The Cheshire director of educa- tion, he was now informed, wrote to the Warrington director who replied pointing out that there was not sufficient accommodation in the secondary school to justify the Corporation coming to an arrangement with Stockton Heath. The Corporation contemplated an ex- tension, and when there was sufficient accommodation they would be pleased to arrange terms with the County Council. Mr. Clarke thought the position of affairs was very unsatisfactory, because it seemed to him that it would be a long time before the Stockton Heath children would be able to receive the advantages of secondary education in the manner desired by the Parish Council. It was pointed out by the Clerk and Mr. Bouchier that already a number of children from Stockton Heath attended the secondary school. No further action was taken. THE SWING BRIDGE.

At the last meeting of the Council a resolution wa passed and forwarded to the Council, requesting that authority to oppose the Manchester Ship Canal Bill. The reason stated was that the company was not fulfilling its obligations with regard to the opening of the Stockton Heath Swing Bridge, and the Council thought opposition to the Bill before Parliament would result in close attention being given to the matter. The Clerk now reported that the County Council had replied to the effect that they did not think they would be justified in incurring the costs of petiqoning against the Bill on the grounds named by the Parish Council.

div.head: FINANCIAL POSITION OF THE PARISH.
div.p: FINANCIAL POSITION OF THE PARISH.

The Clerk produced the statement of accounts for the past half year. On the poor rate account there was a balance in hand of £305 Cs. 2d., and on the special rate account the credit balance was about £l5. Mr. Clarke said he gathered that in the case of Stockton Heath becoming an urban district the sum of £235 at present collected every half year on behalf of the general rate account, for the maintenance of roads &c., would be allocated to the urban authority. That meant that £470 would be received annually, and out of it they would have to pay for the maintenance of roads, officers' salaries, and similar items. Those figures did not agree with the figures supplied to hint by Mr. Ashton, clerk to the Rural District Council, who in- formed him that had the Council been an urban authority the amounts allocated to them during the past three years would have been £197, £268. and .2281. respectively. They would see that the figure was gradually becoming larger. STOCKTON HEATH'S REPRESENTATION.
The Clerk reported the receipt of an order from the Cheshire County Council sanctioning an additional representative of Stockton Heath on the Rural District Council.

div.head: GRAPPENHALL ROAD TREES.
div.p: GRAPPENHALL ROAD TREES.

The Chairman said that at the last meeting it was agreed that he should engage a gardener to cut the trees in Grappenhall-road. He had consulted a gardener who advised that the trees' should be left as they were until nest year. One tree, it was found, was dead, having been broken through an accident caused by a horse taking fright at a County Council steam roller which was working in the roadway. He took it upon himself to have the tree replaced, and wrote to the County Council asking them to defray the cost. Judg- ing from the tone of their reply he did not think they would agree to that. It was decided that in the event of the County Coun- cil refusing to pay for the tree, the cost should be met by the Parish Council.

div.head: PROPOSED VILLAGE IMPROVEMENTS.
div.p: THE PROPOSED VILLAGE IMPROVEMENTS.

The Chairman explained that with reference to the new buildings proposed to be erected by Mr. Piers Egerton-Warburton at the corner of Victoria Square and London road, there was an informal discussion at the conclusion of the meeting of the Parochial Committee at which the plans were approved, as a result of which he wrote to Mr. Egerton Warburton pointing out that there was a unanimous feeling among the mem- bers of the committee that the site on which he proposed to build would eventu- ally have been secured by the parish for the erection of wish offices, as he (Mr. Clarke) did not think it would be many years before Stockton Heath claimed urban powers. He asked Mr. Warburton, if he had not definitely decided upon the erection of the buildings, to bear in mind the wishes of tlie Parochial Committy with regard to the ultimate acquiring of the plot. To.- this letter he received a reply to the effect that Mr. Warburton had decided to build on the plot for the simple object that he wished some- thing sightly to be erected thereon. As the Parochial Committee would see, he pr.aposed to erect handsome buildings, including a club-room, shop, and cocoa room. If required, the large room might be used asa Council room for the Parochial Committee, and the lock-up shop under the central arcade might be used as offices. There would be no diculty in utiliz- ing part of the building for the purposes named. .As Mr. Egerton Warburton was proposing to spend a large sum of money on the building he hoped to make it architecturally an ornament to the parish. To this, Mr. Clarke replied he felt sure from what he saw of the plans, that the buildings would be an ornament to that part of the village.. He thanked Mr. Warburton for his expressions regarding the question of utilizing parts of the building for public or parish business when the , proper time arrived. He suggested that instead of naming the place a cocoa room, if it was to be a place for refreshments it might be styled a cafe or restaurant TIE CHAIRMAN THANKED.

Mr. Whitley said that during the year they had worked together in a very amiable and businesslike manner, and in Mr. Clarke they had had a very excel- lent chairman. He thought it was their duty before closing the meeting, to accord a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Clarke. In the most heated discussion the Chair- man had conducted himself with strict impartiality, and they had always been the best of friends. He thought he could say on behalf of the Council, that they had done their duty during the year for the benefit of the parish. Mr. Bouchier gladly seconded the proposition. They could not have had a b3tter chairman. Mr. Clarke had shown himself deeply interested in parish affairs, and had gone thoroughly into matters. He did not know that they had had heated discussions. They had tried to do their duty, and it was, he considered, a compli- ment to the Parish Council that there were 20 or 30 persons coming out as candidates to take the place of those already in office. That showed that the Council had roused the feeling of the district, and that rate- payers were anxious to get on the Council. (Hear,hear.) The motion was carried. The Chairman, in reply, thought it would be impos- sible to get a number of gentlemen together who would conduct the affairs of the parish in a more capable and energetic way than the present Council had done. Nothing they could possibly do had been overlooked. He hoped the futurG Council would do its work in the same. able way. (Hear, hear).

div.head: TEIE PARISEI MEETING.
div.p: TEIE PARISEI MEETING.

The schoolroom was filled almostto overflowing for the annual parish meeting. Mr. E. Bradshaw was elected to the chair and at eight o'clock asked for nomination papers to be handed in. Immediately eight or nine gentlemen stepped forward and when the papers were examined it was found that nineteen gentlemen had been nominated for the 12 seats. The following were the nominees: Joseph Wallace Bouchier, Whitefield-road, cashier; Joseph Hough- ton Clarke, Grappenhall-road, brewers' agent; BREAD AND PASTRY FOR DYSPEPTICS.

div.head: Great Sankey
div.p: Great Sankey

A well-attended parish meeting was held in the Board schools, Great Sankey, on Monday evening. Mr. George Clarke was voted to the chair and their were present: Messrs. W. Taylor, G. Thompson, J. Fulton Smith, T. Halton, Joseph H. Kilshaw (members of the existing Council): F'. 'l'. Jefferson, A. B. Mellor, A. Birch, W. Furness, J. T. Kilshaw, W. H. Ir4and, B. Grimshaw, F. C. Tonge, J. Blythe, Whitharn, Hope, Dale, H. Craske, H. Bingham, H. Long, Howarth, Unswoith, and J. Smith (clerk).

div.head: REPORT WANTED.
div.p: A REPORT WANTED.

Mr. W. Furness thought if a report on the work of the Parish Council were presented it would be interest- ing to parishioners, as they were anxious to know what the Parish Councillors had done during their tenure of office. Nothing of the kind indicated was, it appeared, to be presented. Mention might have been made or some action taken with reference to the pollution of Whittle Brook by sewage from the Sanatorium. The Chairman thought .this matter might be more correctly dealt with in any cross-examination of candi- dates who might be nominated. The first business of the meeting was the receipt of nominations. Mr. Furness: Could you give us any statement of the attendances of members of the Parish Council? The Chairman : Not at this stage. Mr. Furness: We shall be guided in our choice by the attendance of those who have served on the Coun- cil.
_ The Chairman promised that the Clerk should prepare astatement of attendance and submit it to the meeting before the voting took place. VIE NOMINATIONS.

Nominations were then handed in and the Chairman announced that the following electors had been nomin- ated; Arthur Birch, ironworker; Edwin W. Clarke, agent; Harry Fairclough, farmer; William Furness, gentleman; Thomas Hatton, farmer; George Higgs, works manager; Frederick Thomas Jefferson, plumber; William Taylor, farmer; George Thompson, works manager.
THE ATTENDANCES OF MENIBERS OF THE COUNCIL.

The Clerk stated that the attendances of the members of the existing Council were as follows during the past three years:—Thomas Halton, 19 ; Joseph Wright, 2 ; Joseph H. Kilshaw, 15; William Taylor, 19; G . Thomp- son, 22; J. Fulton Smith, 17; H. Singleton, 11. There were 24 meetings. RESULT OF THE VOTING.

The voting by show of hands resulted as follows : A. Birch 17 • E. W. Clarke, 7•; H.Fairclough, 22 ; William Furness, 20: Thomas Halton, 9; a Higgs 21; F. T. Jefferson 25; William Taylor, 23; G. Thompson, 27. The following sere declared elected : Messrs. Fair- clough,Farness, Higgs, Jefferson, Taylorand Thompson.
PARISH AIXTTERS DISCUSSED. THE POLLUTION OF STREAMS.

Mr. Furness thought the Parish Council ought to leave no stone unturned with a view to compelling the Warrington Corporation to do all they possibly could to obviate the danger of any pollution of Whittle Brook by allowing the sewage of the sanatorium to enter the brook'. There was very little nuisance at present, but there had been a great fresh of water in the brook and this had kept it clear. But what would happen in the summer months when the brook was nearly dry? A large number of the cattle drank out of the brook, and it was a horrible thing to conceive that they had to consume milk from cattle who had been drinking out of a brook ,into which flowed sewage from a smallpox hospital. He thought the Parish Council had been lacking in not insisting upon the Rural Coun- cil taking some action in the matter. Then he thought the Council had been very remiss with regard to Sankey Brook. It was common knowledge that a large portion of the sewage of the Corporation of Warrington was discharged into Sankey Brook, and the Rural Council ought to insist upon the Corporation taking some steps .to stop this pollution. (Hear, hear.) He would also like to call attention to the inadequate sanitary arrange- ments in the Hood-lanellistrict. Mr, Halton said he would like to ask Mr. Furness from what source he had got his information with refer- ence to the pollution of Whittle Brook? I Mr. Farness: From my own observations. _ _
Mr. Halton: You are evidently not aware that the Corporation are treating their sewage in a proper manner before letting it enter the brook. _ .

Mr. Furness: I vry much question that. Mr. Halton, referring to Sankey Brook said the Council had been endeavouring to stop the pollution there for a number of years. There had scarcely been a meeting of the Rural Council lately at which the matter had not been mentioned, and he could assure the meeting that there was not one quarter the amount of pollution that took place twelve months ago in the brook. The Corporation had stopped turning the crude matter into it at Longford, and were also tapping their sewers at Lovely lane. In time he thought the nuisance would be remedied. With regard to the sanitary arrangements in Hood-lane and district, that was a, matter which had been on the tapis at the Rural Coun- cil meetings for some years. These matters could not all be done at once, and if they looked through the Rural Council's work for the past three years they would find that Sankey had had more done for it than any other place in the district. It was absolutely wrong to say that the Rural Coun- cil had neglected their duty with reference to Whittle Brook, as the Corporation had laid down septic tanks, and filtering apparatus at the Sanatorium, the result of which was that there was no danger whatever of pollution. If there was any danger he ought to be the first to complain, as his cattle drank from the brook, and he used the ,milk. He might mention that at the Council meeting held prior to Volt meeting he alluded to the pollution of Sankey Brook, The Rural Council had decided to issue warning notices to the manufac- turers Who were tipping refuse on the embankments near Fox-street and allowing the refuse to fall into Sankey Brook. As their representative on the Rural Council he (Mr. Halton) had done all he possibly could to remedy the evils spoken of, and had time after time been called over the coals for bringing Sankey matters up so frequentlyat the Council meeting. (liehr2 hear.) Mr. Furness said he did not consider the methods of filtration at the Sanatorium at all satisfactory. Mr. Thompson said he would also like to defend him- self. He was a member of the Parish Council, and had done everything he possibly could with reference to Sankey Brook. So far as the Sanatorium was con- cerned, he was one who helped to fight the matter at the Town Hall. They went into the sewage question, and at their request the Local Government Board inspector met them on the spot, and gave them his assurance that the sewage water turned into the brook would do no harm whatever to cattle or anything else. The filtrittion, he said, would be so perfect that they

div.head: Grappenhall,
div.p: Grappenhall,

The annual parish meeting was held in. the school- room on Monday evening, Mr. J. C. Parr being in. the chair. There was a very large gathering, in fact never since the first meeting when the Parish Council was formed have so many ratepayers attended the annual meeting, and this in spite of the very bad weather. It was evident from the first that a keen contest was to take place, and this anticipation was quite justified by the result, which showed that many changes had been made. From the list appended it will be noticed that Mr. F. W. Wareing, Mr. F. It. Roberts, Mr. A. Rathbone, Mr. B. P. N.!Avory, and Mr. S, H. Jenkins, all figure as new-corners to the Council. The last named gentle- man, Mr. Jenkins, was a Councillor some years ago, until he resigned on account of having to leave the dis- trict on business. There were fifteen nominations, but two were disqualified. The election took place by show of hands, and it was found that Messrs. Spence and Smith tied by 22 votes each, for the tenth place on the list. Mr. W. Lomas with- drew his nomination, and the Chairman declared the following gentlemen duly elected councillors for the parish for the ensuing three years.—F. W. Wareing 53 votes; S. H. Jenkins, 51; Joseph Warburton, 45; B. P. N. Avory, 43; A. Rathbone, 40; F. R. Roberts, 39; J. Bradford, 26; F. Ellison, 24; T. Smith, 22; F. T. Spence, 22. Mr. W. Loinas who withdrew had received 28 votes. whilst Mr. T. ITeland received 16 and Mr. R. Boardman 15 votes only. After the election of Parish Council was over, Mr. Jenkins asked the Chairman if anaccount was to be presented to the meeting of the parochial charities. He was informed that there was no necessity to give an account of any parochial charities to the annual meeting. Mr. Jenkins disputed the point, and on the clause of the Act relating to the matter being read, the chairman allowed that Mr. Jenkins was correct, There was no account however prepared to lay before the meeting. On the motion of Mr. S. H. Jenkins. seconded by Mr. W. Lomas. a hearty vote of thanks was accorded the Chairman, and the proceedings terminated.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
WIDNES TOWN CoIINCIL.

The Mayor (Alderman S. Quinn) presided at the monthly meeting held at the Town Hall on Tuesday. Councillor Hemingway, in moving the Health. Com- mittee's minutes reported that the hospital was almost empty, and the smallpox hospital had been emptied. No fresh cases had been notified. The Finance Com- mittee submitted estimates for the borough rate for the ensuing twelve months. These totalled up to £14,624,a net increase on last year of £2,420. CAMDEN P.S.E. MEETING.

Mr. Unsworth presided at the weekly meeting of the above, and an entertainment which was received with cordial appreciation was given by the Misses Water- worth and M. Whynyates, Masters Brimelow and Whyn- yatessnd Messrs. E. Johnson, J. Leathwood, J. Hewitt and J. Johnson. Master Brimelow sang the song for which he received a silver medal at the Widnes Eisteddfod. The accompanist was Miss Waterworth.

div.head: RUNCORN* BOATING CLUB.
div.p: RUNCORN* BOATING CLUB.

The-officers of this club for the ensuing season will be: President, Sir Richard Brooke; vice-presidents, Sir J. T. Brunner and Colonel Hall Walker; captain, Mr. J. W. Wiswell, sub-captain, Mr. R. Johnson ' • treasurer, Mr. H. G. Johnson; secretary, Mr. W. A. Millinger ; and committee, Messrs. F. Abel, R. Benyon, H. Harvey, J. Peacock, J. G. Millington, J. Savage, R. P. Johnson and H. Jones. ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT RUNCORN.

On Monday, at Runcorn, David Martin-, --ii sailor. of Belfast, was charged with attempting to commit suicide in the Bridgewater Canal on Friday. William Green, carpenter to the Ship Canal Company, deposed to seeing the prisoner jump into the Ropewalk Basin. As soon as he get into the water the prisoner struggled to the side, and witness helped him out.—The prisoner's brother, who had journeyed from Belfast. said his mother, who was nearly ninety years of age, was very much upset, and he pleaded to the bench to allow him to take his brother home to Ireland.—Mr. Shaw, 'sea- men's missionary, said the prisoner, had been twenty years an abstainer,and therefore the cause was not drink.—The bench remanded the prisoner.

div.head: -._..,---- ST. HELENS.
div.p: -._..,---- ST. HELENS.
131JRNING FATALITY.

On Monday night Frederick Turton, age thres years, son of George Anderson, Athol-street, Earlestown, died from burns receive in the afternoon. The child's clothes caught fire, and, going to a bed on which an infant lay, was the means of the bedclothes getting alight. The infant had a narrow escape of being burnt as well. ST. HELENS LOVERS' QUARRF.L.

At St. Helens, on Tuesday, a young man, named Bennison, employed at a fruiterer's shop in Peter- street, who had been paying his addresses to a young woman named Brady, quarrelled with her, and Benaison, taking out a rAzor, attacked her and cut her throat and then his own. The girl was not very seriously injured, but the man is in a precarious condition. Both were conveyed to the hospital.

div.head: NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL ELECTIONS.
div.p: NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL ELECTIONS.

Thursday was the last day for the nominations of candidates for the above election, and the result shows that there are contests in two wards oßly, viz., Viaduct and Town Hall. In the former, in consequence of the removal of Mr. J. W. Emmett J.P., from the district, there are two candidates for the vacancy, Mr. W. Beatty of the "Griffin" Hotel, and Mr. E. Worsley, Insurance Agent, Earlestown. In the Town Hall Ward, the retiring member is Dr. Latham and his re-election is being opposed by Mr. John Naylor of the Swan Inn, Newton Common. ,The following is a list of the nominations

Crow-lane Ward.—C. B. F. Borron, The Heights, Golborne, glass bottle manufacturer; proposed by George Goff, seconded by Eli Bunting. Newton Ward.—Lionel Edward Pilkington, The Woodlands, Ashton-road, Newton-le-Willows, colliery proprietor; proposed by Robert Stone, seconded by Walter Stone. Town Hall Ward.—Walter Latham, 86, Cross- lane, Earlestown, medical practitioner, proposed by C. J. Mouncey, seconded by John Potter. div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. --- Rugby Football. By " Ovalist."
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. --- Rugby Football. By " Ovalist."

Last Saturday's ma- tch must be relegated to the background this week to allow cup-tie anticipations to take the premier place. The luck of the draw has been experienced in several places but not at War- rington, who generally get quite as much as they bargain for in the preliminary encounters. The pleasure of entertaining one of those junior teams who are in the competition at the start seldom seems to be Warrington's lot, and the best that could be hoped for was an at home fixture with one of the senior clubs. Even this has been denied, and Warrington have to travel to-day to Swinon,a.district usually fatal to their hopes. Still Fate might have been more unkind -- Swinton and Warrington have met twice this sea- son already and each meeting has emphasized the superiority of the " wirepullers." At Wilderspoll in October Warrington beat the Blues by 10 points to three, while only three weeks ago they made a draw at the colliery village, and had much the better of the day's play. In both encounters, be it noted, Swinton have only once penetrated the Warrington defence. There is therefore good ground for hopefulness in to- day's encounter. I certainly consider that the odds are slightly on the side of the Swintonians, for play- ing at home means a lot in cup-ties. Warrington will, however, have a large following and by sheer determination they should succeed in at least drawing ' the match. In point of weight there is not much to choose between the teams, both of whom favour the open game, but on a decent turf Warrington should prove the epeedier.

For two or three weeks Warrington have been steadily training, and the condition of the men is said to have improved considerably. This week, full teams were out on Tuesday and Thursday, and with every man fit, Warrington should be able to place their strongest fifteen in the field. And Warrington's strongest team should not be behind at Swinton if this season's form is anything to go by. In regard to the attack there are one or two poipts which the players should bear in mind. The wing man is frequently bored into touch, or thoroughly cornered, and yet he seldom thinks of passing inside again to the centre. A judicious return of this kind, before the wing man has gone too far, would probably result in a score,and it is well worth studying to-day, for Fish is going to be paid special attention to. Gartrell has had instructioneto fairly shadow the left-winger and his success in the mud three weeks ago doubtless has filled him with the idea that he can bottle up the re- sourceful Fish. Granted we have dry turf, and Fish ought to be able, one way or another, to open the Cumberland youth's eyes a bit. He probably formed rather a false estimate of the Warrington crack on that rainy day at Swinton. Jack has been rather quiet of late, and if he should come out of his shell to-day it would fairly delight his admirers. They are never so pleased at his success as when there is some obvious shadowing going on.

The Swinton directors picked their team early and the Cup-tie fifteen will be: Chorley, full back ; Hampson, Traynor, Dixon, and Gartrell, threequarters; Molyneux and Wallwork, half-backs; J. Evans, J. Preston, T. Pomfret, R. Tickle,' W. Cheetham, H. Barnett, J. Smith, and W. Simister, forwards. Pomfret has since been suspended, and a substitute will have to be placed in the forward rank.
The draw, for the first round of the Cup-ties is as follows : Swinton v. Warrington. Pontefract v. Brighouse Rangers. Barrow V. Bramley. Dewsbury v. Hunslet. Huddersfield v. Wigan. Hull' v. Widnes.

Lancaster v. Keighley. Halifax v. St. Helens. Brookland Rovers v. Salford. York v. Bradford. Holbeck v. Birkenhead. Parton v. Broughton Rangers. Rochdale H. v. Leigh. Runcorn v. Wakefield Trinity. Batley v. Oldham. Hull Kingston Rovers v. Leeds. Matches to be played on the ground of the first. named clubs.

Warrington's form at Oldham on Saturday was encouraging. They held their own comfortably on the general run of the play, and with any luck would have won.. Fish, for instance, worked his way over in the first five minutes, but was judged to have been held inside. In the end Oldham won by 10 points to eight, each side scoring two. tries. Dickenson and Boardman were the try-getted for Warrington. A dropped-goal and a penalty goal gave Oldham the victory, and they must have been glad when the end came, for Warrington were pegging away near the home line in most determined fashion. The work of the Warrington three-quarters was superior to any- thing on the Oldham side, but the homesters had a useful pull in the scrummage.

The League table underwent no important chanae I on Saturday as both Bradford and Salford won and still tie for premier position. Broughton Rangers and Leeds each dropped a point, at Widnes and Wigan respectively. The League table up-to-date, is as follows : For. Against. P. W. L. D. G. T. P. G. T. P. The honourable part Archie Rigg has played in Rugby football was substantially recognised on Saturday. After the match with Leigh, the popular Halifax player was the recipient of a cheque for £2OO, the result of his recent benefit tnatch,and an illuminated address. The address contains the following Your skilful exposition on the football field, both for your club and county, has made you deservedly popular wherever you have played, and the high position attained by you on the field of sport generally has long been the adinimtion of all. Added to this,your gentlernanly conduct on and off the field has gained the respect of friend and opponent alike. We desire to place on record the invaluable services you have rendered to this club, both as a player for 13 years and captain of the football team for three separate seasons.

William HeNor, of South Shields, who has acted as captain for the Northumberland and Durham team, has signed on for Wigan. Hector, who can play in the positions of either centre three-quarter or full- back, is 23 years of age, and nearly six feet high.

The Warrington team is practically the same as last week, the only changes being Swift and Fairhurst for Edmondson and Lunt in the forwards. The full fif- teen is : Hallam, full back; Fish, Isherwood, Dickenson, and Harris, threequarters ; Davies and Bate half backs; Boardman, Swift, Fairhurst. Thomas Cook, Naylor, Jolley and Harmer forwards. DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MR. R. CHANDLEY .EAELESTOWN.

Mr. R. Chandley, ;TIC.' for several years was head- master at the Wargrave Schools, died on Tuesday morning last after a short illness at the age of 52 years. For the past three years he has been in failing health, but it was only recently that he became seri- ously ill, and last week it was found necessary to call in a specialist, who after examination could hold out po hope of recovery.—Mr. Chandley, who leaves a widow, but no family, comes. of ?n old Earlestown family and was an enthusiastic cricketer, his earlier ;years being spent in that connectior!with the St. Helens Cricket Club, he being 'at that time master at the Windle Schools. When be left to take up the position at Wargrave he joined the Newtoi! Cricket Club, and played for several years with unvarying success, being at one time vice-captain.—The funeral took place oh Thursday afternoon at Wargrave. Church, the deceased having been a member of the choir. The distance from his late residence was very short, and the coffin was borne through the rectory grounds by members of the i Newton Cricket Club. The service n the church was con- ducted by the Revs. J. Carson and T. R. Matthews, and the choir sang the well-known hymn "Peace perfect peace," Mr. George Kidd presiding at the organ.—The coffin was carried to the grave by old members of the choir. and around the grave were Mr. Philip Chandley,brother Mr. H. Molyneux and family and other relatives, be- sides representatlbes of the School Management, Com- mittee and the Newton Cricket and Bowling Club. The church was crowded with a sympathetic congregation, and numerous sympathisers filled the church yard.A large number of floral wreaths were sent, but only the one from the widow was placed on the coffin.

div.head: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.
div.p: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.

The present day walking skirt of Tweed ot cloth requires the wearer thereof to display particular neatness about the feet, which are easily visible, as the hem is so cut as to cleat the ground all round with a tendency to be, if anything, a little shorter at the back than the front. It is, therefore, only an exceedingly ill-advised woman who will venture out of doors with anything except trim, well-fitting shoes or boots. Englishwomen are, I -am glad to say, paying more attention to lheir foot- gear than they used to, with the result that the elegant toilettes worn are no longer spoilt by clumsy or untidy shoes. A really well- turned-out woman devotes as much thought and care to the selection of the details and accessories of dress as she does to the dress itself, for in these very trifles often lies the success of the tout ensemble. It is important as well to be not only smartly !gowned, but to suit the dress to our circumstances and the occasion. It is by no means the most elaborately dressed woman that is the most admired, as a plainly cut gown, if well-fitting and of a becoming colour, will often render
A PRETTY BLOUSE 4

the wearer distinguished-looking amongst a crowd of much more expensively dressed women. The modes of to-day are so unre- stricted that there is plenty of opportunity for the exercise of individual taste.

The pretty blouse sketched is made of cream washing silk and is trimmed with bands of open patterned white lace, finished at the edges by narrow ribbon-edging. The band down the front is very wide, and gives a hand- some look to the blouse, while the sleeves fit the upper part of the arm closely and are full at the wrists, in the manner of all the, smartest blouses. The neck is fini§.hed by a trans- parent collar of the lace, wired to keep it in place; and here it is worth while noting that all the newest blouses are made with very high collars of this style. Some of the collars are, indeed, too high to be really comfortable. As some people object to this lack of freedom for the throat, a modified form of the Medici

div.head: AN ELEGANT COAT 4
div.p: AN ELEGANT COAT 4

collar has been introduced. This arrange- ment leaves the throat uncovered in front except for a piece of velvet or a pearl collar, while at the back a pleating of lace tulle or chiffon gives a finish and can be wired or allowed to fall softly as preferred. In no in- stance is this pleating deep. It is a very becoming fashion for anyone with a long throat, but should not be affected by a short- necked woman, whose lack of throat it would only emphasize. This mode is a revival of a becoming fashion, and will remain in modistic favour during the season.

For evening wear nothing could be more elegant than the coat whose fascinations are portrayed in my second sketch. It is made of fine-faced cloth and lined with wadded silk, and is most comfortable for theatre or restau- rant wear. The cape is bordered with soft fur and embellished with beautiful embroidery in silk and chenille. The collar is of stitched velvet of a ruddy brown, which contrasts charmingry with the champagne tint of the cloth. The fronts are thrown open to show

gimilar embroidery to that on the cape, while the deep gauntlet cuffs are also trimmed in the same way and are bordered with fur 4 There is nothing very 'elaborate about the coat, which is semi-fitting, but the effect is al- together up-to-date and modish. Theatres are, to my mind, both chilly and draughty, and when a decollete toilette -is worn a coat or cloak is necessary if one wishes to avoid the dire consequences of a chill. Nowadays, there is a strong tendency to follow the exam- ple of the Parisiennes, and wear a high derni- toilette, both in ths theatre and restaurant. It is a vastly mot' sensible plan, especially when so many people take advantage of pub- lic conveyances for travelling to and from town. A pretty, fussy toilette always looks nicer at this season of the year when the shoul- ders of the wearer are comfortably covered. This, of course, does not refer to social engage- ments at our own or at our friends' private residences.

The first inkling of the spring fashions is always first apparent in the realms of millinery as the early gleams oi sunshine bring a corres- pondino. touch of brightness in our headgear and early svring flowers or bows of gaily hued ribbon are introduced to lighten the sombre- ness of our attire. The smart hat sketched is descriptive of the inclination towardsi bright- ness, and is made of burnt straw and trimmed with crimson roses and their foliage. It is always in golden yellow or burnt straw. that the first models are exploited for this tint is light and yet not too summer-like when pro- perly treated and trinamedi

div.head: THURSDAY'S LIBERAL MEET!NG.
div.p: THURSDAY'S LIBERAL MEET!NG.
Ftwther [Speeches. by Mr. Arthur,i "..Crosiield and Mr. J. Howes.

IThe National School, Church-street, was filled to its utmost capacity on Thursday evening when another meeting, promoted by the Liberal Association, was held. Captain G. R. Crosfield presided, and he was supported by Mr. A. H. Ciosfield, Mr. Joseph Howes, Mr. C. E. Parker, Alderman Pierpoint, Councillors Tinnion, Maginn, James Evans, and Wilkinson, Mr. C. Jackson Holmes, and others. The CHAIRMAN, in introducing Mr. Howe, said he was sure that his eloquence would convince anys waverersi that Free Trade was the thing for thi country. When they reflected on the artificial disadvantages that this country had laboured under compared with others, the bad patent laws, the unexploited internal communications, the mining royalties, and the want of proper scientific management on the part of so many of our industries, surely they must see that the only thing which had en- abled us to adva"nce in the way we had done was Free Trade. (Applause.) He believed in protection of a certain kind. He believed in protecting the education of the country—by that he meant taking care of tit. What was more, he believed in protection of the physique of the nation—(hear, hear)—that was, he be- lieved in taking care of the bodies of the workers by seeing that they got good food and plenty of it. (Ap- plause.) He was not in favour of anything which mili- tated against that, and he was sure all those present were not. (Applause.) Mr. A. H. CROSFIELD moved a similar resolution to the one adopted on Wednesday evening condemning the Government's policy and affirming belief in the benefits of Free Trade. He had, he said, had the pleasure of attending a great many political meetings in Warring- ' ton in his time, but he had never seen so strongly marked and intense enthusiasm as was manifested at the big meeting they held in the Parr Hall on Wednesday night. He had no doubt that if they had had a larger room that night, knowing who was going to address the meeting, they would very easily have filled it. (Hear, hear.) In regard to national expendititure,certainly was rather astoun4ing, if they came to consider it, how a few years of Tory Government had been sufficient to sweep away all the savings which British 4t atesmanship had effected for thirty or forty years. When he said British statesmanship, he meant the genuine article— (hear, hear,)—and not the Brummagem imitation— (laughter)—he meant the stately edifice of forethought, wisdom and prudence, and not the jerry-built imitation that was foisted upon them, with alterations patched in it every other month of the year. In the next Government, which he saw from the previous night's debate Mr. Balfour anticipated would be a Liberal Government (hear, hear,) —undoubtedly economy would be one of the most pressing questions that the Liberal party would have to consider—economy and efficiency. He felt that at the present stage of national affairs, economy in itself would not suffice; and he thought the \reckless extravagance they had had to face—the distribiltion of doles here and doles there and all the waste of the national resources during late years—had brought much more prominently to the front the question that had been in their minds for many a year,. but which they would now have to give practical

effect to—that was tapping fresh sources -of revenue— (hear; hear)—useful in themselves for the purposes of revenue, but useful also in no less a degree because of the effect they would have upon the physique and di. well-being of the whole of the people. He referred to the necessity of dealing justly and fairly,but thoroughly.with the question of the taxation of land values. (Applause.) Of course, the main purpose of that meeting was the great Free Trade issue which had been joined, and he could quote them from a speech which their member made the other night, a statement that if they went in for the Protectionist policy, they would not increase the food bill of a single ramily in this town. He thought, with all respect to Mr. Pierpoint,that he must fancy they were a great parcel of simpletons if they were going to swallow stuff of that sort. (Laughter.) It was all very well for certain manufacturers who were interested, not in protecting all the stuff that they used—oh no !—they wanted their cheap steel billets coming in, but they wanted to pick out certain finished manufactured articles to increase their profits. It was all very well for men taking that point of view to rivet their attention upon it, but they must never forget for a moment that when once they put their feet on the ! slippery slope of Protection, there was no stopping. If they were going to give Protection to manufactured articles, the great agricultural interest of England i which, after all, was the backbone of the Conservative party,would uot stand it for an instant, unless they got the wholesale protection of food—and to do their member credit, he went in for it. The Tories told them that they had no alternative policy,—that they only went in for laissez-faire. Believe him, that was not true. They heard on Wednesday night a pointed and powerful reference to the intolerable handicap that there was upon our industaies in many cases where the mining royalties amounted to an embargo of ss. or Gs. per ton on the manufactured articles. They i were quite prepared to look into questions of that kind. I (Applause.) They were quite prepared to look into the question Of freights and railway rates—(hear. hear)— and if anybody could find what they never had found. and what they would not find—an instance of an organ- ized attack by a foreign trust upon an industry that was natural to this country, with a view to crushing that industryand raising prices afterwards—they would be quite prepared to deal with that—(applause)—when , the time came, but let the Tories give them the instance first. (Hear. hear.) They must not let them draw red herrings across the trail to confuse;the issue, which, to do them justice, those Tory gentlemen who spoke at the Parr Hall made very clear aud very significant to every man in the town. One would have thought they would -have been content with that, but they knew the old saying of the ancients "Whom the gods wish to destroy they first render crazy" (Laughter). To his mind it was a piece of amazing audacity that the Government should havedared to take a step which, if it were fol- lowed kip, would inevitably create in the Transvaal a ' great slave state in the British empire. (Applause). He ventured to think that many of their Ccnservative friends, even in Warrington,looking back on the patience the courage,and the tenacity with which our army fought our battles out ' ther4ind pulled us out of a very tight place;looking back upon the plucky and able work which , that very distinguished soldier Lord Roberts did for the empire—(applause)—must begin to ask themselves now whether, after all, the game was quite worth the candle, whether we sacrificed all those lives and spent all that money in order to supplant British labour, of whatever colour, by the introduction of Chinese labour under conditions which he would not attempt to des- cribe, because there was a forcible and eloquent descrip- tion from Mr. Howes which, he thought, would go home into the minds of every intelligent man, be he artizan or employer, in the town. (Applause.) In conclusion, Mr. Crosfield said that to all Liberals who took any responsible part in the conduct of the party's affairs in the town, it did their hearts' good to see there was a real, healthy feeling springing up, that thero was a tend- ency to re-union amongst all ranks of the progressive party and,. he thought, a determination to put an end to the domination of a rather reactionary party which they had had to face for so many years in our town. (Cheers.) Mr. JOSEPH HOWES supported the resolution, and went fully into the fiscal question, giving further re- plies to arguments advanced at the Tory meeting. We could, he said, beat the world despite the tariffs if we dealt with internal reforms instead of being dragged away on the false scent of Protection. (tileers.) The resolution was carried unanimously.

Aidernlatt PIERPOINT moved a vote a thanks to the speakers, and alluded to the necessity for a change in the representation of Warrington. contending that the home and foreign policy of the Government had been of a most disastrous character. Urging his hearers not to support a reversion to Protection, the alderman said he could recollect in the days before tho abolition of the Corn Laws when Warrington was suffering the most intense poverty, when there was hunger in nearly every house, when wages were low. and a shop opposite that very building was broken into by ;starving men who wanted to obtain food for their families. He could remember when the highest wages paid in the Warrington tanneries were 12s. per week. They had an expert who came from London and he received 18s. He claimed that all the increased comforts of life had been brought about through the operations of Free Trade. (Applause). Councillor MAGINN seconded, and pointed out that he did not speak to them as a member of any political party, but as an independent citizen. The motion was heartily carried, and the Chairman having been thanked for presiding, the meeting con- cluded.

MR. A. H. GROSFIELD AND THE IRON TRADE.

MR. WILLIAM LONG RE-ENTERS THE LIBERAL RANKS. Further unmistakable evidence of the vitality of I stronger character—(hear, hear)—and if Mr. Balfour Liberalism in Warrington was afforded or Thufsday 1 could only get them to say they were going in for i fiscal reform, he would very soon land them in full- evening, when the Parr Hall was crowded to over- fledged Protection. One thing which he thought had flowing with an interested and enthusiastic audience ' been very cruelly introduced into the controversy was which had assembled to hear replies to the recent I the accusationagainst John Bright and Richard Cobden, Tory-Protectionist oratory in the same building when that infighting the battle of Free Trade they were adopt. Sir Howard Vincent, M.P. was the principal ing a selfish way of getting labour on the cheap for their Sir J. T. Brunner, 'M.P., had been announced to speak, mills. He called that a cruel libel on the men— but to the disappointment of all, important (applause)—and Lancashire, he hoped, would repel it with all tthhoeuschotrnathat was Ams i boll, becausen their Joseph Howes, who is well known to Warrington Richard Cobden. (Cheers). Mr. Long proceeded to P audiences as an able exponent of Free Trade principles quote from a speech of Cobden's which controverted delivered a stirring address in characteristic Style. He the idea that Protection and high prices would increase had no difficulty in proving the hollowness of the the wages of workmen and labourers. "These un- Protectionist proposals, and the cheers with which his fortunate men" said Cobden, "are told that their ivcilgl Nlsillitribs riiicieho f .provisions .advanc(ps. speech was punctuated showed how the viast audience rise as because thee l'. price ?sr fltrovflrsotmonspuinre- was in sympathy with the views he so admirably creases s the demand for labgouf expressed. Mr. William Long J.P., received a cordial charity? The rate of wages has no more connection welcome on his re-appearance in the Liberal ranks and, with the price of food than the moon's changes." (Hear as chairman,opened the meeting with a closely-reasoned hear and laughter.) Again speaking for the abolition speech on the all-absorbing fiscal question. The of the Corn Laws, Cobden said " When Igo down to the resolution condemning the Government's policy and manufacturing districts I know that I shall be return- affirming adherence to Free Trade was carried with I ing to great enthusiasm and practically unanimously. The time before the commencement of the meeting was pleasantly whiled away iii singing a num- ber of topical songs. The "Liberal parch " went with a rare swing to the inspiriting strains of the" March of the men of Harlech," and another popular chorus was "Stamp, stamp, stamp, upon Protection" which was given with much hearti- ness. Mr. J. Rabbitt and Mr. George Wallington led the singing and Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus.- Bac., presided at the organ
A GLOOMY SCI.

I know that starvation is stalking through the land,and that men are perishing for want of the merest neces- saries of life. When I witness this, and recall that there is a law which especially _provides for keening our population in absolute want,l cannot help attribut- ing murder to the Legislature of this country, and wherever I stand—indoors or out of doors—l will denounce that system of legitimate murder. You must not tax the people's bread." Their opponents, continued Mr. Long, were very fond of twitting them with having no programme to bring forward to amend what the American would call the present slump in labour—the backwarding of trade. What war had ever gone on as long as the South African cam- paign,—costing us something over 200 millions of money,—without the country afterwards feeling the reaction? The war was the cause of their bad trade. (Applause). Did they, in addition to bad trade, want to return to the conditions of Cobden's time? No. Let them keep their trade and their open markets, and let them remember that there was too much of THE POLICY•OF GREID. about the question of Protection (Applause). It was not a question that would affect the stomachs of the wealthier men. But how would the working classes feel an addition of a few shillings a week to their food bill? The increase would not stop at three farthings. Liberals could point to many improvements that could be made in the existing state of affairs. They did not believe England was the best of possible worlds. The Associated Chambers of Commerce, which were meeting in London this week, had for years past been trying to urge upon the Government the necessity of better attention to the trade and commerce of the country than it had received in the past. The canalisa- tion of the country was another point upon which a Government department might help them very much, and the excessive railway rates also needed alteration. (Applause.) There were many matters of that kind which the Government might take up, but they wanted more hard-headed business men in the Cabinet. (Applause.) At present, he did not believe there were two members of the Cabinet whom they could recognize as good business men. They would never get legislation such as England needed unless they had men of stability, business knowledge, and tact. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Long quoted from a speech by Mr. Lloyd George, who, he said, ought to be well known to Warrington men, as on• of their employers had gone to wrest his seat from him. (Laughter.) In conclusion he said they could not meddle with Free Trade without breaking into an endless muddle. Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Cobden re- moved the last shackles from the imports in this country. As far as he could remember, between 1100 and 1200 articles were affected, from the pepper that appeared on ttie breakfast table to the smallest things they could imagine. The expenses of collecting the I duty were great, apart from the irritation and annoy- ance to the people—in fact a great deal of it was hardly worth the collection. He had now pleasure in calling upon the gentleman who, they hoped, would soon be their member, Mr. Arthur Crosfield—(cheers)—to address the meeting.

The following were present on the platform ;—Mr. W. Long, J.P. (presiding), Mr. A. HI Crosfield, Mr. C. E. Parker, Mr. Joseph Howes, Mr. T. Birchall, J.P., Alderman Pierpoint, J.P., Councillors D. Tinnion, James Evans, Thomas Barton, Peter Peacock, John Wilkinson, John Maginn, D. S. Duncan, and Thomas Burton, Mr. S. Wright, J.P., Mr. W. Furness, Mr. C. Jackson Holmes, (hon. sec.)' Mr. Nathan Cook, Revs. G. H. Carnson, J. S. Hughes, J. F. Matthews, J. S. Milne, C. Harvey Cook, John Davies, W. J. Roberts Miss Crosfield, Miss Bessie Dutton, Mesdames, C. E. Parker, W. ;Pierpoint, J. Howes, C. J. Holmes, W. Furness, Clay, Osborne, Simpson, Haigh, Barton, Bridgewater, Afillington, and A. G. Webster; Misses, Pierpoint, Walker, Captain G. R. Haigh, Joseph Elwell, Thomas Knowles, George Walker, A. Scriven, H. White, W. Miles, J. Woods, A. Connor, G. Morrall, J. Dolan, B. P. Williams, W. Hayes, G. Pendlebury, J. W. Jowett, W. F. Birch, F.
