SIR J. T. BRUNNER'S ABSENCE. AN IMPORTANT DIVISION. Mr. C. JACKSON HOLMES said he regretted very much that the first apology for non-attendance was from Sir John Brunner. It read: "Gladstone forbids me ab- senting myself to-morrow. Very sorry to be prevented coming to you. BRUNNER." Mr. Gladstone was tele- graphed to twice by Mr. Crosfield,to see if the necessary permission could be granted to Sir John, but he wired back" Division to-morrow night of great importance. Much regret cannot meet your wishes, as the presence of Liberal members here is of great importance." (Applause). Continuing, Mr. HOLMES said that Mrs. Crosfield regretted very much her inability to attend, but he was pleased to see Miss Crosfield on the platform. (Ap- plause.) The Rev. John Yonge wrote explaining that he would be attending Congregationalist meetings at Blackburn on Wednesday and Thursday. He hoped the Liberal meeting would be most successful. (Applause.) Letters of apology for non-attendance had also been received from the Rev. H. Wall, Mr. J. G. Withinshaw, Mr. G. W. Rawlins, Mr. James Horton, Mr. R. G. Henshall, and Mr. B. Percival. In his letter the Rev. H. Wall said "Protection is not reform, but retro- gress.'" Mr. Withinshaw wrote " I trust you will have a first rate meeting and strike a good blow against veiled slavers and Protection." Mr. Rawlins expressed the opinion that the old Free Trade principles which had so far advanced the prosperityof the country would weather the storm raised in Birmingham. THE CHAIRMAN'S ADDRESS. WHAT PROTECTION MEANS TO WORKERS. The CHAIRMAN, who was received with cheers and the singing of "Auld Lang Syne ", said that when the committee of the Liberal Association honoured him by an invitation to preside at that meeting, it might per- haps have been cowardly, but he was obliged to own in truth that the position had no attractions for him. The reason was that when a man had been absent from a party or a political platform for some eighteen years, he began, at his time of life,to lose the zest for that kind of thing. On second thought,and remembering the crisis in which he considered the country now stood, he thought better of the matterand decided that he would come among his old Warrington friends once more. (Cheers). Another fact that helped him to come to that decision waa that the old family of the Crosfields, as he knew them in days gone by, were always to the fore in any public work for Warrington—(hear, hear)— and he felt he would be unworthy of his memories of them, if he did not come forward to support as well as he could, the son of his old friend, Mr. John Crosfield, in his work amongst them. (Cheers). Less than a fort- night ago Sir Howard Vincent, Sir H. Seton Karr, their borough member and others were giving them one side of the great Free Trade question. Agreat many of those present in the hall that night were perhaps not old enough to remember the big struggle of the early forties, and to know something either from their own observation, or from what they bad heard from their fathers, of the condition of trade in England at that date. Lord Rosebery said a short time ago that if only the older men would attend meetings and give the people of two generations later than themselves some idea of what life was in those days, it would do more good than a great deal of ornamental speaking. (Hear, hear.) He (Mr. Long) remembered when their own workmen at Grappenhall tannery were receiving from 12s. to 14s. up to

div.head: 18s. PER WEEK,
div.p: 18s. PER WEEK,

and food was much dearer than it was. to-day. The men doing the same class of work would now be getting from to 30s. per week, and he would leave them to judge how much difference that made. He was very pleased to see present a great many of the gentler sex. The fiscal policy was even more a question for them than for the bread-winners. Reverting to the visit of Sir Howard Vincent,' it was not very long ago— only about twelve months—that no one would hardly have dared to come before a Lancashire audience and stand up for Protection. (Hear, hear.) He supposed Sir Howard Vincent had been at this work, ploughing his solitary furrow for some time, with the help of two or three others, one of whom was their somewhat anti- quated friend Mr. Chaplin—(laughter)---and another, Sir H. Seton Karr. Those men even had to banish the word Protection from their vocabulary and talk first of all about Fair Trade, and then of reciprocity. Now, by the unexampled audacity,of one man, the matter took a different form altogether. and these speakers came here fully-fledged Protectionists. Let them say what they would, the present distinct line on this question was full-fledged or " whole-hogged "Protection, They mast not be led away by

THE DRAWING BACK OF THE PRIME MINISTER. He had played fast and loose with the question quite long enough. (Hear, hear.) When Mr. Chamberlain was resigning his position in the ministry, Mr. Balfour said, in effect "I am going for something smaller than that, but if you can convince the country that a tax on food is desirable then I will go with you." It was, therefore, only a question of degree between the two. They knew who was the more self-willed man and the

div.head: MR. CROSPIELD'S SPEECH.
div.p: MR. CROSPIELD'S SPEECH.

Mr. ARTHUR CROSFIELD. who had a very cordial re ception, said he would like to express on behalf of many Liberal friends, and on his own behalf, the pleasure and.the deep satisfaction if had been to them to listen to the weighty address that had been delivered by the Chair man—(applause)—and to see Mr. Long in the chair. (Hear, hear.) He thought it was typical of the reunion of everyone who had a shred of Liberalism or pro- gressive tendency in his character, and typical also of the ye-union that was taking place in Warrington as in all parts of the country. (Cheers.) He only wished they had had the great pleasure of welcoming Sir John Brunner. (Hear, hear.) He should like just to add that so sorry was Sir John to be prevented from coining to Warrington that he telegraphed offering to come on the following Tuesday or Thursday, if the meeting could be postponed. The Liberal Executive were, however, of opinion that it was impossible to postpone the meeting at the last moment. He thought they might take it for granted that Sir John Brunner would be very pleased to come to Warrington at a later date when he was not hampered by attendance at the Commons. It was now his (Mr. Crosfield's) duty to move

div.head: RESOLUTION.
div.p: A RESOLUTION.

It read as follows: "This meeting of Free Traders views with alarm the enormous growth of our National expenditure under the present Government and with indignation the introduction into South Africa of Chinese labour under conditions that are closely akin to slavery. This meeting also strongly condemns the policy which seeks to impose a tax upon the food of ths people." (Cheers.) Their purpose that night, con- tinued Mr. Crosfield, was to reply to the Conservative speakers who were in that hall the other night. (Hear, Japan) It was a good deal easier to answer them than it was to answer the present Government— (laughter)—because as regarded the Government you certainly never knew when you had them. (Laughter.) the Government policy wobbled about from day To day, and it reminded him very much of man trying to learn to ride a bicycle. (Hear, hear.) A learner who was not accustomed to his machine swerved first in one direction and then in another, and if they cared to carry the simile a little further, they would know that whenever a man was in that unhappy and uncomfortable position, he was very certain of coming a pretty bad cropper,sooner or later. (Laughter). The Government told them that they were in favour of fiscal reform and that it meant nothing. It was just as sensible as somebody telling you to take Inedicine and not telling you what the medicine is. (Hear, hear). That night they were to address themselves to the "whole hoggers "who had been in that hall and who had given them the whole doctrine of protection. He did not know what had converted their friend Mr. Robert Pierpoint to this doctrine of Protection. He (Mr. Crosfield) expected that their member for the Boroughhad been alarmed by what had been said on THE QUESTION. OF DUMPING. They had had very emphatic declaration's in Warrington on this subject, not only by Protectionist speakers but by leading employers in the town who had made a very big bid for support amongst their employs on this very question. (Hear, hear.) Whilst in London he ' (Mr. Crosfield) had the advantage of discussing the matter with Sir James Kitson, who, as they knew,hada very wide experience of the iron trade of Great Britain. He (Mr. Crosfield) simply asked Sir James whether taking the iron trade as a whole, dumping had been an advantage or a disadvantage. Sir Jams said most dis-, tinctly in reply,that the dumping of cheap foreign semi- manufactured material had been of advantage to the iron trade as a whole. (Cheers.) Not long since they had in Warrington, Mr. Cox, the most able secretary of the Iron and Steel Workers,'who had proved that case for them up to the hilt. (Hear, hear.) Dealing with that part of the resolution referring to the

CHINESE LABOUR QUESTION IN SOUTH AFRICA, Mr. Crosfleld quoted with approval the speeches of Sir Henry Fowler and Mr. John Burns in the House of Commons on the sttbject. Sir "Henry Fowler quoted the words of Burke who said that "whatever is morally wrong cannot be politically right." He (Mr. Crosfleld) was afraid that if they included the whole House of Commons there was perhaps scarcely a statesman who could compare with Burke's mighty genius, ^ vast learning and stately eloquence, with all its wealth of imagery and splendour of diction (Cheers.) None the less. although perhaps it was more difacult for men in these dayto stand out prominent amongst their fellows owing to the ' high level of average . talents, they as Liberals might be satisfied that t hey had in the present. House of Commons probably a larger number of statesmen of all round ability than was ever contained there before. (Hear, hear.) They could not excuse themselves for lack of leading. They had plenty of able and earnest men to lead them and they could not say, as a larda

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, March 12, 1904
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, March 12, 1904

employer of labour in this town wrote him that morning "that the progressive party has got no policy." They had got leaders—(cheers)—and with all due deference to his friend who wrote him, 1 they had got a policy too. (Cheers.) There were many questions ripe for consideration. There was, for , instance, the question of the reform of the land laws. 1 (Cheers.) That was a cause sufficient in itself to rally them. (Hear, hear.) Further, there were the questions of temperance—(cheers)—and of education—(cheers.) There was also this very question of stamping out the first beginnings of this system of slavery in South Africa. (Cheers.) It seeined to him that any one of ' , these questions was good enough a cause for a progres- sive party to tight for. (Cheers.) They needed first of all to form a solid phalanx of the whole progres- sive party to resist the preposterous and pernicious fiscal proposals. (Applause.) Having made sure of the ground that had been won for them by the statesmen , who had gone before, let them press forward,determined that they would continue in the direction of orderly •and well reasoned and legitimate progress towards 1 ideals that could be realised, and towards a higher and better civilisation, carrying reforms which he ventured to say in future time the pen of the historian would delight to trace. (Loud cheers.)
MR_ HOWES REPLIES TO THE TORY SPEAKERS ADVICE TO WORKINGMEN. THE CHINESE LABOUR QUESTION.

Mr. A. flowEs, who had a hearty reception, said we had had a government in office for eight years which had done some very peculiar things, and some people seenod to be somewhat astonished at the nature of the work performed. (Laughter). The Government found the national expenditure little more than half what it had now become. The Government had succeeded in doubling it in eight years. (Hear, hear.) Then the Government on coming into office found a surplus of four millions, and in the first three years of their existence, thanks to Sir William Harcourts death duties —(ch cers)—had a surplus of nine millions. No w the sur- pluses had disappeared and deficits had taken their place. When the Government had money they gave it away to the rich—(hear, hear,)—when their foreign policy developed and they wanted money they came to the poor. (Hear, hear.) When the Government had taxes to take off they went to the mansions—(hear, hear); when they had taxes to nut on they came to the cot- tages. (Cheers.) The Government had increased the price of food enormously. By increasing the duty on tea, by increasing the price of sugar, and by increasing the price of meat one penny per pound owing to the stoppage of the importation of live cattle, every man who spent a sovereign on food received two shillings' worth less food than he did before the Government came into office. (Cheers.) That meant that working- men who earned a sovereign had had to sub- mit to a ten per cent. reduction from the Chancellor of the Eichequer. Our liabilities in conse- quence of the 'Government's colonial and foreign pelicy had been appalling. We knew now what we went to war in South Africa for (Hear hear). We knew now why we spent 200 millions of monoy,and poured out the life blood of our brave sons. Some people did not profess to know it when the war wis going on. Some did (Hear, hear). There were a few men who went about the country stating the truth. They were called Pro- Boers. Now we knew that all they said had literally come to pass,unfortunately. Such was the present con- dition of things—national expenditure doubled,taxation made much heavier, the burdens of the people in- creased, the purchasing power of the worker pulled down, foreign cemolications created and inten sifted, and slavery introduced into British dominions (Applause.) After all that, they had Mr. Chamberlain and Sir Howard Vincent telling them that trade was in a deplorable condition. (Laughter.) If all they said. was true it was not to be wondered at. (Loud laughter.) Eight years of Toryism was enough to destroy any- thing. (Hear, hear,) He did not wonder at things being bad; he wondered that the Tories had the impudence to admit it. (Laughter.) But unfortunately after creating a great deal of the poverty that existed the Tories proposed to use that condition of poverty as a plea for placing us in a deeper condition of degrada tion, for they asked us to return to protection (Cheers). The gentleman who was the central figure at the Tory meeting in that hall a short time ago told them that he came as a business man to talk to business men on business matters. (Laughter:) Nothing was funnier than to be introduced to • SIR HOWARD VINCENT AS A BUSINESS MAN.

The London " Daily News "had given them some idea of Sir Howard Vincent's business con' nections. It appeared fthat he was a director of four concerns. One of them—the Eastern Investment Company—was interested in South Africa., That was what one would expect after reading Sir Howard Vin- cent' speeches. (Hear, hear, and laughter). Sir Howard also owned claims in the Western district of the Trans- vaal, and was a director of a South Africm shipping company, whose dividends were ,limited to ten per cent. (Laughter). He was the only protectionist director of Hadftelds Limited which had been paying 25 per cent. The audience would gather from this, that trade had not altogether disappeared. There werea few prosperous companies still left and this gentleman had managed to •onnect himself with a few of them. (Laughter.) Sir Howard' Vincent told them some curious things. They were asked once more to reopen and discuss the ques tion of protection—a subject which many of them thought was closed for ever. (Hear, hear.) Now that they were asked to resuscitate the corpse of protection they came across some interesting matters. It reminded him of the story of the Irishman, who, having pulled a body out of the canal, was called upon to appear at the Coroner's inquiry. When asked by the Coroner whether he did anything to resuscitate the corpse he replied "Yes, yer honour, I remember I did; I felt in both his pockets." (Loud laughter.) If they allowed anyone to resuscitate the corpse of protection it would be on the principle of feeling in both their pockets. (Loud laughter.) Sir Howard Vincent commenced the argumentative part of his speech by referring to the prosperity this country had experienced. Even protec- tionists had to admit that. " We have made progress during the last 50 years," said Sir Howard Vincent, "but the progress has not been equal to the progress of other nations, notably the United States of America, under an entirely different commercial system." He (Mr. Howes) noted that protectionists were fond of comparing this island with the United States of America. Before the protectionists could make out a case they would have to find some protected country better off than Free Trade Britain. (Hear, hear.) If ever they were able to find a protectionist country better off than ours they would have a better case than they had to-day. (Hear. hear.) Those of them who were associated with the labour movement received statistics from time to time bearing on the labour question. He would read them a report from Pittsburg in the United States which Sir Howard Vincent had not read. This report stated that of the7s independent tin plate mills in the United States 45 were closed , down, and of the 251 mills under the control of the I American trust, 133 were closed down owing to the de- pressed condition of trade. The proportion of mills idle to those employed was larger than in Wales in the worst years. It was singular how unfortunate the in- dustries of the United States were at this moment. A receiver had been appointed in connection with an American company with a capital of three million I dollars, which attributed its difficulties to the recent revelations in connection with the United States Ship- building Trust. ("Oh, oh.") That was one of the great ; difficulties of Protection. It encouraged trusts and corners. (Cheers.) Mr. Howes proceeded to. give statistics relating to the wholesale discharge of men in many American manufacturing centres and stated that the wages of 32,000 cotton operatives were to be reduced eleven ner cent. and a further reduction ' was contemplated. It was estimated that 75,000 opera- tives in New England were to have their wages reduced. In the last report published by the "American World," only two months ago, the following statistics were given: Men idle by reason of improvemonts on rail- ways, 20,000; men idle by the shutting down of paper I mills, 15.000; miners idle by partial closing of copper I mines, 4,000; men idle in Pennsylvania, 2S,000; men I idle in Birmingham (United States) steel and iron I industry. 15,000: workers affected by ten per cent. wage reduction in New England textile mills, 65,000. So much for the prosperity of the fJnited States.(Hear,hear). He contended that there was no country in the world.' that had so low a percentage of unemployed in propor- tion to its population as we had in these isles. (Cheers). To-day we were the greatest traders in the world. To.' day we were the greatest shipbuilders in the world. To-day we were the greatest. carriers in the world. (Cheers.) Our trade was so great that we
THE YEIR 1888 TO 1874

r. Howes said what Sir,Hovrard Vincent omitted to say he would say. (Hear, hear.) During that period there ; existed a Liberal Government presided over by that great statesman Mr. Gladstone. (Cheers). In 1871 he. • (Mr. Howes) was president of a large labour organisa- tion and he knew that the highest rate of wages was paid in thatperiod. From 1803 to 1874 the 'prosperity of this country increased by leaps and bounds. (Hear, hear). Sir Howard Vincent SA d other influences were at work. The very party Sir Howard Vincent was associ- ated with did its level bast to drag us into the war that was going on during this period between Germany and France. (Hear, hear.) They opposed Gladstone because he did" not go to the assistance of what they called "our old allies in the Crimea." They held meetings and denounced the Liberal party. Mr. Gladstone wisely kept us at peacz and while Germany and France were fighting we were 'working. (CheerSa) There we estah- lished the truth of the old adage that "no nation ever fights itself rich ; all nations work themselves rich." (Loud cheers.) Was it not singular that Sir Howard Vincent should conclude his period of progress with the year 1871? Why did he conclude it at that date? The explanation was to be found in the fact that the Liberals were defeated in 1874 and the Tories came in (Loud laughter). From 1874 to 1880 things went from bad to worse under the Tory government. After describing the extreme poverty which existed during this period, when relief works had to be started, Mr. Howes addressed himself to THE QUEST lON OF E IGR XT lON alluded to by Sir Howard Vincent,in which Sir Howard stated that in the year 1893, 23:1,009 of our own flezh and blood :ead to leave England for a foreirmcountry where their labour would be protected for the livelihood they could not get in their own land, and at the Same time, 70,000 or 80,000 foreigners arrived in this country to fill our prisons." (Laughter). Where did these foreigners come from? They must have come from those pro- tected countries where the workers interests are pro- tected (Laughter). What foolish people, to flee from the golden land of protection and come to this wretched country of Free Trade (Loud laughter). It was a very silly thing for them to do to fill our prisons. It certainly did not show a very lofty ambition. Of course, Sinftoward Vincent could not p-ove such a thing as that. (Hear, hear.) • That was just a bit of platform rhetoric. (Laughter.) In the first place his figures were not right. Sir Howard Vincent certainly, did not gat them from the bluebook. In 1893 the num- ber of emigrants from this country was 203,003. Of this number 49,000 went to our own colonies. Surely Sir Howard Vincent knew that. Was he so unpatriotic that he already considered that our colonies had torn themselves from us, (Laughter.) Mr. Chamberlain suggested that if we did not adopt preferential tariffs they would do so. That was the result of IVlr.Chamber- lain being at the Foreign Office. (Laughter.) The Colonies were all right before he want there. (Hear, hear and laughter.) Well, in addition to the 49,000 who want to the Colonies,l49,ooo want to the United States and only 10,000 to other places of the world. Those were the correct figures in reference to the question of emigration. Proceeding to deal with Sir Howard Vin- cent's references to the trade of Warrington, Mr. Howes said it was the practice of protectionists to settle upon a town where there are one or two indds- tries suffering, and then play the suffering for all it is worth. Suppose it be true that a particular industry is suffering because of foreign competition. He (Ar. Howes) knew that

FREE TRADE HAD INJURED SOME INDUSTRIES. Any system of trade must iniure another to some extent. He remembered that at Congleton there was once a large fustian cutting industry for the making of coiduroy for the workers. The moment Free Trade was introduced, workingmen began to wear cloth and down] went fustian. (Laughter.) What fustian was now made went chiefly to protected countries where the workers still wore it. (Laughter and cheers.) The Protectionists never mentioned the num- ber of industries that Free Trade had creatsti. (Hear, hear.)There were a few manufacturers who would lik• to go to Parliament to get the legislature to protect them against the foreigner. It was very cowardly to go cringing to Parliament and pleading "Please protect me from the German and the Frenchman." (Laughter.) What they had to remember was this, that if one trade got Protection they would have a number of other trades demanding Protection. It must not be forgotten that if one man had one article to sell he had to be the purchaser of six. (Hear, hear.) If what he sold had to be protected then what he bought must also be pro- tected. If we could buy everything cheap and sell everything dear it would be glorious. (Laughter.) But we could not and it was no use crying for the moon because it would not come down. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Sir Howard Vincent said Warrington used to be noted for its many industries. The glass industry, he said. was once flourishing here. Then we had the iron and wire trades and others: In what condition, asked Sir Howard, did we find the great majority of these trades to-day'? Then, according to the report, he left it there. He asked the conundrum, but did not give the answer. Their opponents generally presented themselves as a kind of Christy Minstrel troupe. They were. like the corner men' always asking conundrums. (Laughter.) Sir Howard Vincent told them that

more than W 3 parted with. It u3ed not be c3niidered bad for a min to get mare than he parted with. (Laughter.) Wa got all these imports in return for our exports. We did not pay for the ts withimpormon ey ; there was not ,money enough in the wand to enable us to do so. If we purchased imports with money, all the coins in the country would only allow us to do our present rate of trade for about six months. We got an increased importation of goods and of bullion every year, because Free Trade had been so beneficial that it had enabled us to carry our goods to all parts of the world, despite their walls of tariffs, and we had ' planted British investmeats in every civilized country on the face of the earth. (Cheers.) I Into this country rolled the goods and the bullion which was the ir terest on the foreign invest- ments. As long as we could • have an increased importation of goods in return for what We setit out, it showed that we warn making a profit. Sir Flowarci Vincent talked about the balance of trade. Suppose there was a local shopkeeper balancing trale,it would mean that he bought as mach as he sold, and received as much as he expended. The result would be that he would soon put up the shutters. We did not want to balance trade. We wanted the scale to go bump down on one side, If we sent £l,OOO worth of goods abroad and got in return £1,500 worth, we ought not to grumble. Let the other chap grumble at the other end. (Laughter.) Mr. Chamberlain said ,we were buying more than we ware selling, and that by doing so we were going to ruin. Fancy a man who had ever been in business talking like that! It all depended on how we bought and sold. Sir Howard Vincent said "he would undertake. to say on • behalf of Mr. Piernoint, and the member for St. Helens, indeed on behalf of the entire Unionist party, that if their opponents could suggest a remedy for the existing state of things, which all men of all parties admitted to be deplorable, it would be most carefully and earnestly considered by the Govern- ment." There was no other man in the universe who could speak on behalf of the entire Unionist party. (Laughter.) Mr. Chamberlain could not, and Mr. Balfour could not. (Laughter.) But Sir Howard Vincent said ha could. (Laughter.) Then again,it was strange that when the present Government had had the management of affaiis for eight years, Sir Howard Vincent should admit that the existing state of things Was deplorable. He was a brave man who would speak ,on behalf of the Government. (Laughter.) There were not many who would do so. Tory candidates at bye-elections dare not. (Cheers). If they, could propose a remedy, Sir Howard Vincent promised them on behalf of the Unionist party that their suggestions would be con- sidered. "So here goes" said Mr. Howes. "The first proposition I have to make is

TFIE DESTRUCTION Oir THE PRESENT GOVERNMENT. (Cheers). Let them earnestly consider that. That is a remedy. They admit themselves that this condition of deplorable poverty exists now, and they have had the management for eight years. Therefore it is a safe thing to say that the one advantage you get from a Tory Government is that you touch the bottom. Any Government that comes after this must do ,better, because they can't do worse." (Laughter.) Continuing, Mr. Howes said they had many more suggestions to make. nave people talkedabout dumping. They talked about the wicked foreigner sending us steel and iron. They also spoke of the depressed condition of the iron trade, when they knew or ought to know that the cause was not dumping, but

THE QUESTION OF ROYALTIES. (Cheers.) Sir Howard ought to know that we could not make a ton of steel in this country until we first paid the landlord Os. 6d; for allowing us to make it. (Cheers). He ought to know that this was the only country in the world where the land-owner claimed the minerals under the surface of the earth. He did so because a landlord Parliament gave him the privilege before the people had votes, when his party had supreme control of the legislative machinery, before there was anything like organized Liberalism in the country. These men when they claimed the minerals in the bowels of the earth, handicapped our industries and lived like leeches on the vitals of the nation. After they had thus taxed our industries till we felt the burden, the protectionists said" You have submitted to it so long. Please sub- mit to another tax." At a time when Liberals wanted to call the attention of the people to the great necessity of home refornt, they cried "Look abroad. It is the wicked foreigner !" Liberals said "Nothing of the sort. It is the bad English land laws and the greed of certain landlords. Look abroad, and you will discover some day that while yonare looking abroad your pocket is picked at home." (Cheers). Sir Howard Vincent asked them to consider the policy' put forward by the statesman under whom they were all proud to serve. Whom did he mean ?—Josephrhamberlain. The present Government were not proud to serve under Joseph Chamberlain. They had repudiated him. They were bound to repudiate him. ':WHO STOOD WITH CHAMBERLAIN NOW? Why, even CSamberlain had fled to Egypt. (Laughter.) The other Joseph went to Egypt. (Laughter.) The other Joseph had a coat of many colours. (Laughter.) Sir Howard Vincent talked as if Mr. Chamberlain and the Government were synonymous. They knew very well that the Government dare not accept Mr. Chamber- lain's proposals. He believed Mr. Balfour would be ready to dp so if the people had foolishly accepted the suggestions made from Birmingham. Mr. Balfour said "I will not tax raw material." Mr. Chamberlain said "You must tax tha people's food." Mr. Balfour forgot that food was the raw material for the produc- tion of human beings. No food for the boys and girls, no men and women. No men and women, no Empire. That ought to frighten them. (Laughter.) When Mr. Cavre-Jerlain snake at the Guildhall to the bankers and millionaires he said: "I want the nation to think imperially." That was very good for a man with a heavy purse and a full cupboard. (Hear, hear.) Ho knew lots of people who thought very locally, because all their thought wart taken up with the problem of how to get the next meal. There were net many imperial aspirations for the dwellers in the slums. We could all THINK IMPERIALLY if we could eat imperially. That was the problem. (Cheers.) Sir Howard Vincent said one of the most painful features of the debate in the House of Commons was the way in which their opponents sneered at the action of Canada in giving a preferential tariff to British goods. Who did they think it was that sneered at the action of Canada? Not the opnonents at all, but Mr. Chamberlain. Addressing the Colonial premiers, he told them that "in spite of the preference which Canada has given us- their tariff has Dressed and still presses with the greatest , severity upon its best customers, and has favoured the foreigner. - • • • While I cannot but gratefully acknowledge the intention of your proposal and its sentimental value, vet its substantial results have been altogether disappointing to us." Howdid we treat our colonies? We gave them open ports and allowed them to send -us what they liked and how they liked. They Was equally wicked did not return the compliment, but built up a wall of tariffs against us. Mr. Chamberlain said ii t ‘vas wofietkheedfoerfeeigunreeretloentaiaxl fourriends goods.te dlefese. Al:uding too, t w SOUTH AFRICA

Sir Howard Vincent said "we fought for South Africa. Our sons bled and died there. It cost us millions of money. Was it fair therefore that our exports to South Africa should not have a substantial preference?" He (Mr. Howes) should say that our British workers ought to have a preference also. (Cheers.) If Sir Howard believed in preference for British goods and workers, why did he vote for slavery out there? (Cheers.) Sir Howard tried to prove that after all, it was not slavery. (A voice: It is not slavery). One of the questions asked of the Secretary of State for the Colonies in Parliament last week by Mr. C. wagon, Wig if, while the system of indentured Chinese labour was in force in the Transvaal, measures would be taken to prevent the introduction of free Chinese labour. The answer was " Measures are already in force in the Peace Preservation Ordinance by which the introduction of free Chinese labour can be restricted by withholding per- mits." The Government. therefore, would not allow free Chinese labour. (Cheers.) If it was not free Chinese labour, what would they like him to call it? (Cries of " Slavery.%) Th 3 conditions under which the labourers were to be imported told him that there was to be an individual known as an importer, that the importer was to bring in these Chinese labourers, and that when they arrived they were to be imprisoned in the compounds. ("Shame.") They were to have no right to leave the compounds without the permission of the employer or importer. If he gave permission it must be on a written permit, stating the number of the labourer. (Cries of" Shame "and cheers.) They were to be TICKETED AND NUMBERED LIKE CONVICTS. If the employer gave a permit, it must not allow the man to be absent more than 4S hours. If the Chinese workman indulged in any other labour, he was liable to be sent to prison for three months. If any man induced him to leave the compounds that man wouldalso be liable, to three months. But that was not the worst. The employer when he liked could sell a man for a money payment, hand him over to another employer, and when the man had been handed over he was bound to the second. employer under the same conditions that were signed for the first. If .that was not slavery, there was no other name to know it by. The English people were not to be deceived. (A Voice: `.` What about the Non- conformist telegram ?") Whenever they mentioned this question. Tories .always wanted to know about some- thing else. (Cheers.) The question was sufficiently grave to be discussed on its own merits. (Hear, hear.) This was

WHAT OUR BRAVE LADS DIED FOR. (Cheers). When their opponents sal I they had got a programme, he would be in favour of banishing every- thing but that, and fighting the next election on the question. (Cheers). They could meet the so-called tariff reformers on every point. They knew what the people in this country suffered when Protection was the order of the day, when food was dear and wages were low, when there were no trade nnions,when a man on leaving his employ- ment received a ticket with a corner torn off and no employment could be given to him withina radius of per- haps 100 miles from the spot he had just left. A con- stable would track the man until be had stepped over the border, and then arrest him as a vagrant. In the old Protection days—so late as 1830—six labourers were transported for asking for an increase of wages. They were receiving 6s. a week and they met and asked for Bs. They agreed before they went that if the

employer would. not give them Bs. they would leave him. The meeting was a conspiracy under the old Tory Conspiracy Laws. Telling t'neemployor that they would leave if he did not grant an advance, was threatening under the old laws. Conseqtfbntly the men went to penal servitude. In those ditys all the rich interests were protected. Only the poor man was left unprotected. Wages were small because the area of trade was narrow WHEN THE LIBERAL PARTY CAME AND TORE AWAY

• PROTECTION trade began to spread itself out. (Cheers). I\l4 Chamberlain now raised the cry again and said "You must tax the people's food." If they taxed the people's food, they taxed the poorest people in the country and the smallest incomes in the country. They struck at the children of the country, and when the Government struck his child, he was going to strike the Government back. (Loud and prolonged cheers). The CfIA.IRNIA.N then put the resolution to the meet- ing and it WAS carried with enthusiasm, only two persons voting against it.

div.head: COULD NOT AFFORD TO GO IN FOR PROTECTION.
div.p: COULD NOT AFFORD TO GO IN FOR PROTECTION.

Our workers worked fewer hours than the workers in any other country, andwhile working fewer hours they got a higher ware than the workers of any other coun- try in the world, save those in the United States (Cheers). The United States oufht to be far more Prosperous than they were. They had opportunities for the development of wealth that we knew nothing of. They comprised a great self-containing continent. Everything the human family required could be pro- duced in the United States—coal. iron, silver. copper, brass, tin, grain. oil, cotton, cereals and fruits in abund- ance. and millions of acres of virgin soil not yet touched. (Hear,hear.) The United States had a sparse population in pronortion to the acreage and they \VP rag free from the feudal obligations which still existed in this country and ham- nered and impeded our industries. (Loud cheers.) If it were possible to freeze up the great waters around that continent and shut them off from the rest of the world, the American people would 'revel in luxury. They would be able to produce all they wanted and more than they could consume, hut if it were possible to freeze up the waters around these little islands, we should commence to starve in less than six months. (Applause.) We were bound to LAY THE WHOLE WORLD UNDER CONTRTRETIOV for our sustenance and Free Trade had enabled us to do it. We had tapped all the world and made it contribute not. only to our necessities but to our luxuries. Bananas, oranges, grapes. apples, and the fruits of the sunny climes were brought to our door, grain enriched our granaries from all partgof the world,and if there was a scarcity in one corner of the earth, in the Providence of God there was abunlance elsewhere, and our norts being wide open it flowed in and enabled our people to be better fed. (Cheers.) Not only were webetter fed, but we were better clothed and better housed than any other people. and he who would shut a single port was a traitor to his country. (Loud cheers.) Referring to Sir Howard Vincent's statement that the greatest pro- ress of this country was between

div.head: FALL IN EXPORTS
div.p: THE FALL IN EXPORTS

_ during the ten years from 1891 to 1900, as compared with the previous ten years, was 137 millions. Accord- ing to the Blue Book, these figures were all wrong. He (Mr. Howes) found that from 1881 to 1890 the total exports to all destinations amounted to 2,314 millions, while from 1891 to 1900 the figures were 2,379 millions—an increase of 35 millions according to the Government return. (Cheers.) They could not. however, gather from the speech whether Sir Howard Vincent meant that the decrease was in the trades he had previously referred to, or whether, having asked the conundrum about them, he proposed to leave the rintter there. What about the glass industry? He (the speaker) did not know what the condition of the glass trade was in Warrington, but he did know what its con- dition was in the country. In the Government Blue Book they gave periods of six years for them to com- pare. Our export of glass in 1897 amounted to £870,000; in 1898 it was £885,000; 1899, £917,000; 1900, £l,034.000; 1901, .21,057,000 ; and 1902, £1,093,000. (Cheers.) The iron trade had been gloriously increas- ing everywhere. Of course, as their member said, that brought them to the

div.head: QUESTION OF DUMPING.
div.p: QUESTION OF DUMPING.

Dumping was a ,word which their opponents used when they were hard up for argument. It was like the blessed word Mesopotamia. (Laughter.) It was sup- posed to cover a multitude of sins. (Laughter.) The wicked foreigner kept dumping goods on our shores. The wicked foreigner did it because we wanted the goods. There was no law in England to compel us to take anything the foreigner sent us, if we did not want it. The remedy was entirely in our own hands. We took the goods because we knew it was to our advan- tage to do so. "Where the customers are, there will the goods be also," added Mr. Howes, "so the goods keep coming." (Hear, hear.) If their opponents said "Yes, but look how cheaply they have dumped them" he would say "I wish they had, dumped them free of cost. Cheapness doesn't trouble me much." (Laughter). They knew that in al- most all their industries—in the wire industry—they depended upon dumping, and they used the dumped material to stimulate the industries of this very dis- trict. (Applause). Mr. James Cox. the workmen's secretary of the Manufactured Iron and Steel Trade Board of Conciliation for the North of England, deliv- ered a speech to the Staffordshire ironworkers a short time ago. He said ;" they would be told it was an awful shame that there should have been• so muzlh foreign material dumped down into the English market at a very low price. He for one welcomed the fact. He was glad that during the last two or three years we had been able to buy at a cheap rate. By reason of depression, German manufacturers had been compelled to sell at ridiculously low prices. rhat simply meant that many industries which depended upon materials sent here, would not have been able to go on, if they had not come." With reference to

div.head: WIRE TRADE
div.p: THE WIRE TRADE

the exports in 1898 amounted to £772,000. In 1902 they were £1,042,000. There were two Chamberlains in the field—Joseph and Arthur (cheers.) Arthur had some- thing to do with wire nails, and this was what he said: "Onbehalf of my own company and on behalf of any manufacturer who is fit to be in the business, I altogether repudiate the suggestion that we need protective tariffs, or would benefit by them. My company has always done a good business in the better qualities of wire nails, both for home and export, and that business we are increasing year by year. It is a fact that we have not been able to com- pete in the commoner lines, but I no more attribute it to unfair competition on the part of till foreigner,than I attribute their inability to compete with us in other lines to unfair competition on one part. I have in- variably found the explanation of the foreigner's suc- cess to lie in some natural advantage." Mr. Chamber- lain went on to contend that Protection would "re- ward dullards for th.ir dulness." They knew, continued Mr. Howes, how well

div.head: PHILOSOPHY OF TARIFFS
div.p: THE PHILOSOPHY OF TARIFFS

would prove in a moment or two the fallacy of the Protectionist agitation. When they nut on a tariff they increased theprice of the article. When they increased the price of an article they pulled down the purchasing Power of.the buyer. When they pulled down the purchas- ing power of the buyer, they narrowed the area of trade and threw paonle out of work. On the other hand, if they took off a tariff, they cheapened the article. increased the purchasing power of the buyer, widened the area of trade And brought people into work. That was thephilosophy of the whole thing. (Cheers.) A tariff was never the worker's gain. Whoever else might prosper, tie worker could not. They should remember that all the people who were out of work had to he kept by the people who were in work. Whether those out of work were peers or tramps, it mattered not.. (Laughter.) It cost them more to keep a peer than it did to keep a tramp—(loud laughter)—but if they were not associated with the industries of the country, they must be sunported by those who were. From the induitries of the country came all the wealth the country produced. Sir Howard Vincent said there was a yearly average excess of imports over exnorts to the tune of 145 millions. Surely we ought not to grumble at that. Yet they knew it was one of the fallacies that Protectionists tried to create in the public mind. True, our imports did exceed our exports. What did it mean ?—that we were getting

div.head: COUNCILLOR MAGINN SPEAKS OUT.
div.p: COUNCILLOR MAGINN SPEAKS OUT.

- . Councillor MA.Grxx, in proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. Crosfiald and Mr. Howes, said he was sure that after the speeches, they had heard, they were all agreed that to alter the Free Trade policy of this country would mean ruin to the working-classes and the downfall of the British EMpire. The United Kingdom was the hub of the Empire. (Hear; hear.) If we went down he was afraid that the spokes of the wheel—the Colonies would be of little use. (Hear. hear.) The Tories at their meeting told them. that their sole interest was to better the workingman and on the same platform they said they wanted to:import the Chinese labourer into South Africa in order to reduce the wages of the work- ingman. The government bad spent 200 millions sterl- ing and lost some 25,000 of our best soldiers in order that they might import Chinese labourers, whilst at the same time making it practically impossible for English workingmen to get there. Under the South African Emigration Act of 1803 it was stipulated that English emigrants must land with at least £2O in their pockets. The lowest fare to South Africa was 15 or 17 guineas., and were not these conditions preventing our unem- ployed from going there? (Hear, hear.) The country's first duty was to its own citizens before they gave free p islages to these yellow slaves—Mr. Joe Chamberlain' yellow; cousins. (Laughter.) History proved that wherever, the yellow man went he became a curse. America in its foolishness imported the yellow man, but they had stopped doing so, and they would give millions to get rid of those they had got. (Hear, hear.) Yet we were told by these self-styled friends of the working- people that they would improve our wages by raising the cost of food, and at the same time they would make fortunes—the poor millionaires—by importing Chinese slaves and keeping English workmen out of the country altogether. What did they think of the men who told theft that a tariff on corn would not increase the cost of food? The speaker at the Parr Hall meeting quoted the authority of Mr. Chamberlain. (Laughter.) Four Tears agd ihey had the authority of Mr. Joseph Chamberlain that he was only playing at bluff. (Rear, hear.) They had also his authority that the Boers would not fight. (Laughter.) Mr. Chamber- lain's bluff cost £200,000,000 and-if he (Mr. Magian) re- membered rightly the Boers dida little fighting. (Loud laughter.) They had the same mighty authority that South Africa would be aFi open market and that it would pay off every penny of the war debt. We had got none yet and he was afraid never would. (Hear. hear.) The same great authority told them that the war was over three years ago,and as soon as the Govern- ment got into power it was found that the warliad only practically commenced: So much for juggling Joe. (Laughter.), Mr. Magma proceeded to prove from his own experience of foreign countries that tariffs instead of increasing wages kept them down. By altering the Free Trade policy of .the country for Protection they would not only be bringing misery on the present generation but upon future'generattons. He urged them not to throw away lightly the ,privileges their fore- fathers wan for them. (Lend applause.)

div.head: "OUR ARTHUR."
div.p: "OUR ARTHUR."

Mr. NATEIA.N CiOIC seconded the vote of thanks. He was sure, he said, that everyone was delighted with the eloquence of Mr.. Howes. The popularity of Mr. Arthur Crosfleld was steadily increasing and he had already heard him spoken of as "Our Arthur." (Hear. hear, and laughter.) -That spoke well for Mr. Crosfleld's success at thenext general election. (Hear, hear). Mr. Cook proceeded to refer to the unfulfilled promises of Mr. Chamberlain when he visited Warrington. " Free education" and" three acres and a cow" were promised, but those promises were still unfulfilled. Mr. Cook expressed the hope that every Trades Unionist in War- rington would see to it that they did not submit meekly to a tax on food—(hear, hear,)—but that they would do their best to defeat Mr. Chamberlain's retrograde proposals. The vote was carried with acclamation. ALDERMAN PIERPOINT WELCOMES MR. LONG. Alderman PIERPOINT in .proposing a vote of thanks to the Chairman, said it was a matter of great gratifica- tion to him, as he was sure it was to the audience, to welcome Mr. Long, after so long an absence from the Liberal party of Warrington—an absence which had been far too long in his opinion. (Hear, hear.) The re- union was one of the happiest things that had taken place in his political recollection. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Long left the Liberal party from conscientious convic- tions and he (Mr. Pierpoint) did not blame him at the time because he liked a man to be honest in his opinions and to. fight for them. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Long believed that he was justly entitled to his opinions at that tirae and there were other leading members of the Liberal party in Warrington who left them at that time. He (Alderman Pierpeint) only hoped that the return o, Mr. Long to the Liberal party would herald the return of others. (Hear, hear.) No one could say that the Liberal party was a party disorganised. (Hear, hear.) The; were determined to go forward to the great fight that was before them with renewed energy, assured of the success which was awaiting their effort. (Applause). Councillor JAMES.EVANS briefly seconded the vote of thanks, which was unanimously carried.

div.head: MR. LONG AND HIS POSITION.
div.p: MR. LONG AND HIS POSITION.

In acknowledging the compliment, Mr. LONG said it was with a certain amount of pain that he came into the room because he could not forget the past. (Hear, hear.) He did not think he would have left the privacy of his home for the sake of taking up party politics if he had not been convinced that the present occasion was as important to him—more important in fact— than that which took him away from the Liberal party. (Hear, hear.) Well, there he was, and he was quite open to do what he could to support Mr. Gros- field. In saying that, he wished to remark that he res- pected the present member for the Borough. He knew that Mr. Pierpoi4 had the interests of Warrington at heart. (Hear, hear). He (Mr. Long) would like to see a scion of the Crosfield stock returned. (Loud applause.) Sir John Brunner, whom he (31r. Long) looked upon as one of the most sincere and liberal"- minded men, anxious for the good of his country and anxious to do all he could for the working-cluses, had written him a letter in which he stated that he looked forward very much to having Mr. Crosfield amongst them in the House of Commons. Sir John further remarked that when that was the case he would see that Mr. Crosfield bbeved the Whips just as he (Sir John) had had to do. (Applause.) The meeting then terminated. A report of the Liberal meeting in the National Schools on Thursday evening will be found on page 7.
LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.

Authors of letters intended for publication must in all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith. Matter intended for publication must be written on one side only of the paper and sent in, if possible,not later than Thursday.

The " Observer" and the Sermonettes. Sir,—Whena bad boy gets punished for his sins you can measure the suffering he endures by the row he kicks up about it. I never knew My " Sermonettes " appear in any town for many weeks without the Tories making a desperate attempt to kick me out,and a similar attempt is being made now in Warrington. My attention has been called to an article in the "Warrington Observer" of March sth, criticising my statements on the Fiscal Policy. I have no doubt that article was inspired by the gang of young men who tried to tackle me when I was lecturing near Warring- ton, recently, for the Knutsford Division. The writer says I described Joseph "as an accom- plished liar and a gay deceiver." The Tory scribe who can say that about me, can say anything. If he knows anything at all he knows it is not true. Then he goes on to rave and talk for a column of space but he takes good care to steer clear of the points 'he has got to answer. When he has answered any one of the points at issue deal with him as he deserves. He has got to pr)ve 1. That "for the last twenty pr thirty years our export trade has been practically stagnant" though itlhas increased £83,000,000, or over forty per cent. 2. That •" our exports of manufactured goods have actually declined" during the same period, though they have increased by £42,§00,000. 3. That "Protectionist countries have taken much less from us during the last thirty years than they took before," though they had increased by £20,646,000 in the year 1900. 4. That" Protectionist countries shut us out of their markets" though we sold them £62,200,000 worth of our goods in 1902. I do not know whether you have got a Lunatio Asylum in Warrington or not, but the Tory who tries to prove these propositions ought to be sent there in hot haste. Such a rabid dangerous creature ought not to be running loose. Lock him up by all means and look after him. At present lam spending a month in lecturing for the Yorkshire Liberal Federation in York, Hull, Rich- mond, Think, Mahon, &c., but I will keep an eye to the wandering lunatics who are making white into black, and lies into gospel truttis.—Yours truly, JOHN TAYLOR. [ln a further letter to us Mr. Taylor says his engage- ments will prevent him entering into a lengthy cor- respondence.—ED. " Ex."]

Ebenezer Church, Buttermarket-street. The anniversary services in connection with the above church were held on Sunday. The preacher should have been Mr. Morris Jones, of Liverpool, but that gentle- man was taken suddenly ill. The morning service was taken by Councillor Thornton, who delivered an interesting address, on the words, "Blessed is the man who walketh not in the counsels of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in ithe seat of the scornful," Psalm 1,1.—1 n the afternoon, the choir gave an excellent rendering of the cantata, " Judah's Captivity and Restoration." Councillor Forshr pre- sided and read the connective passages. The soloists, who all acquitted themselves credit- ably, were Misses K. Bowyer, E. Littlewood (sopranos), E. Lee (contralto), Messrs.T. Hughes, R.W Cook (tenors) and C. J. Sheath (bass). Mr. F. Wright of Padgate, preached at the evening service, and based an earnest address on "For the Son of Man is come to seek and save that which was lost," Luke xix, 10. The anthem "The Lord is Loving" was creditably rendered' by the choir. Mr.' W. Jowett presided at the organ with his customary ability.—On Monday evening, the usual tea and entertainment were held. A goo 4 tea was provided by the ladies, after whic`` Councillor Thornton presided and gave a brief address. The programme was a long and varied one and was thoroughly enjoyed. Miss E. Lee sang "The Children's home,". in a pleasing manner. The violin solos by Miss Thornton were well received and she had to respond to a recall. Mr. C. J. Sheath gave a good rendering of "The Diver." The voice of Miss E. Littlewood was heard to perfection in" The Kerry dance," and "Scenes that are brightest," and in response to an enthusiastic encore for the latter, she further scored in "On the banks of Allan Water." Recitations were well rendered by Mr. Walmsley, "How to nail 'em " ; Miss M. E. Hughes, "Your duty"; Mr. J. Sheath, "The burial of Moses"; Master 11. Wakefield, "Begin at once"; and Miss G. Hughes, "Returned from the war." A dialogue entitled "The Outcast," was admirably taken part in by Miss E. Littlewood, Messrs. F. Merlin, P. Bate, and T. Hughes. Mr. Jowett discharged the duties of accompanist. The singing of the Doxology brought a pleasant meeting to a close.

div.head: PROGRESSIVE ASSURANCE COMPANY.
div.p: A PROGRESSIVE ASSURANCE COMPANY.
Remarkable Year's Work.

Year by year the business of the Prudential Assurance Company, Ltd., increases by leaps and bounds, and the summary of the report presented at the fifty-fifth annurl meeting, which appears in our advertising columns, is another record of remarkable pro- gress. The company was started in 1818, and the number of its policies is now nearly 160,009,000, with an income which exceeds £10,000,000, and invested funds of over £50,000,000. Upwards of 1,403 clerks—inCludinl 332 ladies—are employed in the head Offiee alone. besides 165 more in the district offices in all the more important towns throughout the king- dom. It is interesting to be told that the weather has proved the friend of the company dnring the past year. The mortality in both branches was exceptionally favourable, and confirmed the opinion the company have always held that a wet year means a low rate of mortality. As showing the wide extent, of the com.panyis business we may quote the follow- ing from the spAch of the Chairman at the annual meeting;—lnorder to show that if an accident involving loss of life does oecnr anywhere in the British Isles we are sure to be in it, I may mention that the explo- sion at Woolwich Arsenal last June occasioned the loss of sixteen lives, and we had in consequence to pay ten claims: also when four coastguardsmen were drowned from a boating disaster maths Lincolnshire coast, three of the in were found to be assured with us. A local instance of thecompany's generosity has come to light. A short time ago a. man was killed by falling' from a ladchr in Wilderspool road, and it was found that the widow held a long-lapsed policy on his life. Although she had no actual claim on the Company, she was awarded .25. Mr. .T. T. Rowlands, Sankey street. is the enegetic superintendent of the Warrington District.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

STOCKTON HEATH GARDEN SOCIETY.—On Tuesday evening in the Church Room a paper was read by Mr. Ryan on "Roses." There was a very good attendance of members, the gathering being above the average. Mr. W. H. Woodcock was in the chair. IVlr.Ryan dealt with his subject in a very lucid and practical way andhaving a rose tree with him demonstrated how it should be planted and primed with the view of obtaining the best productive result in roses. After the demonstration, a discussion took place on rose culture in general, the following gentlemen among others taking part in the discussion:—the Chairman, Messrs. J. Warburton, W. Skelton, Moore. Vernon, and Plinston. PASSIVE RESISTERS.—We learn that the Rev. H. Dunnico, the Pastor of Golborne-street Chapel and who resides at Fairfield-road, Stockton Heath, and the Rev. J. S. Hughes, the Pastor of Hill Cliffe Chapel, and who resides at Cliffe View, Stockton Heath, have declined to pay the Edwation Rate, a 3 a protest we presume against the use of public money, for what they consider to be sectarian and dogmatic teaching in Stockton Heath school and other schools in the Cheshire district. As the rev, gentlemen will have to appear shortly before the Daresbury Bench the legal proceedings should be interesting.

Candid ates must be not more than 14 years ;of age on August Ist. 1904. 180 SCHOLARSHIPS for boys and girls desirous of be- coming pupil teachers, and who are in attendance at any school.—Elementary or otherwise; and who will not be more I ban 15 or less than 12 vesrs of age on August Ist, 1904. COUNTY BOROUGH OF W A KAI N UTON.— EDUCATION COMMITTEE. ADMISSION EXAMINATION FOR PUPIL TgiII.CHERS. The Board of Education will hold an EXAMINA PION on SATURDAY. MAY 14Th, 1904, to enable candidates to qualify for engagements as pupil teachers. The examination is open for boys and girls who will be sixteen years of age on or before Augnst Ist, 1904. Pupil teachers are paid, Boys £25 in the first year and £3O in the second, and Girls £l5 and £2O respectively. ADMISSION EXAMINATION FOR PREPAitATORY PUPIL TEACHERS. The Board of Education will hold an examination on Sat- urday, May 14th, 1904, to enable eandldades to qualify for engagements as Preparatory Pupil Teachers. The examina- tion is open to boys and girls who will be fifteen years of age on or before August let, 1904. 'V h, successful candi- dates will attend the Pnparatory Pupil Teachers' Classes for one year. They' will not be required to pay fees nor for their books, and will receive a scholarship of £5. Both examinations are open to Boys and Girls from Private Secondary, or Elementary schools. There are several vacancies in the schools in the Borough, and intending candidates can obtain on or before Friday April Bth. the syllabus of assimilation and further informa- tion from the undersigned. J. MOORS MURRAY, M.Sc. Secretary and Director of Education.
